# Front Binding of the Manuscript

->[The exterior cover of the volume]<-

The manuscript is bound in dark, aged leather that shows signs of significant wear. The decoration is executed through **blind-tooling** <term>blind-tooling: a technique where decorative patterns are impressed into the leather using heated metal tools, leaving a recessed design without the application of gold leaf or ink</term>.

The decorative layout includes:

*   **Central Panels:** An arrangement of interlocking diamond shapes or "lozenges" occupying the middle of the cover.
*   **Border Work:** An intricate **interlace pattern** <note>interlace: a style of decoration common in medieval and early modern manuscripts featuring ribbons or lines that loop, braid, and knot together</note> that frames the central geometric designs.
*   **Geometric Design:** A strictly symmetrical composition that suggests the volume was bound with a high degree of professional craftsmanship.

# Of the Holy Dionysius

As we recount the many radiant miracles of these blessed men, we have striven to record them in these final sacred scrolls as a tribute to Christ, for the glory of the martyrs, and as a memorial. We do this so that we might not—by looking down upon them or being negligent, or by yielding to our ancient, watchful, and envious enemy <note>The "ancient enemy" is a common epithet for the Devil.</note>—keep silent. For if we were silent, as some say, and let their writings be consumed by a scorching flame, we would lose the benefit of their grace.

**W**ith our thoughts awakened by this same grace, and proceeding from even these few written accounts, the things understood and spoken here have the power to be great.

**W**e believe without hesitation that they endured many other struggles for the sake of Christ, because even until now, the divine power deigns to manifest such wonders through them that all those who dwell there or happen to pass by are filled with wonder.

**T**he blessed martyrs of Christ—Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—suffered their martyrdom on the seventh day before the Calends of October <note>original: "ἑβδόμῃ καλανδῶν ὀκτωβρίου" — Traditionally, the feast of St. Denis is celebrated on October 9th. In the Roman calendar, the 7th day before the Calends of October would be September 25th; this discrepancy may reflect a local variant or a scribal error in the Greek tradition.</note> under the Emperor Domitian, in the regions of Gaul and the city of Paris.

->While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns,<-
->together with the Father and the Holy<-
->Spirit, now and ever<-
->and unto the ages<-
->of ages.<-
->Amen.<-

<insert>STAMP: NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME</insert>

## Martyrdom <unclear>of the saints</unclear>

And she, with every effort and toil as much as she was able, with all prayer and great desire, having built a church over the blessed <term>bodies</term><note>The OCR shows "σωματ̅", an abbreviation for "somata" (bodies). In hagiography, the physical remains of saints were considered conduits of divine power.</note> of the holy martyrs, and in the holy glory of the Holy Trinity, worthily laid down the holy bodies, three in number, with fragrant spices. This was done with the help of God the Almighty, whose goodness shines forth daily through miracles and signs. What word, then, or what tongue of the faithful could suffice to recount these <term>miraculous powers</term><note>original: "δυνάμεις" (dynameis) — often translated as "powers," but in this context, it specifically refers to miracles.</note>, 
<margin>15</margin> since people cannot even comprehend their own affairs with human reasoning? For they grant health to the sick, the ability to walk to the lame, light to the blind, and hearing to the deaf. They give speech to the mute, and by driving out the unclean <term>spirits</term><note>original: "πν̅ατα" (pneumata) — another sacred abbreviation.</note> that beset their bodies, 
<margin>20</margin> they ceaselessly provide healings. And we, drawn by good prayer and blessed obedience—especially we who are most unworthy—believe that we are helped toward salvation by their prayers; or rather, being in awe as unworthy men, we yet attempt to present their worth to you. For we have not been called by our own ways or by our own foreknowledge, but an ancient narrative has brought these things to you. In part, from a firm and ancient source, we have set down in writing a few things as we were able, which we have heard from long ago. 
<margin>30</margin> We have not acted on our own accord regarding this explanation, as has been said, but have written as we learned the accounts from the great teachers, fearing God and with the care of love...

### Of Saint Dio<unclear>nysius</unclear>...

O praiseworthy <term>theft</term><note>original: "κλεψισύνη" (klepsisynē) — This refers to a "pious theft," a common motif in lives of saints where relics are taken secretly to protect them from desecration by pagans or to ensure they receive a proper Christian burial.</note> which brought about no loss, but rather a profitable gain! Just as it is the custom for those who toil upon the land to wait for their beasts of burden to carry in the harvest, so too is that land of the blessed martyrs filled with a gift and guided by grace, so that the believing farmers may reap a hundredfold fruit. Thus, they are deemed worthy of <term>salvation</term><note>original: "σωτηρίας" (sōtērias).</note> and leave behind a great treasure of <term>holiness</term><note>original: "ἁγιωσύνης" (hagiōsynēs)</note> for those who come after them.

**T**he aforementioned most honorable woman, not forgetting the sanctification of the martyrs—as the fury of the tyrants had already subsided—sought with all diligence for the suitable place that ought to guard the <term>bones</term><note>original: "ὀστᾶ" (osta).</note> of the holy martyrs. And having found a great <term>vaulted building</term><note>original: "τροῦλον" (troulon), referring here to a tomb or a domed structure.</note>, she sealed it. We believe this most wonderful and <term>noble matron</term><note>original: "μητροφαμίλιον" (mētrophamilion) — a term indicating a woman of high social standing or a respected mother of a household.</note> was not without merit, being likened to the very reverence of these holy martyrs; for indeed, the <term>Redeemer</term><note>original: "λυτρωτής" (lytrōtēs) — a title for Christ.</note> of all deigned that she too should come to faith in His own name. Never of its own accord did her heart bring forth such a plan; rather, because of this, we believe without any contradiction that she guarded the bones of the blessed martyrs through a godly purpose, as she became worthy of them and advanced in the truth of the faith through their intercessions.

**A**nd the multitude of the Christians, being like a city through the teaching of the blessed martyrs, turned—

# Martyrdom

But God the almighty, good, just, and merciful, who never overlooks His mercy toward the <term>human</term><note>original: "ἀνθρωπίνου" (anthrōpinou)</note> <gloss>human</gloss><note>original: "ἀν̅νου," a scribal contraction for "anthrōpou" (of man/human).</note> race; who submerged the counsel of Pharaoh in the Red Sea and cut off the neck of Ahithophel with a hanging rope <note>Ahithophel was a biblical counselor who betrayed King David and ultimately took his own life; here, he represents the failure of evil plots.</note>; He Himself also cast down the unstable counsel of these men by His mercy, so that the two brilliant lights <note>Likely referring to the two companions of St. Denis, Rusticus and Eleutherius, whose bodies were also recovered.</note> should not be hidden by the depth of the waves. For the Church of Christ always possesses powerful warriors.

**A**mong these things, an honorable woman named Catulla, who was still being held by pagan fears, turned then to the faith of Christ through the miracles of the martyrs and gave herself over to holy desire. Both in her mind and in her deeds, she showed the power of her longing; and being moved by the mercy of God, as a power from above came upon her, she received a sign. And indeed, she entreated the persecutors to come to a banquet; and when she had presented many gifts to them, she subtly removed the memory of their evil intent against the martyrs. To the faithful, however, she revealed the secrets of her heart and commanded that they should secretly steal the honorable bodies of the martyrs. They were to hide them in a certain part of the city, in the rocky ground that lay like a small field prepared for sowing, burying them there in place of a future [harvest]. Those who were commanded fulfilled these orders and quickly carried out what had been enjoined upon them.

<meta>This page provides the historical and spiritual context for Saint Dionysius’s life. While the previous page described his arrival in Rome and his commissioning by Pope Clement, this section steps back in time to establish the "apostolic succession"—linking the authority of the Church from the Ascension of Christ, through the conversion of the Apostle Paul, to the eventual conversion of Dionysius himself in Athens.</meta>

### [Life] of the Holy Dionysius

<margin>1.</margin>
**T**his authority, in its fullness, has been left behind as an inheritance for those perfect and worthy men who followed in the churches. Having briefly recounted these matters according to the sequence of that time and the history of the apostolic church, let us now turn our account to the struggles of the blessed **Dionysius** <term>Dionysios</term>; so that, as has been stated, we may go through a few details concerning him according to the chronological order.

<margin>2.</margin>
**A**fter the most glorious **Ascension** <term>analēpsis</term> <note>The departure of Jesus Christ from Earth into Heaven, traditionally celebrated forty days after the Resurrection.</note> of our Lord and God Jesus Christ; when the blessed Apostle **Paul** <term>Paulos</term>, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, turned from the error of unbelief to the way of salvation; so that the faith which he formerly fought against, he might now preach in its glorious fullness in these latter days; and that, according to the Lord’s decree, he might become a **chosen vessel** <note>original: "σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς" — a reference to Acts 9:15, where God describes Paul as His chosen instrument.</note> among the nations.

<margin>3.</margin>
**F**or when he who preaches the name of our Lord Jesus Christ came to the ignorant nations in **Athens** <term>Athēnais</term>, he also guided and converted to the way of salvation this holy man Dionysius, who was previously immersed in **pagan customs** <note>original: "ἐθνικοῖς ἔθεσι" — referring to the polytheistic traditions of ancient Greece before his conversion to Christianity.</note>. Having reborn him through holy baptism, he strengthened him further in divine holiness. Then indeed, when he cut away the thorns and briars of error from the depths of his heart through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he produced fruit and a new sprout, as if in good soil, watered by the divine word and the spiritual contemplation that comes from it...

# Martyrdom

Having reached the most exalted imperial Rome of the Romans for the sake of the same preaching, he <note>Referring here to the Apostle Peter.</note> was entrusted from heaven to preach there as well. So that, as the **leader** <term>koryphaios</term> <note>original: "κορυφαῖος" — a title frequently given to Peter in Eastern tradition, meaning the head or "peak" of the apostolic group.</note> of the holy apostles, having become first in the order of the apostolate, he might also be first in the **struggles** <note>original: "ἀγῶσι" — This term refers to the "contests" or trials of faith, particularly martyrdom, often compared to athletic competitions in early Christian writing.</note> in Rome, becoming a sharer in the sufferings of Christ. For indeed, the city, being gripped by great errors, needed to be corrected by greater means. So that where the wound was heaviest, there also the grace might be great. <note>A thematic echo of the Epistle to the Romans 5:20: "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."</note>

Then, as has been said, the tyrant and impious **Nero** <term>Nerōn</term>, thinking to subject both land and sea to his own tyranny; raging with the fury of his own cruelty and the recklessness of madness, he was inflamed against the servants of Christ. And in the fourteenth year of his tyrannical reign <note>Approximately 68 AD, the final year of Nero's rule.</note> he condemned the blessed **Peter** and **Paul** to an unjust death by the shedding of their blessed blood; and through the victory of martyrdom, he worthily—though unwillingly—sent them forward into the Kingdom of Heaven. 

However, before the blessed Peter was deemed worthy of the life in the Kingdom of Heaven through the victory of martyrdom, he entrusted the authority of the Church to the blessed **Clement** <term>Klēmenti</term>, <note>Traditionally regarded as the third or fourth Pope/Bishop of Rome, and a key figure in the establishment of apostolic succession.</note> saying: "Just as the authority **to loose and to bind** <note>original: "λῦσαι καὶ δῆσαι" — A reference to the 'Power of the Keys' granted by Jesus to Peter in the Gospel of Matthew 16:19.</note> was granted to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I also eternally grant and give this same authority to you; so that whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven."

<summary>This page describes the Apostle Peter's mission to Rome and the subsequent martyrdom of both Peter and Paul under the Emperor Nero. It concludes with Peter formally bestowing his spiritual authority and the "power of the keys" upon his successor, Clement.</summary>
<keywords>Apostle Peter, Apostle Paul, Emperor Nero, Saint Clement, Rome, Martyrdom, Apostolic Succession, Power of the Keys, Persecution</keywords>

Beholding the extraordinary beauty of divine concepts as they appear through the mirror of their names. <note>This poetic opening suggests that the names given to holy people reflect their inner spiritual reality.</note>

**E**usebius of Pamphilus <note>original: "Eusebios ho Pamphilou"; the 4th-century "Father of Church History"</note> also mentions this. Some claim that Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a 1st-century Jewish philosopher</note> said these things regarding the common Jews. Others say he meant the Essenes <note>a Jewish sect known for asceticism and communal living</note> or Ebionites; others, the Nazarene Jews. Still others believe he spoke of the "believers from the circumcision" <note>Jewish converts to Christianity</note> who believed in Christ yet continued to keep the Law of Moses in a symbolic <term>typikōs</term> <note>meaning they observed the law as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christian truths</note> manner. Others say he refers to the "perfect" Christians. Regardless of which sect they belonged to, because they lived a monastic life, they were fittingly called "Therapeutae" <note>original: "Therapeutai"; meaning "Healers" or "Worshipers/Attendants of God"</note>. It was not only Eusebius of Pamphilus and Philo the Jew who noted this; the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite—the disciple of the holy Apostle Paul who became the Bishop of Athens—also stated in his work *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* that in ancient times, monks were also called "Therapeutae."

# Philo on those of the circumcision in Egypt who believed, both Christians and monks, from his discourse titled:
# On the Contemplative Life; or,
# On Suppliants.

<margin>T</margin>his race of people <note>original: "genos"; referring here to the group known as the Therapeutae</note> is indeed found in many parts of the inhabited world, for it was necessary that both the Greek and the non-Greek worlds should share in a perfect good. However, they abound in Egypt in each of the so-called nomes <note>administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>, and especially around Alexandria. From all over, the best of them are sent as if to a fatherland, a colony of <term>Therapeutae</term> <note>original: "Therapeutōn"; meaning "Healers" or "Worshippers," a group of Jewish ascetics described by Philo</note>, to a most suitable place. This location is situated above Lake Mareotis, lying upon a somewhat low hill, very well-positioned for the sake of safety and the mildness of the air.

### By the same author from the same discourse.

<margin>I</margin>n each house, there is a sacred room which is called a <term>semneion</term> <note>a sanctuary or place of holy retreat</note> or a <term>monastērion</term> <note>original: "monastērion"; this is one of the earliest uses of the word that would become "monastery," originally meaning a place of solitary devotion</note>. In these rooms, they live in seclusion and are initiated into the mysteries of the holy life. They bring nothing into these rooms—neither drink, nor food, nor anything else necessary for the needs of the body—but only the laws and the oracles declared through the prophets, and hymns, and the other things by which knowledge and piety are increased and perfected.

### Letters.

I am persuaded to perceive that these things are judged justly; as for those who wrong you and think they can hem in the sun of the Gospel, unjustly accusing it, I pray that they may be released from these things. I see that instead of the good, they turn upon themselves, yet you draw them toward yourselves to partake of the light. Nor, on the contrary, will He deprive us of the all-shining ray of **John**; for now we delight in the memory and the renewal of your true <term>theology</term> <note>original: "theologias"; in the early church, this often referred specifically to the study of the divinity of Christ or the inspired words of the Evangelist.</note>. A little later—for I see it, even if it is a bold thing to say—we shall be united with you. ...to those guided by goodness; for this reason, the divine and intelligible words are compared to dew and water, and to milk, <margin>D</margin> and to wine and honey. This is because of their life-generating power as found in water, and their power for growth as found in milk; their reviving power as in wine; and their cleansing and simultaneously preserving power as in honey. For just as among us, in the lesser sense, drunkenness is an immoderate over-filling and a displacement of the mind and wits, so in the <margin>I</margin> better sense regarding God, one must not think of "drunkenness" as anything other than the super-full immeasurability of all good things pre-existing in Him as their cause. 

Furthermore, regarding the **ecstasy** <term>ecstasy</term><note>original: "ekstasis." Literally meaning "to stand outside oneself." For humans, it is a loss of reason; for God, it is His absolute transcendence beyond all categories of being.</note> that follows this drunkenness, one must describe it as the transcendence of God which is beyond all understanding. <margin>X</margin> In this state, He is removed from the act of thinking by being above thought itself, and above being thought of, and even above being itself. Simply put, God is both **drunk** and **ecstatic** with all good things at once, as He is the cause of all of them at once...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of symbolic theology found in Pseudo-Dionysius's ninth letter. ### Dionysius

He is the cause of all things, and proceeds to all things, and comes to be in all things, and contains all things. And yet, He is again the <margin>Ξ</margin> same in the same state according to His transcendence; He is nothing in anything according to any mode. Instead, He is set apart from the whole. Being in Himself identically and eternally, both standing and remaining, always in the same way and in like manner. And in no way does He come to be outside of Himself, nor is He departing from His own seat and immovable station and **hearth** <term>hearth</term><note>original: "hestia." A term referring to the center of the home, used here to describe God's stable, central essence from which He never departs.</note>. But <margin>Δ</margin> even while remaining within it, He performs His complete and total providences, doing good and proceeding to all things, yet remaining within Himself. He is always standing and moving, and yet neither standing nor moving. Rather, as one might say, He possesses His providential activities within His permanence, <margin>Ο</margin> and His permanence within His **Providence** <term>Providence</term><note>original: "pronoia." The benevolent care and guidance God exercises over all creation.</note>, having them both naturally and supernaturally at once.

<margin>Α</margin> But what is the **solid food** <term>solid food</term><note>original: "sterea trophē." A reference to Hebrews 5:12-14, distinguishing between "milk" for spiritual infants and "solid food" for the mature.</note> and what is the liquid food? For Good Wisdom is praised for granting both of these while simultaneously providing care. <margin>Η</margin> I believe that the solid food brings symbols of intellectual and permanent perfection and identity, according to which divine things are participated in through a stable, powerful, <margin>Ξ</margin> unified, and indivisible knowledge by those intellectual senses. It is from this truly solid food that the most divine <margin>Ο</margin> **Paul** <note>The author writes in the persona of a disciple of the Apostle Paul, referencing the biblical distinction between spiritual food and milk.</note>, having received it from Wisdom, shares with others.

<margin>Τ</margin> The liquid food refers to the influence that is both diffusive and eager to proceed to all things. It leads those being appropriately fed by it from various, many, and divided things toward the simple and calm **knowledge of God** <term>knowledge of God</term><note>original: "theognōsia." This refers to a mystical or contemplative understanding of the Divine that transcends mere factual information.</note>...

<margin>K</margin> Indeed, the impassive <term>impassive</term><note>original: "apathes." # Dionysius

...most holy things. These are revealed only to those who are genuine lovers of holiness, who cast aside all **childish imagination** <note>original: "paidariode phantasian." Dionysius warns against taking religious symbols literally or "childishly" (e.g., imagining God has physical hands), urging a more mature, spiritual interpretation.</note> regarding the sacred symbols. Such seekers are capable of crossing over, with a simplicity of mind and the power of contemplation, toward the divine—moving toward the simple, supernatural, and transcendent truth that lies beyond the symbols.

Furthermore, one must understand this: the tradition of the <term>theologians</term><note>original: "theologon." In the early Church, "theologians" usually referred to the writers of the Bible (the Apostles and Prophets) rather than modern academic scholars.</note> is twofold. One part is **secret and mystical**, while the other is **manifest and more well-known**. One part is **symbolic and initiatory**, while the other is **philosophical and demonstrative**. 

The "unspoken" <note>original: "arrheton." That which cannot or should not be expressed in common words.</note> is interwoven with what is "spoken." The spoken part (philosophy) persuades and binds together the truth of what is said, while the unspoken part acts and establishes the soul in God through <term>untaught initiations</term><note>original: "adidaktos mystagogia." A form of spiritual guidance or "mystagogy" that comes directly from a divine experience rather than formal classroom instruction.</note>. 

Indeed, neither in the rites of the most holy mysteries <note>The "mysteries" here refer to the Sacraments, such as Baptism and the Eucharist.</note> did the leaders of our tradition, or those of the legal tradition <note>Dionysius refers to the "legal" (Old Testament) tradition of the Jewish priests, contrasting it with the "our" (New Testament) tradition.</note>, abstain from symbols befitting of God. We see even the most holy angels mysteriously bringing forth divine things through riddles. We see **Jesus** himself speaking of God in parables and handing down the <term>divine mysteries</term><note>original: "theourga mysteria." Literally "God-working" or "wonder-working" rituals that convey divine life to the participant.</note> through the symbolic setting of a table <note>This refers to the Last Supper and the institution of the Eucharist.</note>.

**F**or it was fitting—not only so that the "Holy of Holies" <note>The innermost, most sacred part of the Temple, used here as a metaphor for the highest truths of God.</note> might be preserved undefiled from the common crowd, but also because human life itself is both undivided and divided. 

<margin>M</margin> Therefore, it is appropriate to human nature that divine enlightenments be granted in a way that suits it <note>Dionysius argues that because humans are a mix of spirit (undivided) and body (divided), God uses both spiritual truth and material symbols to teach us.</note>.

# Epistles, Volume 4
y iiii

...by spreading out **chariots and thrones**, and arranging certain **all-consuming feasts** <note>original: "holophoikas." This likely refers to the "sumptuous" or "all-burning" sacrificial banquets described in the Old Testament, where God is depicted as a guest or host.</note>, and depicting those who drink first, those who are drunk, those who sleep, and those suffering from hangovers.

The act of describing the formless God using physical shapes or human characteristics.</note> which appear as veils for hidden things. 

These symbols are multiplied and divided to represent the **unified and undivided**; they are symbolic and multiform to represent the **formless and un-typable**. If one were able to see the beauty hidden within them, they would find that all these things are mystical, god-like, and filled with a great abundance of **theological light**.

<margin>Note</margin> For let us not imagine that the outward appearances of these symbols were fashioned for their own sake. Rather, they have been set forward as a shield for a knowledge that is **unutterable and invisible** to the many, so that these most holy things might not be easily handled by the profane...

## Of Dionysius

<margin>T</margin>herefore, let those who have been appointed by God to rule over others distribute what is appropriate to themselves and to those under them. But let Demophilus assign what is appropriate to **reason**, to **anger**, and to **desire** <note>Dionysius employs the Platonic concept of the "tripartite soul," consisting of Reason (logos), Spirit/Anger (thymos), and Appetite/Desire (epithymia). In this system, virtue is achieved when Reason governs the other two</note>, and let him not wrong his own rank <term>taxis: an order or position within a hierarchy</term>; rather, let the underlying **reason** rule over the lower faculties.

<margin>F</margin>or if we saw in the marketplace a servant reviling his master, or a younger man reviling an elder—or even a son reviling his father—and attacking him and striking him, we would think ourselves to be acting impiously if we did not run to help the superiors; and this is so even if those superiors had perhaps previously done wrong themselves. How then shall we not be ashamed to look on while **reason** is wronged by **anger** and **desire**, and is cast out from the authority given to it by God? How can we stir up an impious and unjust disorder <term>ataxia: the opposite of order (taxis); a state of confusion or rebellion</term>, a rebellion and a lack of harmony within ourselves?

Rightly does our blessed Lawgiver <note>Original: "nomothetes." Dionysius refers here to St. Paul, specifically referencing 1 Timothy 3:5: "For if a man see not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?"</note> from God judge that one is not worthy to preside over the Church of God who has not already presided well over his own house. For he who has ordered himself will also order another; and he who orders another will order a house; and he who orders a house, a city; and he who orders a city, a nation. To speak simply, as the oracles <note>original: "ta logia"—Dionysius’s standard term for the Holy Scriptures</note> say: "He who is faithful in a little is also faithful in much; and he who is unfaithful in a little is also unfaithful in much." <note>A quotation of Luke 16:10</note>

<margin>Y</margin>ou yourself, then, must assign what is appropriate to **desire**, **anger**, and **reason**. And to you <note>Demophilus, as a monk/therapeutes</note>, the divine ministers <term>leitourgoi: here referring to the deacons, the rank immediately above the monks</term> shall assign what is appropriate; and to these, the priests; and to the priests, the hierarchs <term>hierarchai: the bishops, the highest rank of the clergy</term>; and to the hierar—... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page</note>

<unclear>H</unclear>aving proximity to the Divinity. He thinks that God is ignorant of what he himself is conscious of within his own soul, and he imagines he can deceive the one he falsely calls "Father." He even dares to utter his abominable blasphemies. 

For even if I were to say that he recites the prayers over the divine symbols <note>The "divine symbols" refer to the bread and wine of the Eucharist. In Dionysian thought, these are not just signs but participants in the divine reality.</note> in a seemly manner, such a man is not a priest. He is not; rather, he is a hostile, deceitful mocker of himself, a **wolf** against the divine people, armed in a sheepskin <note>This is a direct reference to Matthew 7:15, "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."</note>.

But it is not lawful for **Demophilus** to correct these things. For if Theology <note>original: "theologia." In this context, Dionysius often uses this word to refer to the Holy Scriptures or the divine word itself, rather than the modern academic discipline.</note> rightly commands us to pursue what is just—and it is just to pursue it when one wishes to assign to each person what is according to their worth <term>axia: merit or fitness for a specific rank</term>—then this must be pursued by all, and not in a way that goes against one's own worth or rank <term>taxis: the fixed order of the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies</term>. 

For it is just that even the **angels** are assigned what is according to their worth and are set apart. However, it is not for us to do this, O Demophilus. Rather, divine things come to us from God through the angels, and to the angels through those who are pre-eminent among them. To put it simply: among all things that exist, what is according to merit is assigned by the first to the second by the well-ordered and most just **Providence** <term>pronoia: God's purposeful and sustaining care for the universe</term> of all things.

<summary>Dionysius argues that a priest who lacks internal illumination is not a true priest, but a wolf in sheep's clothing; however, he insists that it is not the place of a monk like Demophilus to correct them, as this violates the divinely established hierarchy.</summary>
<keywords>ecclesiastical hierarchy, priesthood, Demophilus, justice, divine order, Providence, illumination, Eucharist</keywords>

# Dionysius

"He who sacrifices an ox to me is as one who slaughters a dog" <note>A quotation from Isaiah 66:3, where God rejects the rituals of those who are inwardly wicked.</note>. The perfect justice of God does not tolerate the sight of what is contrary to the Law. And even when they say, "In your name we have performed many miracles," He answers, "I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of lawlessness" <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:22-23.</note>.

**As** is right, and as the sacred scriptures say, one should not pursue even what is just in an unworthy manner. Each person must attend to himself and not contemplate things that are too high or too deep for him, but should reflect only on those things which have been commanded to him according to his rank <note>Dionysius refers to the "rank" (axia) or worth of an individual within the Church's structure. In his view, attempting to perform a task assigned to a higher rank is a form of spiritual pride.</note>.

**What** then do you say? Should priests who act impiously, or who are caught in other absurdities, not be called to account? Shall it be permitted only to those who boast in the Law to dishonor God by breaking the Law? And how are the priests revealers <term>revealers: original Greek "ekphantores," those who bring the divine light into view for others</term> of God? For how can they proclaim the divine virtues to the people when they have not known their power? Or how will those who are in darkness provide light? And how will they distribute the divine Spirit when they do not even believe, through faith in the truth, that there is a Holy Spirit?

But I shall answer these things for you—for you, Demophilus, are not an enemy, and I will not allow you to be taken advantage of by **Satan**. For indeed, every rank in the divine arrangement is more "god-like" the closer it is to God; and those things closer to the true Light are simultaneously more luminous and more capable of illuminating others <note>This is a core principle of the "Celestial Hierarchy": the higher ranks receive the light of God directly and then pass it down to the lower ranks.</note>.

**And** do not take this bitterly, but according to the divine—

<summary>Dionysius argues that ritual acts by the lawless are rejected by God and asserts that while a corrupt priest is a contradiction in terms, it is still not the place of a subordinate to overstep their rank to correct them. He explains that the hierarchy is designed so that those closer to the "True Light" illuminate those below them.</summary>

# Epistles XI <note>original: "Ἐπιστολαί ΙΑ" — Although the heading indicates the eleventh letter, the content continues Letter 8 from the previous page.</note>

...battles that lead to the ruin of those who listen. If a local governor <term>local governor: original Greek "ethnarchia," a subordinate ruler over a specific region</term> undertook a task not commanded of him by the king, he would be justly punished. And if a lowly subordinate dared to cross-examine a magistrate who was either acquitting or condemning someone—and I am not even speaking yet of insulting him or attempting to cast him out of office—it would be seen as a grave offense.

<margin>B</margin>ut you, O man, are so bold as to act against the ordinances of the Gentle and Good One <note>Referring to God</note> and His hierarchical legislation <term>hierarchical legislation: the "thesmothesia," or the divinely established order and laws governing the ranks and duties within the Church</term>. You have attempted these things even though they are unbefitting and beyond your rank; yet you seemed to think you were acting appropriately. However, this is not permitted to anyone. What was so "absurd" in what Uzziah did when he burned incense to God? <note>King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for performing a priestly duty—burning incense—that was not permitted to a king (2 Chronicles 26).</note> Or what of Saul when he offered sacrifice? <note>King Saul lost his kingdom because he offered a burnt offering himself instead of waiting for the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 13).</note> Or the tyrannical demons when they spoke the truth about Jesus’s divinity? <note>Referring to instances in the Gospels where demons recognize Jesus, but are silenced because they have no rightful place in the ministry.</note> On the contrary, everyone who acts as a "foreign bishop" <note>original: "allotrios episkopos," meaning someone who interferes in or takes over duties that do not belong to their specific rank or office.</note> is barred from the sacred proclamation, and each person shall remain in the order of his own liturgy <term>liturgy: "leitourgeia," the specific sacred service or official duty assigned to one's rank</term>. Only the High Priest shall enter the Holy of Holies, and only once a year, and even then only in the full purity required by the Law. The priests are to veil the holy things, and the Levites must not touch the holy things, lest they die.

<margin>A</margin>nd the Lord’s anger was kindled by the audacity of Uzziah. And Miriam was struck with leprosy when she attempted to lay down laws for the Lawgiver <note>Miriam, Moses' sister, was punished for challenging Moses’s unique authority (Numbers 12).</note>. And the demons leaped upon the sons of Sceva <note>The sons of a Jewish priest who tried to exorcise spirits using Jesus' name without having the authority or faith to do so (Acts 19).</note>. And He said, "I did not send them," yet they ran; and "I did not speak to them," yet they prophesied. And even the impious man...

<summary>Dionysius warns the monk Demophilus that unauthorized interference in the duties of higher church ranks is a sin, citing biblical figures like Uzziah and Miriam who were punished for overstepping their bounds.</summary>

...they teach by their actions what it means to be a servant <term>servant: original Greek "therapōn," which Dionysius uses here specifically to refer to the rank of monks</term> of the worthy. Or do the sacred symbols themselves not cry this out? 
<margin>2</margin> For it is not simply the case that the "Holy of Holies" <note>The most sacred part of the sanctuary, usually partitioned by a veil or screen</note> is open to everyone. Rather, the order of the initiators <term>initiators: "hierotelestai," referring to the bishops who lead the sacred rites</term> approaches them most closely; then comes the arrangement of the priests; 
<margin>3</margin> and following these, the rank of the ministers <note>original: "leitourgōn," referring to the deacons</note>. To those who are appointed as servants <note>the monks</note>, the gates of the inner sanctuaries are not permitted to be crossed. It is within these gates that the rites are performed and where the higher ranks stand—not merely to guard the place, 
<margin>3</margin> but to maintain order and to ensure that the people recognize their own station by seeing the servants standing closer to the priestly ranks. From this, the holy order <term>holy order: "taxiarchia," the structured arrangement of the hierarchy</term> of sacred things ordains that the servants participate in divine things through the mediation of others, namely those ranks more internal than themselves, to whom the distribution of the holy gifts has been entrusted. 

For those who stand symbolically around the divine altar always see and hear divine things, which are revealed clearly to them. They then proceed, in a manner reflecting the Good, toward those outside the divine veils <note>The curtains or screens that separated the altar from the rest of the church</note>—to the subordinate servants and the holy people. There, they reveal the sacred things according to what each rank is worthy to receive, keeping them beautifully undefiled, until the moment when you, jumping upon them tyrannically, forced the "Holy of Holies" to be paraded before you against its will. You claimed to possess and protect the light of these sacred things.

<margin>K</margin> But such a thing you have neither seen nor heard, nor do you possess any of the qualities belonging to the priests; just as you have not even known the truth of the Oracles <note>original: "logiōn," referring to the Holy Scriptures</note>, even though you recite them every day...

<summary>Dionysius explains the strict hierarchical structure of the Church, where only bishops and priests may enter the sanctuary, while monks (servants) must remain outside the gates to receive the mysteries through mediation. He rebukes Demophilus for "tyrannically" breaking into the sanctuary, an act that violates this divinely established order.</summary>

# Letters

...good, and he lays down his own life for those who have fled to him <note>A reference to the "Good Shepherd" imagery from the Gospel of John, contrasting Christ’s mercy with Demophilus’s harshness</note>.

<margin>Σ</margin> But you—as your own letter makes clear—when a man whom you call ungodly and a sinner fell down before the priest, I do not know how you, having lost your temper to your own detriment, kicked him away. 

<margin>Ε</margin> Then, that man begged and confessed that he had come seeking a cure for his evils. 

<margin>Σ</margin> But you did not tremble; instead, you insolently insulted the good priest, claiming he was to be rebuked for showing mercy to a penitent and for justifying the ungodly <note>original: "ton asebē dikaiōsanta." You disturbed the <term>Holy of Holies: "hagia tōn hagiōn," referring here to the most sacred objects or the area around the altar</term>, and you wrote to us saying: "The sacred things were about to be defiled, so I providently rescued them and keep them undefiled." 

Now then, hear our response: it is not permitted for a priest to be corrected by the <term>ministers: "leitourgōn," refers to the rank of deacons</term> who are beneath you, nor by the <term>servants: "therapeu-tōn," the rank of monks</term> who are of the same rank as you. This holds true even if the priest seems to act irreverently toward divine things or is caught doing something else that is forbidden. For if disorder and <term>confusion: "ataxia," literally a lack of order or a breaking of the ranks</term> represent a departure from the most divine boundaries and laws, it makes no sense to overturn the God-given <term>order: "taxis," the structured arrangement of the universe and church</term> on behalf of God. 

For God is not divided against himself; for how then shall his kingdom stand? And if judgment belongs to God, as the <term>Scriptures: "logia," literally "the oracles"</term> say, and the priests are messengers <note>original: "angeloi"</note> and interpreters of divine judgments ranking after the <term>hierarchs: "hierarchas," the bishops or highest rank of leaders</term>, then the divine will should come to you from them in the proper way, through the mediation of the ministers, whenever the occasion— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing on the next leaf</note>

# Dionysius

Let us be <term>led by the light: "phōtagōgēthōmen," a term for spiritual illumination or guidance into the divine mysteries</term> toward His divine acts of goodness. Is it not a sign of an unspeakable goodness—one that is beyond all understanding—that He makes things exist in the first place, that He brought all things into being, and that He desires all things to always become like Him and to share in His gifts according to the <term>capacity: "epitēdeiotēta," the individual fitness or readiness of a soul to receive grace</term> of each? And what of the fact that He holds an affectionate longing even for those who depart from Him? He strives and even begs not to be rejected by those He loves <note>This bold imagery suggests that God is the one "striving" to win back the human soul, reversing the typical roles of seeker and sought</note>. Even when they are broken and accusing Him, He bears it and even defends Himself, promising all the more to heal them. Even when they are far away, He approaches them; He runs toward those who are coming back and meets them; He embraces them entirely with affection <note>original: "pothikōs," meaning with longing or passionate love</note>. He does not complain about what happened before, but loves what is present; He holds a feast and calls together His friends—that is, the good angels—so that everyone may rejoice. 

But Demophilus, if anyone else does, hates what is good; he is justly rebuked, and he must be taught what is beautiful so that he might be made good.

<margin>C</margin> For, as the text says, should not the Good One rejoice in the salvation of those who were lost and in the life of those who were dead? <note>A direct allusion to the Parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:32</note>

<margin>D</margin> He cares for and carries on His shoulders that which barely returns from its wandering, and He rouses the good angels to joy. He is kind even to the ungrateful, and He makes His sun rise upon the wicked and... <note>The text breaks off here, quoting the Gospel of Matthew 5:45 regarding God's universal providence</note>

<summary>Dionysius rebukes Demophilus by illustrating God's proactive mercy, using imagery of the Good Shepherd and the Prodigal Son to show that God seeks out sinners rather than shunning them. He argues that divine goodness is characterized by a "longing" for the return of the lost, contrasting this with Demophilus's judgmental anger.</summary>

# LETTER 8
<note>The original heading "Letter 4" reflects a specific manuscript numbering; however, this text is traditionally known as Letter 8 in the Dionysian corpus.</note>

Every lover of good works must realize this. Why should we listen to the <term>ancestor of God: "theopatōr," a title for David because Christ was born of his lineage</term> David, who was so beloved by God? It is because he was good, and even toward his enemies he was found to be good. The one who is <term>Super-good and the Lover of Good: "hyperagathos kai philagathos," referring to the transcendent and proactive nature of God's goodness</term> said of him: "I have found a man after my own heart." 

Indeed, even a good law was given to provide for the pack animals of one’s enemy. Job was also justified because he held fast to <term>innocence: "akakia," literally "lack of malice" or "guilelessness"</term>. Joseph did not take revenge on the brothers who plotted against him. And Abel followed along simply and without suspicion with the brother who would eventually kill him. 

<term>Theology: "theologia," here referring to the Holy Scriptures</term> proclaims that all good people are those who do not plan evil things and do not resort to them; they are not even changed from their own good nature by the wickedness of others. On the contrary, in a God-like way, they treat even the bad with goodness. They extend their great goodness over them and, with <term>gentleness: "epieikeia," meaning fairness, moderation, or kindness</term>, call them back to become like themselves. 

But let us strike a higher chord and return to the <term>Cause: "aition," meaning God as the source of all things</term>. We are not just recounting the gentleness of good men, nor the goodness of the philanthropic angels who pity the nations and <term>watch over them: "hyperechomenōn," suggesting protection or standing over for their benefit</term> with good intent. These angels rebuke the destructive and evil-working multitudes; they are grieved by evils, but they rejoice in the salvation of those who are called back to good things—along with everything else <term>Theology</term> teaches us about the <margin>A</margin> good-working angels. 

Rather, receiving in silence the good-working rays of the truly Good and <term>Super-good: "hyperagathou," meaning beyond all categories of human goodness</term> Christ, let us be led toward...
<note>original: "pros" (towards). This is the catchword for the following page.</note>

<summary>Dionysius uses the examples of David, Job, Joseph, and Abel to argue that a truly godly person shows goodness even to enemies. He asserts that even angels and God Himself act with proactive mercy rather than vengeful judgment.</summary>

## To Demophilus the Minister concerning attending to one's own work
## and concerning piety and kindness.

<margin>4</margin> O noble Demophilus, the histories of the Hebrews declare that even the holy Moses was deemed worthy of the <term>appearance of God: "theophania," a direct manifestation of God to a human</term> because of his great <term>meekness: "praotēs," a combination of gentleness, humility, and strength</term>. And if they ever record him being excluded from the <margin>1</margin> divine vision, they do not attribute this to a loss of his meekness; rather, they say that the Lord was moved to anger when Moses was acting too presumptuously and resisting the divine counsels. <note>original: "ἐπαυθαδιαζομένῳ καὶ ἀντιτείνοντι," likely referring to Moses' hesitation at the burning bush or the incident at the waters of Meribah.</note>

However, when the scriptures proclaim him for his God-chosen honors, he is heralded because of his pre-eminent <term>imitation of God: "theomimēsia," the act of mirroring God's character, particularly His goodness</term>. For he was indeed exceedingly meek, and for this reason, he is called the <term>servant of God: "therapōn theou," a title of high honor implying a close, personal attendant</term> and was considered more worthy of the vision of God than all other prophets. 

Furthermore, when certain men <note>Referencing Korah, Dathan, and Abiram from Numbers 16.</note> were contending with him and Aaron for the <term>high priesthood: "archierōsynē"</term> and the <term>leadership of the nation: "ethnarchia"</term>, he remained above all personal ambition and lust for power. He yielded the leadership of the people to the one chosen by God. But when they stood against him, reproaching him for past events and making threats—even to the point of nearly attacking him—this meek man called out to the Good One for salvation. With great <term>fairness: "epieikeia," a quality of being reasonable, moderate, and just</term>, he spoke with confidence, asserting that he was innocent of any wrongs against those under his rule. 

For he knew that it is necessary for one who communes with the Good God to be molded, as far as possible, into the closest likeness of Him. And to himself...

<sig>iii *</sig>

<summary>Dionysius holds up Moses as the supreme example of meekness, explaining that his worthiness to see God came from his "imitation of God." He contrasts Moses' gentle refusal to seek power for himself with the rebellious ambition of Korah.</summary>

### Page 160

...at <term>Heliopolis: the "City of the Sun" in Egypt</term>, being present together and standing in company, we saw the moon unexpectedly encroaching upon the sun. For it was not the <term>time of conjunction: "synodos," the natural point in the lunar cycle when an eclipse is possible</term>. Furthermore, from the ninth hour until evening, we saw the moon unnaturally returned to the point opposite the sun's diameter.

<margin>A</margin> Remind him <note>Referring to Apollophanes, a pagan philosopher and friend of Dionysius.</note> of something else as well. For he knows that we saw the <term>encroachment: "emptōsis," the start of the eclipse</term> itself beginning from the east and proceeding to the edge of the sun; then it retreated, and again, the encroachment and the <term>clearing: "anakatharsis," the end of the eclipse</term> did not happen from the same side, but from the diametrically opposite side. Such were the supernatural events of that time, possible only for Christ, the cause of all things, who does great and marvelous things without number.

<margin>T</margin> If it is lawful and possible for you, refute Apollophanes with these facts. Address me as one who was present with you then, who saw it with you, and who examined everything with you. Indeed, I do not know where Apollophanes began his prognostications <note>original: "μαντείας," meaning his attempts to explain the event through pagan divination or astrology</note> then, but to me, as he compared the events as they were happening, he said: "O noble Dionysius, these are the exchanges of divine matters." Let this much be said by us by way of a letter. You are capable of filling in what is missing and leading this man—who is wise in many things—fully to God; perhaps he will not disdain to learn gently the most wise truth of our <term>religion: "thrēskeia," here referring to the Christian faith</term>.

**Vocabulary:** City of the Sun, Moon, Time of Conjunction, Encroachment, Clearing, Apollophanes, Dionysius, Religion.

<meta>This page continues Letter VII to Polycarp. ### Dionysius

...determined by the completely immovable state of the universe, and as the measure of a whole day, all the signs of the zodiac stood still in the same place, or even longer than that. For if the whole of the higher and encompassing spheres were moving in such a way, the encompassed things would not have been carried along with them. And when another day was nearly tripled in length—even in twenty-four hours—either the whole universe retreated in its course for that amount of time and turned back with such supernatural reversals, or the sun, in its own course, contracted its <term>five-fold motion: a reference to the complex planetary paths or the "climates" of the sun's path</term> into ten hours, and then retraced its path again in another ten hours along a new track. This indeed rightfully amazed the Babylonians <note>According to 2 Kings 20, the Babylonian king sent envoys to Hezekiah to inquire about the miracle of the shadow retreating</note>, and without a fight, it subjected them to Hezekiah as if to a god-like and superior man.

<margin>K</margin> And I do not speak only of the great works performed in Egypt, or other divine signs that occurred elsewhere, but those common and heavenly events proclaimed throughout the whole universe to everyone. Apollophanes, however, insists that these things are not true. Yet, these very things are recorded in the priestly accounts of the Persians, and even now the <term>Magi: Zoroastrian priests and scholars of the stars</term> perform the memorial rites of the <term>Triple Mithras: a title for the Persian sun-god Mithras, here interpreted by Dionysius as a pagan memory of the "triple-length" day</term>. But let him be allowed to disbelieve these things because of his ignorance or his lack of experience.

<margin>B</margin> Ask him then: what do you say about the eclipse that happened at the time of the Savior’s cross? For both of us were then...

## Letters

...and the <gloss>39</gloss>path thereafter, as it is necessary to speak of it.
<margin>S</margin> You <gloss>40</gloss>say that the <gloss>41</gloss>sophist <gloss>43</gloss>Apollophanes <gloss>42</gloss>insults me and <gloss>44</gloss>calls me a "patricide" <note>Greek: "patraloian," meaning one who strikes or kills his father; here it refers to Dionysius being a "traitor" to his Greek intellectual heritage</note>, on the grounds that I am unholily using the things of the Greeks <gloss>45</gloss>against the Greeks. Of Dionysius

You ask; and you will do so if you follow my advice: you will refrain from speaking against others, but you will speak as you ought on behalf of the truth, so that what you say might be entirely unrefutable.

# To Polycarp, a <term>Hierarch</term> <note>original: "hierarchē," a high-ranking religious leader or "sacred ruler"</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **I** do not know if it is enough for good men to simply speak against the <term>Greeks</term> <note>original: "Hellēnas"; here referring to those following pagan philosophy or religion</note> or others, thinking that this alone is sufficient. In my view, it is better if the truth itself can be known and spoken as it truly is. For once the truth is correctly demonstrated according to the law of truth and stands pure and firm, everything that is otherwise—even if it pretends to be the truth—will be exposed as being different from that which truly exists. It will be seen as something dissimilar, appearing to be the truth rather than actually being it.

<margin>P</margin> **I**t is therefore unnecessary for the revealer of truth to battle against this group or that. For everyone claims to possess the <term>royal coin</term> <note>a common metaphor for authentic, divinely-sanctioned truth or "orthodoxy"</note>, even if they perhaps only hold a deceptive image of some small part of the truth. If you refute one person, another—and then yet another—will argue about the same thing. But if the true account of truth itself is correctly established and remains unrefuted before all others, then anything that is not in total agreement with it is overthrown of its own accord by the unbeatable stability of the truly real truth.

<margin>T</margin> **H**aving well understood this, I think, I have not been eager to speak against Greeks or others; but may God grant me this: to know, first, enough about the truth...

<summary>Dionysius advises Polycarp that the most effective way to address error is to present the truth clearly rather than engaging in endless polemics. He uses the metaphor of a "royal coin" to explain how partial truths can be deceptive and how the "truly real truth" naturally exposes falsehood.</summary>

## CHAPTER V

**That He who is the pre-eminent Cause of everything perceived by the mind is Himself nothing perceived by the mind.**

---

<margin>A</margin>
**A**gain, ascending yet higher, we say that He is neither soul nor mind; nor does He possess imagination, opinion, reason, or understanding; nor is He reason or understanding; nor is He spoken of or understood. He is not number, nor order, nor magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality, nor likeness, nor unlikeness. He does not stand, nor move, nor maintain silence. He has no power, nor is He power, nor light, nor life. He is not essence <note>original: "ousia"; the fundamental substance or being of a thing.</note>, nor eternity, nor time; nor is there any intellectual grasp of Him. He is not knowledge, nor truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom. He is not one, nor unity, nor deity <note>original: "theotes"; even the term "Godhead" is seen here as a human category that the ultimate Reality exceeds.</note>, nor goodness. He is not spirit in the sense that we understand it, nor sonship, nor fatherhood. He is nothing else known to us or to any other being. He does not belong to the things that do not exist, nor to the things that do exist. Existing things do not know Him as He is, nor does He know existing things as existing things <note>This suggests God’s knowledge is beyond the subject-object relationship of created beings.</note>. There is no reason for Him, nor name, nor knowledge. He is not darkness, nor light, nor error, nor truth. There is no <term>affirmation</term> <note>original: "thesis"; the act of stating what God is.</note> nor <term>negation</term> <note>original: "aphaeresis"; the act of taking away or stating what God is not.</note> that can be made of Him at all. But when we make affirmations or negations of those things that come after Him, we neither affirm nor deny Him. For the perfect and unique Cause of all things is beyond every affirmation.

Why then, you may ask, do we start from the highest point when we set forth divine affirmations <note>original: "thesies"; the positive names or attributes given to God.</note>, but start from the lowest point when we perform the divine negation <note>original: "aphairesis"; the process of "taking away" or stripping attributes to reach a higher truth.</note>? It is because when affirming that which is above all affirmation, we must start from that which is most closely related to it. But when negating that which is above all negation, we must strip away those things which are most distant from it. For is He not more truly "Life" and "Goodness" than He is "Air" or "Stone"? And is it not truer that He does not suffer from "drunkenness" or "wrath" than it is to say He cannot be "spoken of" or "perceived by the mind"?

Just as now, as we enter the <term>darkness</term> <note>original: "gnophos"; the divine gloom or "cloud of unknowing" where God dwells beyond human reach.</note> which is beyond mind, we shall find not brevity of speech, but a total <term>speechlessness</term> <note>original: "alogia"; literally "without word" or "without reason," describing the state where human logic fails.</note> and an absence of thought. In the former case, the discourse descending from the heights to the lowest things was widened according to the quantity of the descent; but now, ascending from the below to the transcendent, it is narrowed according to the measure of the ascent. And after every ascent, it will become wholly silent and will be completely united with the <term>Unspeakable</term> <note>original: "aphthegkto"; the ineffable reality that cannot be voiced.</note>.

And then he is released from the things that are seen and from those who see, and he enters into the truly mystical **darkness of unknowing** <note>original: "gnophos tēs agnōsias"; a state where the mind is blinded by the excess of divine light.</note>, in which he shuts out all perceptions of knowledge and comes to be in the altogether intangible and invisible, being entirely of the One who is beyond all, and of no one—neither himself nor another; and by the complete cessation of all knowledge, he is united in his higher part to the altogether Unknown, and by knowing nothing, he knows beyond the mind.

# [On] Mystical Theology

It seems to me that [the Apostle Bartholomew] has understood this in a supernatural way: that the Good Cause of all things is both prolific in words and yet brief of speech—and at the same time wordless—since it possesses neither word nor thought. This is because it is **super-essentially** <note>original: "hyperousios"; existing beyond the very category of "being" or "essence." This is a key term for Dionysius, suggesting God is not just "a" being, but the source above being.</note> set above all things. It reveals itself truly and clearly only to those who pass beyond all things both impure and pure, and who climb beyond every ascent of every holy height, leaving behind all divine lights and sounds and heavenly words, and who plunge into the **darkness** <note>original: "gnophos"; often translated as "the cloud" or "divine gloom." It represents a state where the human mind's light is extinguished by the overwhelming brilliance of God.</note> where, as the Scriptures say, He truly is who is beyond all things.

<margin>p.</margin>
For it was not without reason that the divine **Moses** was first commanded to be purified himself, and then to be separated from those who were not so purified. After every purification, he hears the many-voiced trumpets and sees many lights flashing with pure rays and widely-diffused beams. Then he is separated from the multitude and, with the chosen priests, reaches the summit of the divine ascents. Yet, even in these circumstances, he does not come to be with God Himself; he beholds not Him—for He is invisible—but rather the place where He stood.

And this, I believe, signifies that the most divine and highest of the things seen and understood are but certain <term>provisional suggestions</term> <note>original: "hypothetikous logous"; these are the preliminary concepts or symbols that serve as a foundation for understanding the Creator.</note> of the things subject to Him who transcends all. Through these, His presence—which is beyond all human conception—is shown, stepping upon the mental heights...

...things that are and things that are not, and strive toward union, as far as is attainable, by unknowingly reaching upward toward that which is beyond all essence and knowledge. For by the unattached and absolute <margin>l</margin> ecstasy <note>original: "ekstasei"; a standing outside of oneself or moving beyond ordinary perception.</note> from yourself and all things, you will be led up to the **super-essential** <note>original: "hyperousion"; refers to God existing beyond the very category of "being" or "substance."</note> ray of the divine darkness, having stripped away all things and been released from all things.

**S**ee to it that none of the uninitiated hears these things. By these, I mean those who are entangled in the things that exist, and who imagine nothing to exist super-essentially beyond the things that are, but think they know through their own knowledge Him who has made **darkness His hiding place** <note>A reference to Psalm 18:11, suggesting God's nature is hidden by the very intensity of His being.</note>.

**B**ut if the divine **initiations** <note>original: "mystagogiai"; the process of being led into sacred mysteries.</note> are beyond these people, what can one say about those even more uninitiated? These are the ones who characterize the Cause that lies above all by using the lowliest of created things, and who say that this Cause in no way excels the godless and many-shaped forms they fashion for themselves. It is necessary to both attribute and affirm all the qualities of existing things to It, as the Cause of all, and yet more properly to deny them all, as It exists super-essentially beyond all. One should not think that the **negations** <note>original: "apophaseis"; the "negative way" of describing God by what He is not (e.g., "immortal" or "infinite").</note> are the opposite of the **affirmations** <note>original: "kataphaseis"; the "positive way" of describing God (e.g., "God is good").</note>; rather, that the Cause which is beyond all deprivation is far prior to and above both every denial and every assertion. <meta>Ghosted text from verso visible here</meta>

**T**hus it is that the divine Bartholomew says both that theology is extensive and yet very brief, and that the Gospel is broad and great, and yet again concise.

### What is the divine darkness.

<margin>T</margin>rinity beyond essence <note>original: "Trias hyperousie"; refers to the Trinity existing beyond the very category of "being" or "substance."</note>, beyond divinity, and beyond goodness, guardian of the divine wisdom <note>original: "theosophias"</note> of Christians: guide us to the beyond-knowing, beyond-luminous, and highest summit of the mystical oracles <note>original: "logion"; sacred utterances or scriptures.</note>, where the simple, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of theology are veiled in the beyond-light darkness <note>original: "gnofos"; a thick, intentional darkness or cloud, often used to describe God's presence on Mt. # **On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy**

**T**herefore, the hierarch <note>original: "hierarches"; the presiding bishop or high priest.</note>, according to the sacred ascent, requires the child who is being admitted to make the renunciations <note>original: "apotagas"; the formal rejection of evil and the devil during the baptismal rite.</note> and the sacred confessions <note>original: "homologias"; the public profession of faith.</note>. It is not as those mockers <note>Referring to critics who argued that infant baptism was invalid because the child could not understand the commitment.</note> might say, that one person is initiated into divine things in place of another. For he [the sponsor] does not say this: "I am making the renunciations or the sacred confessions on behalf of the child." Rather, it is the child who renounces and joins himself [to Christ]. That is to say: "I promise to persuade the child, when he reaches a holy understanding through my God-inspired guidance, to renounce completely all opposing things, and to profess and enact the divine confessions."

<margin>T</margin>**T**herefore, I think there is nothing absurd <note>original: "atopon"; literally "out of place" or illogical.</note> if the child is led according to a
<margin>H</margin>divine upbringing, having a holy guide and sponsor <note>original: "anadochon"; literally "one who receives"; the godparent who receives the child from the baptismal font.</note> who imparts
<margin>T</margin>to him a habit <note>original: "hexin"; a stable disposition of character or a "state of being" developed through practice.</note> of divine things and keeps him untried by the opposing forces.

**T**he hierarch shares the sacred symbols with the child so that he might be nourished by
<margin>O</margin>them, and might have no other life than that which always contemplates divine things,
<margin>O</margin>becoming a partaker of them in holy progress, possessing a sacred habit in these things and being led in a holy manner by the God-like sponsor. Such things, my child—and so beautiful—are the unified visions <note>original: "henoeide theamata"; sights that bring the soul back to a state of oneness with God.</note> of our hierarchy. But perhaps to other minds with sharper vision, not only these things were seen, but things much clearer and more God-like. And you also, I think, will see more far-reaching and more divine beauties by using what has been said as stepping stones <note>original: "epanabathmois"; literally "rungs of a ladder" or "ascending steps."</note>.

<summary>This passage defends infant baptism by explaining that the godparent (sponsor) acts as a spiritual guide who promises to lead the child into a holy life, rather than simply speaking in the child's place. It emphasizes the importance of a "divine upbringing" where the child is nourished by sacred symbols from infancy.</summary>

## **Of Dionysius on the...** <note>The title continues "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy."</note>

...they do not understand, they randomly hand over the sacred traditions; and what is even more ridiculous, as they say, is that others perform the renunciation <note>original: "apagoges"; the turning away from evil.</note> and the sacred professions <note>original: "homologias"; the declaration of faith.</note> on their behalf.

**I**t is necessary that your hierarchical understanding <note>Addressing the reader, traditionally Timothy, with a title reflecting his spiritual maturity.</note> not be vexed by these mocking echoes; but rather, both reverently and for the sake of their enlightenment <note>original: "photagogias"; literally "bringing to the light."</note>, you should lovingly respond to the objections brought forward by them. You should set this forward according to sacred law: that not all divine things are circumscribed within our human knowledge. Many things unknown to us have God-befitting causes that are hidden from us, but known to the ranks of beings superior to us <note>Referring to the angelic hierarchies.</note>. Many things also remain hidden even from those highest beings, and are known accurately only by the all-wise and wisdom-creating Thearchy <note>original: "thearchias"; the divine source or Godhead.</note>. 

Nevertheless, concerning this matter, we affirm those things which our godlike consecrators <note>original: "hierotelestai"; high-ranking priests or initiators.</note>, having been initiated by ancient tradition, have passed down to us. For they say—and it is true—that children being brought up according to sacred law will arrive at a holy habit <note>original: "hexin"; a stable state of character.</note> of mind, being kept free from all error and remaining untried by an unholy life. This having come to the minds of our divine leaders, it seemed good to receive infants in this sacred manner: that the natural parents of the child being brought forward should hand the child over to one of the initiated who is a good educator in divine things. For the rest of his upbringing, the child would live under him as if under a divine father and a sponsor <note>original: "anadocho"; literally "one who receives" or "takes up"; a godparent.</note> of sacred salvation.

### Of Dionysius the Cit<gloss>y-dweller</gloss>

...having initiated him into the appropriate rites, he declared. Therefore, the divinely-inspired **Hierarchs** <note>A term for a high-ranking priest or bishop who leads the sacred rites.</note> must use their distinctions and all their **hierarchical** powers just as the **divine sovereignty** <note>original: "thearchia"; the ruling power of God as the source of all order.</note>, which is the **source of the rites**, might move them. As for the others, they must pay attention to the Hierarchs when they act in a hierarchical way, as if they were moved by God. *For he who rejects you,* He says, *rejects me* <note>A quotation of Jesus' words to his disciples in Luke 10:16.</note>. But let us return to what follows the prayer we mentioned. For once the **Hierarch** has finished the prayer, he himself kisses the **one who has fallen asleep** <note>original: "kekoimemenon"; a traditional Christian term for the deceased, implying that death is a temporary sleep before the resurrection.</note>, and after him, all those present do the same. For one who has reached his completion in the divine life is sweet and precious to all who are god-like.

<margin>M</margin> After the kiss, the **Hierarch** pours the oil over the one who has fallen asleep. Remember that during the sacred **divine birth** <note>original: "theogenesis"; referring here to the sacrament of Baptism, where a person is "born again."</note>, before the most divine **baptism**, the first participation in a sacred symbol is granted to the one being initiated—after the total removal of their former clothing—through the oil of anointing. Now, however, it is at the very end of everything that the oil is poured over the one who has fallen asleep. At the beginning, the anointing with oil called the initiate to sacred struggles; but now, the oil poured out shows that the deceased has fought those same sacred struggles and has reached completion.

<margin>T</margin> When the **Hierarch** has finished these things, he places the body in an honorable house along with other sacred bodies of the same rank. For if the deceased lived a life beloved by God in both soul and body, the body will be held in honor alongside the holy soul.

## Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

**T**o the righteous Scripture <note>original: "logion"; literally a 'divine word' or 'oracle,' used here to refer to the Bible.</note> he himself also quite appropriately listens: *You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.* <note>A quotation from James 4:3.</note> Therefore, the divine **Hierarch** <note>The high-ranking leader of the sacred rites.</note> asks for those things promised by God, which are dear to God and will certainly be granted. In doing so, he demonstrates his own **good-like** <note>original: "agathoeidous"; having the form or character of the Good (God).</note> disposition to the good-loving God, and clearly reveals to those present the gifts that will belong to the holy ones. In this same way, the **Hierarchs** also possess the powers of **separation** <note>original: "aphoristikas"; the power to set apart, exclude, or excommunicate.</note>; they act as the revealers of divine judgments. This is not as if the all-wise **Divine Sovereignty** <note>original: "thearchia"; God as the supreme source of all order and rule.</note> followed their own irrational impulses in a subservient way, but rather that they, as **interpreters** <note>original: "hypophetikos"; one who speaks for a deity.</note>, are moved by the **Spirit who initiates the rites** <note>original: "teletarchiko pneumati"; the Holy Spirit as the source of all sacred mysteries.</note>. They separate those who have already been judged by God according to their merit. For He says: *Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.* <note>Quoting Jesus’s words to the Apostles in John 20:22–23.</note> And to the one enlightened by the divine revelations of the most holy Father, the **Scriptures** say: *Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* <note>Quoting Matthew 16:19.</note>

**S**o it is for him and for every **Hierarch** like him. According to the revelations of the Father's judgments occurring within him, he acts as a revealer and a **messenger** <note>original: "diaporthmeutikos"; one who carries something across or acts as a conduit.</note>, welcoming those who are dear to God and rejecting the godless. For as the **Scriptures** say regarding that sacred theology, it was not by their own motion, nor did **flesh and blood** reveal these things, but they were revealed intellectually by God. <note>An allusion to Matthew 16:17, where Jesus tells Peter that his confession was revealed by the Father rather than human means.</note>

<summary>This page explains that a Hierarch's prayers and his power to forgive or retain sins (binding and loosing) are not based on personal whim, but on his role as an enlightened interpreter of God's pre-existing will.</summary>
