### Dionysius on the... <note>The title is truncated here but refers to the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.</note>

->The divine **Hierarch** <note>original: "hierarchēs"; the high-ranking leader of the sacred rites.</note> is a **manifestor** <note>original: "ekphantorikos"; one who reveals or brings divine truths to light.</note> of the **Divine Sovereignty's** <note>original: "thearchikōn"; pertaining to the 'Thearchy,' the supreme source of divine order.</note> judgments, just as the **Scriptures** <note>original: "logia"; literally 'divine utterances' or oracles, used here to refer to the Bible.</note> say; for he is a messenger of the Lord God Almighty.<-

He has, therefore, learned from the God-delivered **Scriptures** that for those who have lived holily, the most radiant and divine life is rendered according to their merit by the most just scales of God. The **divine benevolence** <note>original: "thearchikēs philanthropias"; God’s love for humanity.</note> of the Sovereignty overlooks the **stains** <note>original: "kelidas"; blemishes or spots on the soul.</note> that occurred within them due to human weakness; for as the **Scriptures** say, "no one is clean from filth." <note>A reference to Job 14:4.</note>

The **Hierarch**, then, knows these things have been promised by the true **Scriptures**. He asks that these things come to pass and be gifted to those who have lived holily, along with the sacred rewards. On one hand, he is being **good-like** <note>original: "agathoeidōs"; taking on the form or character of the Good (God).</note> by imitating God, asking for the gifts of others as if they were his own favors. On the other hand, he is **manifestly** showing to those present that these true promises will surely come to be. He reveals that the things he asks for according to sacred law will certainly belong to those who have been perfected in the divine life.

For the **Hierarch**, the **interpreter** <note>original: "hypophētēs"; one who speaks for or interprets the divine will.</note> of divine justice, would never ask for things that are not most dear to God and which have not been promised by Him to be given in a **God-like** manner. This is why he does not pray these things for the unholy who have **fallen asleep** <note>A common early Christian euphemism for death.</note>. This is not only because he would be straying from his ordered role as an **interpreter** and would be audaciously daring to act on his own authority as a **Hierarch** without being moved by the **Initiator of rites** <note>original: "teletarchou"; the supreme source of the sacraments, usually referring to the Holy Spirit or God.</note>, but also because he would fail to obtain the effective prayer...

<summary>This page explains that the Hierarch's prayer for the dead is an act of "revelation" rather than a petition to change God's mind, asserting that God's mercy overlooks human weakness for the righteous. It also clarifies that the Hierarch only prays for those who died in a state of holiness, acting as a mouthpiece for divine will.</summary>

## **Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy**

...in this manner: if anyone, longing for **sacred gifts** <note>original: "hierōn dōrōn"; refers to spiritual graces or the benefits of the sacraments.</note> and possessing a sacred habit for partaking in them—being mindful of his own insignificance—goes to one of the **holy men** <note>original: "hosiōn andrōn"; individuals of recognized sanctity or the clergy.</note> and requests that he become his **helper and fellow-supplicant** <note>original: "syllēptora kai syniketēn"; one who assists and joins his prayers to the petitioner’s own.</note>, he will certainly benefit from this. Indeed, he will attain the primary benefit of all things, for he will obtain the most divine gifts he requests. This is because the **Divine Goodness** <note>original: "thearchikēs agathotētos"; the goodness of the Thearchy or Godhead.</note> of the Sovereignty accepts him for his own reverent self-awareness, his respect for the holy ones, his praiseworthy longing for the sacred requests, and his fitting and **god-like disposition** <note>original: "theoeidous hexeōs"; a state of being that reflects the divine character.</note>. For this also has been established by the **Divine Judgments** <note>original: "thearchikois krimmasin"</note>: that divine gifts are shared with the worthy in a most god-fitting order—bestowed through those who are worthy of imparting them.

<margin>Therefore,</margin> if anyone should dishonor this sacred order and, having arrived at a wretched **self-conceit** <note>original: "oiēsin"; an inflated sense of one's own spiritual standing or pride.</note>, should think himself sufficient for direct communion with the **Divine Sovereignty** <note>original: "thearchikēn homilian"; direct conversation or fellowship with God.</note> and should look down upon the holy ones...

<margin>And indeed,</margin> if he makes requests that are unworthy of God and not sacred, and if he does not have an intense and suitable desire for divine things, he will fail [to receive them] because of himself and his **ignorant request** <note>original: "anepistēmonos aitēseōs"; a request made without true spiritual understanding.</note>.

<margin>Regarding</margin> the aforementioned prayer which the **Hierarch** <note>original: "hierarchēs"; the bishop or presiding priest.</note> prays over the **one who has fallen asleep** <note>original: "kekoymēmenō"; the standard early Christian term for the deceased, implying the hope of resurrection.</note>, it is necessary to speak of the tradition that has come to us from our **divinely inspired leaders** <note>original: "entheōn hēmōn kathēgemonōn"; the teachers or apostles who established the liturgical traditions.</note>.

<summary>Dionysius explains that divine grace is granted through a sacred order, where humble individuals seek the intercession of holy men. He warns that prideful attempts to bypass this hierarchy or making unworthy requests leads to a loss of divine favor.</summary>

# # Of Dionysius, Concerning the <note>original: "Dionysiou peri tēs"; the title is continued from a previous section, likely referring to "The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy."</note>

By what **hierarchical prayer** <note>original: "hierarchikēs euchēs"; a prayer offered by the Bishop or Hierarch.</note>, then, will he be transferred to another destiny <note>original: "lēxin"; an allotment or state of being in the afterlife.</note> contrary to his merit and the reward for his life here?

<margin>I</margin>
know, however, following the **Scriptures** <note>original: "logiois"; literally "oracles," referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note>, that each shall have a reciprocal allotment. For the Lord, it says, has closed the door against him; and "each shall receive for the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:10.</note>

<margin>But</margin>
that the prayers of the righteous during this life—and perhaps after death only for those worthy of **sacred prayers** <note>original: "hierōn euchōn"</note>—are effective, the true traditions of the Scriptures teach us. Otherwise, what did Saul benefit from **Samuel**? Or what did the **prophetic prayer** benefit the people of the Hebrews? For it is as if someone—while the sun is granting its proper light to healthy eyes—seeks to partake of the solar light while destroying his own vision. Such a person gapes after impossible and empty hopes. He who requests the prayers of the saints, while driving away their natural sacred influence <note>original: "energeias"; activities or operations.</note> by neglecting the divine gifts and departing from the most bright and **good-bestowing commandments** <note>original: "agathodotidōn entolōn"</note>, acts in vain. I say, following the Scriptures, that the prayers of the saints are entirely beneficial in this life in this manner...

They will also see that the divine promises will result in unending consequences for those who are unholy like themselves. For it will be a benefit to them to see the person who has been sacredly perfected <note>The deceased believer.</note> being announced by the **liturgical proclamation** <margin>L</margin> as truly being a partaker of the saints from all ages. 

**W**hen they are sacredly announced in this way, perhaps these observers too <margin>T</margin> will come to a similar desire and will be taught by the **liturgical science** <note>original: "leitourgikēs epistēmēs"; the systematic understanding of the church's rites.</note> that the perfection <margin>Z</margin> in Christ is truly blessed.

<margin>5</margin> **T**hen the divine **Bishop** <note>original: "hierarchēs"</note> approaching, offers a **sacred prayer** over the **deceased** <note>original: "kekoimēmēnō"; literally "the one fallen asleep."</note>; and after the prayer, the Bishop himself kisses him; and then all those present do likewise.

# On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

The **Hierarch** <term>Hierarch: a leader of sacred rites, specifically a Bishop</term> brings the one who has fallen asleep <note>A traditional Christian euphemism for death, implying the hope of resurrection.</note> to the place designated for those of the same rank and sets them there. This sacredly signifies that in the **rebirth** <note>original: "paligenesia"; referring to the general resurrection at the end of time</note>, all will receive their <margin>A</margin> allotments based on how they lived their individual lives here. For instance, if someone lived a **godlike** <note>original: "theoeidē"; meaning a life that reflects the character of God</note> and most holy life—as far as imitating God is possible for a human—he will dwell in divine and blessed allotments in the age to come.

<margin>E</margin> But if he lived a holy life that fell short of the highest godlikeness, he too will receive holy rewards of a similar kind. For this **divine justice**, the Hierarch offers thanks and makes a holy prayer, praising the venerable **Godhead** <term>Godhead: the original "thearchia," referring to the Trinity as the source of all divine order</term> as the power that destroys the unjust and tyrannical rule <note>A reference to the power of death and spiritual darkness over humanity.</note> over us all and translates us to our own most just judgments.

<margin>A</margin> The songs and readings of the **divine promises** <note>Referring to scriptural passages regarding the afterlife and the kingdom of God.</note> reveal those most blessed allotments into which those who have achieved **divine perfection** <note>original: "teleiōsin"; the completion of the spiritual journey through the sacraments</note> will be eternally assigned.

<margin>T</margin> These rites are welcoming for the one who has holily fallen asleep, and they act as an exhortation for those still living toward a similar perfection.

<margin>S</margin> Observe that now, not all the orders currently undergoing purification are dismissed as is usually the custom. Only the **catechumens** <term>Catechumens: those receiving instruction in the faith but who have not yet been baptized</term> are excluded from the sacred spaces. This is because this group is entirely uninitiated into any sacred rite and has no part in any of the things sacredly performed... <note>The text cuts off here; Dionysius is explaining that while penitents (baptized people who have sinned) can stay for funeral prayers, the unbaptized cannot.</note>

<summary>This page describes how the funeral rite mirrors the soul's future state, with the Bishop praying for the deceased according to their level of holiness. It explains that while some "purified" orders may attend, the unbaptized catechumens are strictly excluded from these mysteries.</summary>

# Dionysius on the **Ecclesiastical Hierarchy** <note>original: "ekklēsiastikēs hierarchias"</note>

...[deprived] of instruction, they do not properly deprive those who have reached the end of the most divine races of their rewards. <note>This fragment likely concludes a sentence from the previous page regarding those who misunderstand the rewards of a holy life.</note>

->Of the **Ecclesiastical Hierarchy**<-
<sig>t iii</sig>

# **Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy**

...knowing that their salvation will likewise be accomplished through their future total resurrection.

<margin>A D</margin> For holy souls, which in this present life are liable to fall into a **turn** <term>turn: "tropēn," referring to the mutability or instability of the human will in the material world</term> toward what is worse, will, in the **regeneration** <term>regeneration: "palingenesia," the "rebirth" or restoration of life at the resurrection</term>, receive a most godlike reassignment to an unchangeable state.

<margin>T</margin> Moreover, the pure bodies—which were yoked to and traveled the same path as the holy souls, being enrolled with them and having struggled alongside them during their divine labors—will receive their own resurrection together with the souls' unchangeable establishment in the divine life. For having been united to those holy souls to which they were joined during this life, and having become **members of Christ** <note>original: "melē Christou," the Pauline idea that the physical bodies of believers are parts of Christ’s own body</note>, they will receive a godlike, incorruptible, immortal, and blessed **allotment** <term>allotment: "lēxis," the final state or destination assigned to a person in the afterlife</term>. In this, then, is the "sleep" of the holy: it is a state of gladness and unshakable hope, as it reaches the goal of their divine contests.

<margin>T o</margin> But regarding the unholy: some irrationally imagine that they pass into non-existence; others believe that the physical union with their own souls is severed once and for all, as if a body were unsuitable for them in a godlike life and blessed destiny. This is because they have not considered, nor have they been sufficiently initiated into divine knowledge, that our most godlike life in Christ has already begun.

<margin>A</margin> Still others assign unions with *other* bodies to these souls <note>Dionysius is here refuting the concept of metempsychosis (the migration of souls into new bodies), which was a common idea in some Platonic and Gnostic circles.</note>. In doing so, they do an injustice—at least in my opinion—to the bodies that labored with the divine souls, and they deprive the holy...

<summary>Pseudo-Dionysius explains that the resurrection involves the reunion of the soul with its specific, original body, which shared in its earthly spiritual labors. He rejects alternative views such as annihilation, the permanent shedding of the body, or reincarnation into different bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the systematic conclusion of "The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. Having previously discussed how the heavenly ranks receive and pass on divine light, the author now correlates these celestial functions with the specific ranks of the earthly Church (the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy) and addresses a potential contradiction regarding the nature of "purification" among the sinless angels.</meta>

<lang>English (translated from Greek)</lang>
<sig>t ii</sig>

# On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

It has therefore been concluded by us that while the holy rites <note>original: "teletai," referring to the sacraments or initiations</note> are purification, illumination, and perfection; the ministers <note>original: "leitourgoi," referring specifically to the rank of deacons</note> are the purifying order; the priests are the illuminating order; and the god-like hierarchs <note>original: "hierarchai," the bishops</note> are the perfecting order. The order being purified is that which does not yet share in the sacred vision and communion, as it is still being cleansed <note>This refers to the catechumens or those undergoing penance who were excluded from the Eucharist</note>. The contemplative order is the holy people <note>the lay faithful</note>. And the perfected order is that of the solitary monks.

For in this way, our hierarchy, being sacredly arranged according to the God-given orders, is of the same form as the heavenly hierarchies, preserving—as much as is possible among men—the god-like characters and features of the divine imitation.

<margin>See how</margin>
But you will say that the heavenly hierarchies altogether lack "purifying" orders; for it is neither lawful nor true to say that any heavenly arrangement is defiled. I would certainly agree—and let us not fall away entirely from a most holy understanding—that they are completely unblemished and possess a super-worldly purity. If any of them had been seized by wickedness, they would have fallen away from the essence and unmixed harmony of the divine minds, and would have been carried down into the lightless fall of the rebellious multitudes. But one can say sacredly regarding the heavenly hierarchy that "purification" for the lower beings <note>subordinate ranks of angels</note> is the illumination from God of things previously unknown, leading them to a more perfect knowledge <term>knowledge: "epistēmē," a spiritual and certain understanding</term> of the divine-governing <note>original: "thearchikōn," meaning the rule or origin of God</note> understandings. It is as if they are being cleansed of the ignorance of things for which they did not yet have the knowledge, being led up through the first and more divine beings toward the highest and most brilliant glimmers of those who behold God.

<vocab>Ecclesiastical hierarchy, purification, illumination, perfection, hierarchs, monks, god-like characters, heavenly hierarchies, Dionysius the Areopagite</vocab>

<summary>Dionysius defines the three functions of the Church (purifying, illuminating, perfecting) and assigns them to specific ranks, from deacons to bishops. He explains that even sinless angels undergo "purification," which in their case means the removal of ignorance through the reception of new divine revelations.</summary>
<keywords>ecclesiastical hierarchy, deacons, priests, bishops, monks, purification, illumination, perfection, angelic ranks, divine light, Pseudo-Dionysius</keywords>

While this usually means "sophistic" or "rhetorical," in this context it refers to a state of spiritual wisdom. Some manuscripts suggest "photistiken" or "illuminating."</note> disposition.

<margin>E</margin> Since even now, the priest and all the holy ones who are present embrace the one who has been perfected <note>the newly initiated monk</note>; consider this the holy communion of those who are god-like, as they share in joy with one another in a state of divine gladness.

<margin>H</margin> And at the end of all things, the priest calls the one who has been perfected to the **divine communion** <term>thearchic koinonia: the Eucharist</term>. He shows in a sacred manner that the one who has been initiated—if he truly arrives at the monastic and unified state—will not only be a contemplator of the sacred rites appropriate to his rank, nor will he come to the communion of the most holy symbols according to the middle rank <note>the ordinary lay faithful</note>. Rather, with a divine knowledge of the sacred things he has partaken in, and in a manner different from the holy people <note>the laity</note>, he will come to the **participation** <term>metalepsis</term> of the divine communion. 

For this reason, the communion of the most holy **Eucharist** is also imparted by the **hierarch** <term>the bishop</term> who performed the rites to the various priestly ranks during their own sacred consecrations, at the very end of those most holy initiations. This is not only because the participation in the divine mysteries is the "head" <note>the summit or completion</note> of every hierarchical participation, but also because <margin>αι</margin> all the sacred ranks participate in that communal and most divine gift in a way proportionate to themselves, leading toward their own proper **deification** <term>theosis: the process of becoming like God</term> and perfection.

# Of Dionysius the Elder
## The Mystery of Monastic Perfection.

**The** priest stands before the divine altar <note>original: "thysiasterion." In the Eastern tradition, this refers specifically to the altar table within the sanctuary.</note>, pronouncing the sacred monastic invocation; the one being initiated stands behind the priest. He does not bend both knees <note>In certain ordinations, such as for a deacon or priest, the candidate kneels on one or both knees. The monk stands, symbolizing a different kind of dedication.</note>, nor does he have the God-given words <note>original: "theoparadota logia." This refers to the Holy Gospels, which are placed on the head of a bishop during his consecration.</note> held upon his head; but he stands only beside the priest, who pronounces the mystical invocation over him.

<margin>10</margin> **H**aving completed this prayer, the priest, coming to the one being initiated, first asks him if he renounces all "divided" lives <note>original: "diairetais... zoais." In Dionysian thought, a "divided" life is one distracted by worldly cares, whereas the monk seeks a "unified" life focused solely on God.</note>, and not only lives, but even imaginations <note>original: "phantasiais." These are the mental images or sensory distractions that pull the mind away from pure contemplation.</note>. Then he sets before him the most perfect way of life, testifying that he must rise above the middle state <note>The "middle rank" refers to the ordinary lay faithful who are being perfected but have not taken monastic vows.</note>. When the initiate has readily confessed all these things, the priest, having signed him with the sign of the cross, tonsures <term>tonsure: the ritual cutting of hair, signifying the casting off of worldly vanity and the dedication of the mind to God</term> him, calling upon the Trinitarian personhood <note>original: "triadike... hypostasis." A reference to the three persons of the Holy Trinity.</note> of the divine blessedness; and having stripped off all his clothing, he puts different clothes on him. Then, along with the other holy men who are present, he kisses him and makes him a participant in the divine-ruling mysteries <note>original: "thearchikon mysterion." This refers to the Holy Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>.

**The** fact that he does not bend either of his knees, nor has the God-given words upon his head, but stands beside the priest as the invocation is pronounced, indicates that the monastic order is not one that leads others <note>Unlike the orders of the clergy (deacons, priests, bishops), the monk does not have the authority to lead or initiate others into the mysteries.</note>; but...

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

...through sacred contemplation and communion. And being entrusted to the perfecting powers of the hierarchs <term>hierarchs: the highest rank of the clergy, specifically bishops, who have the authority to perform initiations and perfect the lower orders</term>; and through their divine illuminations and hierarchical traditions, the soul is taught the sacred rites of the ceremonies that belong to it. According to the measure of their holy knowledge, it is led upward proportionately toward its most complete perfection <note>original: "teleiosin." In this context, it refers to both spiritual maturity and the finality of the ritual itself.</note>.

<margin>5</margin> **H**ence our divine leaders have deemed them worthy of sacred names: some calling them "servants" <note>original: "therapeutai." This Greek term implies both a servant of God and one who seeks spiritual healing.</note> and others calling them "monks" <note>original: "monachoi." Derived from the word for "alone" or "single," referring to their focus on the "One" (God) and their withdrawal from the many distractions of the world.</note>. This is due to their pure service and attendance to God, and because of their undivided and unified life. This life folds them together, drawing them away from "divided" things <note>Dionysius uses "divided" to describe the fragmented nature of worldly, material life compared to the unity of the divine.</note> into a god-like oneness and a god-loving perfection. Therefore, the sacred legislation of the Church has granted them a grace that brings perfection, and it has deemed them worthy of a specific consecrating invocation—though not a "hierarchical" one <note>Dionysius is distinguishing between monastic consecration and the ordination of clergy (bishops, priests, deacons). Monks are consecrated, but they do not receive the "hierarchical" power to perform sacraments themselves.</note>.

<margin>5</margin> **F**or that hierarchical invocation is reserved for the priestly orders alone; but this monastic rite is a sacred service performed by holy priests through the hierarchical rite of perfection in a secondary degree.

<note>The following technical terms appear in the source text:</note>
*   **Ecclesiastical Hierarchy:** The ordered structure of the Church.
*   **Contemplation:** Deep spiritual vision or "theory."
*   **Communion:** The shared participation in the divine.
*   **Monks:** Those who live a unified, solitary life for God.
*   **Servants:** Another term for those dedicated to God's service.
*   **Perfection:** The state of spiritual completion or the rite that bestows it.
*   **Sacred Rite:** The liturgical act or "hierurgy."
*   **Legislation:** The established laws or ordinances of the Church.

<margin>Δ</margin> <margin>LV</margin> ...of the hierarchy. For even the most lover of mankind, Jesus, who became [human] for our sake, did not glorify himself, as the scriptures say, but it was the one who spoke to him:

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

How the hierarchical arrangement of the divine, undefiled things divides itself into distinct ranks and powers, actively demonstrating the divine <term>energies: the outward workings or activities of God</term> as they stand without suffering and without confusion in most holy and unmixed orders.

### The Mystery of Hierarchical Completions.

The <term>Hierarch: bishop</term>, being brought to the hierarchical completion, bends both feet before the altar; he has the God-given <term>oracles: (logia) the Book of the Gospels</term> and the hierarchical hand placed upon his head. <margin>H</margin>
<margin>O</margin>

<margin>O</margin>
The <term>minister: (leitourgos) here referring to the deacon</term>, bending only one of his feet before the divine altar, has the right hand of the ordaining Hierarch placed upon his head, being completed by him with the perfecting invocations designated for ministers.

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy
∫ iii

...completing those who approach and making them partakers of the holy rites; then sending up to the <term>Hierarch: bishop</term> those who desire the knowledge of the sacred acts they have beheld.

<margin>H</margin> The order of the <term>ministers: deacons</term> is the purifying rank and the one that discerns between those who are unlike [the holy things]. 
<margin>Δ</margin> Before bringing them to the sacred rites of the priests, it cleanses those who approach, making them free from anything contrary [to the divine] and fit for the sacred <term>vision: epopsia</term> <note>original: "ἐποψίαν" — a term borrowed from ancient mystery religions meaning the highest level of initiation where one "beholds" the truth</note> and communion. 

Hence, in the sacred <term>divine birth: baptism</term> <note>original: "θεογενεσίας" (theogenesias) — Dionysius uses this term to describe Baptism as a spiritual rebirth into God's family</note>, the ministers strip the one approaching of their old garment; they even take off their shoes; and they stand them facing the West for the renunciation; and then they breathe upon them. For it belongs to the purifying order and power to command those who approach to cast off entirely the clothing of their former life, pointing out the darkness of their previous way of living, and teaching them that once they have renounced those things without light, they should cross over to the things of illumination.

<margin>K</margin> Therefore, the ministerial arrangement is purifying; it leads those who have been cleansed to the radiant sacred rites of the priests. It purifies the uninitiated and acts as a midwife to them through the purifying illuminations and teachings of the <term>Holy Scriptures: oracles</term> <note>original: "λογίων" (logion) — literally "divine sayings" or "oracles," referring here to the Bible</note>. Furthermore, it completely separates the unholy from the holy things. For this reason, the hierarchical law places this order at the sacred doors, determining that the entrance of those approaching the sacred things must happen within a state of complete purification.

Now, the capacity of those being initiated is threefold. The first is that which is being **purified**. The middle, following purification, is that which is being **illuminated** and is capable of contemplating certain sacred things. # On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

...[understand]ing by means of **intellectual contemplations** <note>original: "νοεραῖς θεωρίαις"—spiritual insights perceived by the mind rather than the physical eyes</note>; and on the other hand, because it is adorned with **sensible symbols** <note>original: "συμβόλοις αἰσθητοῖς"—physical objects like water, oil, or bread that represent spiritual truths</note> and through them is sacredly led up toward the divine.

<margin>T</margin>he threefold nature likewise holds for the hierarchical division, being divided into the most holy **rites of the sacred services**, the **god-like ministers** of the sacred things, and those who are proportionately **led by them** toward the sacred mysteries.

<margin>E</margin>ach of the three divisions of our hierarchy follows the pattern of the <term>Legal Hierarchy: the Old Testament law</term> and the more divine hierarchy of our own era. It is arranged by power into a **first**, **middle**, and **last** rank, having been pre-taught the sacredly-fitting proportion and the well-ordered, harmonious, and binding fellowship of all things.

<margin>H</margin>ence, regarding the most holy ministry of the <term>rites: the sacraments</term>: first, it possesses a god-like power for the **sacred purification** of the uninitiated; second, the **illuminating initiation** of those already purified; and finally, as a summary of the preceding stages, the **perfection** <note>original: "τελείωσιν"—the final state of spiritual completion or "finishing"</note> of those initiated into the knowledge of the mysteries they have received.

<margin>H</margin>owever, the order of the sacred ministers <note>the clergy</note> also operates this way: in its first power, it **purifies** the uninitiated through the rites; in its middle power, it **leads the purified to the light**; and in the last and highest of the ministerial powers, it brings to **perfection** those who have shared in the divine light, through the <term>scientific perfections: certain knowledge</term> of the illuminations they have contemplated.

# [Dionysius] On the [Ecclesiastical Hierarchy]

...the radiance of the <term>Thearchy: the rule of God as the source of all divinity</term> <note>original: "θεαρχίας"—God as the origin of all sacred order</note>; the ranks being perfected are called holy and true. After that heavenly and <term>super-cosmic: beyond the physical world</term> hierarchy, the Godhead—bringing forth its most sacred gifts to our level in a spirit of goodness—granted the <term>Legal Hierarchy: the religious system of the Old Testament Law</term> to those who were "infants" <note>original: "νηπίοις"—referring to those not yet spiritually mature enough for direct revelation</note> according to the Scriptures. This was composed of faint images of the truth and distant reflections of the archetypes. It utilized riddles difficult to behold and symbols that do not easily reveal the <term>contemplation: spiritual insight</term> <note>original: "θεωρίαν"—perceiving the divine meaning behind a physical act</note> hidden within them, shining a light proportional to the needs of those with weak eyes, so as to enlighten them without causing harm.

In this Legal Hierarchy, the rite is the <term>anagoge: leading the soul upward</term> <note>original: "ἀναγωγή"—the process of lifting the mind from physical symbols to spiritual truths</note> toward spiritual worship. The guides toward this were those sacredly initiated into that holy Tabernacle by Moses—the first mystic and leader of the hierarchs under the Law. In his <term>sacred writing: the Pentateuch</term> <note>original: "ἱερογραφίαν"</note>, Moses, leading us away from the physical, called all the priestly duties performed under the Law an "image of the pattern" shown to him on **Mount Sinai**.

<margin>T</margin>hose who are being perfected by means of the legal symbols are led up proportionately to a more perfect initiation. Scripture <note>original: "θεολογία"—literally "theology," but often used by Dionysius to mean the Bible itself</note> calls this more perfect <term>initiation: the process of entering into sacred mysteries</term> our own hierarchy, naming it the fulfillment of the former and a sacred inheritance.

<margin>E</margin>ach [part of our hierarchy] is both heavenly and legal, partaking in the middle ground between the two extremes; for on one hand, it is **sharing in**... <note>original: "κοινωννοῦσα"—the text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the thought continues with how the church shares in both spiritual and physical realms</note>

<summary>Dionysius explains that the Old Testament Law was a "Legal Hierarchy" of faint symbols designed for spiritual "infants," which has now been fulfilled by the more perfect "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" that bridges the gap between the Law and the Heavenly hosts.</summary>

# [On the] Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

...and the triad of subordinate ranks beneath them; so that the arrangement of our own hierarchy might be demonstrated. This system clearly separates and excludes everything that is disordered, formless, and confused, while revealing what is orderly, structured, and stable through the proportions of the sacred ranks within it. ### [Dionysius Concerning] the [Ecclesiastical Hierarchy]

**The** fragrant essence that is beyond all intellect loves to be stirred into manifestation by the fiery and most pure minds; and it grants its most divine inspirations in all-blessed distributions to those who call upon it in a way that transcends the world.

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

...an intent and unwavering <term>contemplation: "theoria," the spiritual act of seeing beyond the physical to the divine</term> of the fragrant and hidden beauty will grant the unseen and most godlike image. Naturally, then, the divine painters <note>A metaphor for the clergy or holy men who "paint" the image of God within their own souls through virtue</note>—who unswervingly conform their own <margin>O</margin> intellectual powers to the <term>supersubstantial: "hyperousios," a term used to describe God as being "above" or "beyond" all categories of being or essence</term> fragrance and spiritual beauty—do not look upon any of the god-imitating virtues within themselves for the sake of being "seen by men" (as the Scripture says). Rather, they sacredly shroud the most holy mysteries of the Church in the divine ointment <note>original: "myron," the consecrated oil</note> as if in an image.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, by sacredly veiling the things of virtue—which are holy and most godlike—within their god-imitating and god-inscribed minds, they look only toward the <term>archetypal: the original divine pattern or "first draft" from which all earthly things are copied</term> perception. For these things are not visible to those who are unlike them; nor do these holy men allow themselves to be dragged down toward the gaze of the uninitiated. Consequently, following their own nature, they do not love those things which merely *seem* beautiful and just, but those which truly *are* so. They do not look toward the glory that is irrationally praised by the masses, but they judge what is good or bad in itself in a god-imitating way.

<margin>X</margin> They are divine images of the most supreme divine fragrance. This fragrance, possessing true sweetness within itself, does not turn toward what *seems* fragrant to the many who are unlike it; <margin>D</margin> rather, it imprints its unfeigned character upon its true images.

<margin>Ph</margin> Come then, since we have now looked upon the outward beauty of this entire beautiful sacred rite, let us look toward its more divine beauty. ### Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

**T**herefore, let these first, and more importantly than the others, be set apart by the minister's discriminating voice. For it is not lawful <note>original: "themiton"</note> for them to participate in any other sacred rite than the teaching of the scriptures <note>original: "logion," literally "divine oracles"</note>, which turns one back toward better things.

**F**or the supramundane <term>supramundane: "hyperkosmios," existing beyond the physical or material world</term> sacred service of divine things remains hidden from both those in repentance <note>original: "metanoia," referring here to those undergoing formal church discipline for sins</note> and those who have already reached that state; for it does not admit that which is not yet entirely most-holy. It proclaims this most purely: that even to those who are in any way too weak to reach the peak of the godlike <term>godlike: "theoeidous," having the form or character of God</term> state, it remains invisible and unshared. For the voice, which is entirely unmixed, drives away those who are unable to be joined with the worthy communicants <term>communicants: "koinonois," those sharing in the fellowship of the Eucharist</term> of the most divine things. Much more so shall the unholy multitude of those driven by passions <note>referring to those controlled by earthly desires rather than spiritual discipline</note> be excluded from every vision and communion of the sacred mysteries. For the uninitiated and unperfected in the ceremonies remain outside the divine temple and the sacred service laid out before them. Alongside them are the apostates <note>those who have abandoned the holy life or the faith</note> from the holy life; and following these are those who, through cowardice, are susceptible to the terrors and phantoms of the enemy, because they have not attained—through a strained and unyielding leaning toward divine things—the immovability and activity of a godlike habit. Then, in addition to these, are those who have turned away from a life of opposition [to God], but even so, they must be purified of its fantasies by a divine and unmixed love. And after them, those who are not pure...

### Dionysius on the <unclear>Hierarchy</unclear>

**I**f indeed it is true that the entirely divine man—the one worthy of sharing in divine things, who has been raised to the peak of the godlike <term>godlike: "theoeidous," having the form or character of God</term> state through perfect and perfecting deifications <term>deifications: "theosesin," the process of becoming united with God (theosis)</term>—will not even act according to the flesh except for the most necessary of natural things, and even then, only incidentally.

**H**e shall be at once a temple and a follower of the Divinely-Sovereign <note>original: "thearchikou," referring to the Godhead as the principle or source of all things</note> Spirit in the highest deification belonging to him; for the Spirit establishes like within like. Such a man would never be moved by opposing fantasies or impulses.

**H**e will laugh at these things and wrestle them down as they approach; he will drive them away, acting upon them rather than being acted upon by them. In addition to the lack of passion <note>original: "apathei," the state of being undisturbed by worldly desires or "apatheia"</note> and the unyielding nature of his own character, he will appear to others as a physician for such disturbances.

**B**ut I think in addition to this—or rather, I know clearly—that the most unmixed discrimination <note>referring to the hierarchical duty of discerning who is fit to remain for the liturgy</note> of the hierarchy knows those who are being "energized" <note>original: "energoumenous," a term often used for those possessed or driven by external spirits</note> more clearly than the examples mentioned before. These are they who, having fallen away from the godlike life, become like-minded and similar in character to the destructive demons. Through an ultimate and self-destructive folly, they turn away from things that truly exist—the immortal and attainable goods which are eternally sweet. Instead, they desire and act upon material <term>material: "prosylon," literally "towards matter" or "immersed in matter"</term> and most passionate change, seeking those fleeting and ruinous pleasures and that unstable "well-being" found in alien things—a state which does not truly exist, but only appears to be.

<summary>Dionysius describes the "divine man" (the perfect initiate) as a temple of the Spirit who is immune to worldly passions, contrasting him with those "energized" by demons who prefer material pleasures over eternal truths.</summary>

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

<margin>1</margin>...miscarriages and abortions, being an unborn, lifeless, and separated falling-away from the earth, as it were. No one of sound mind, looking at the reality of the situation, would say that such things have been brought into the light simply because they have been released from the darkness of the womb. For the scientific guardian of bodies—the art of medicine—would say that light acts only upon those things capable of receiving light. So too does the all-wise science of sacred things: first, it acts as a midwife <note>original: "maieuetai," a term used by Socrates and Dionysius to describe the process of bringing truth or spiritual life to birth</note> for them through the introductory nourishment of the formative and life-giving scriptures. When it has brought them to full term, it grants them a salvific place in the rank of <margin>7</margin>Divine Birth <term>Divine Birth: "theogenesian," the spiritual rebirth or "begetting" of a person into the life of God through the Church</term>, providing them communion with the light-filled and perfecting mysteries. But for now, it separates these uninitiated ones from the final rites, providing for the good order of the sacred things, and acting as a midwife of life and godly order <margin>0</margin> for the catechumens <term>catechumens: those receiving instruction in the faith but not yet baptized</term> through the hierarchical rank.

<margin>H</margin>The multitude of the "energized" <note>original: "energoumenon," referring to those troubled by spirits or internal passions</note> is likewise unequal; it is second in rank after the outermost group of the catechumens.

<margin>O</margin>For it is not the same thing, I believe, to be entirely uninitiated and a stranger to the divine rites, as it is to have held some participation in the most holy sacraments but to be currently ensnared by contrary charms or disturbances. Nevertheless, the vision and communion of the all-holy things is also restricted from these people, and quite rightly so.

## Of Dionysius on Theology, the Divine Work as Summary

<margin>T</margin> ...theology, the divine work <term>divine work: "theourgia," the sacred activity of God through the liturgical rites</term> is the summary. <margin>T</margin> But the regulation of the holy hierarchy allows the catechumens <term>catechumens: individuals receiving instruction in the Christian faith but not yet baptized</term>, the "energized" <note>original: "energoumenous," referring to those troubled by contrary spirits or the "possessed"</note>, and those in a state of penance, to listen to the sacred chanting of the psalms and the divine reading of the most holy scriptures. <margin>E</margin> For if the godlike hierarchy is full of sacred justice and salvifically assigns to each according to their merit, it grants a harmonious participation in divine things to each, bestowing it in due measure and proportion at the proper time. Therefore, the lowest rank is assigned to the catechumens. For they are without a share and uninitiated into every hierarchical rite, not yet possessing a divine existence through the merit of attainment. Instead, they are still being "midwifed" <note>original: "maieuomenoi," the Socratic metaphor for bringing truth or life to birth</note> by the paternal scriptures and are being shaped by life-giving forms toward the life-originating, light-originating, and blessed advancement that comes from the Divine Birth.

<margin>W</margin> For just as infants according to the flesh, if they fall out <note>i.e., are born prematurely or miscarried</note> while still unformed and incomplete, [are deprived] of their proper midwifery...

**I** believe it is necessary for us to go within these most sacred things. We must strip away the mental coverings from the first of the images <note>original: "agalmaton," literally "statues" or "ornaments," here referring to the outward symbols of the ritual</note> to gaze upon its godlike beauty and to behold the bishop <term>bishop: "hierarchen," the leader of the sacred mysteries</term> acting in a divine manner. We see him moving from the divine altar to the furthest edges of the temple, carrying a sweet fragrance <note>the ritual of censing the entire church with incense</note>, and then returning again to the altar to complete the rite. 

For the divine Blessedness <term>Blessedness: "thearchike makariotes," the sovereign and divine state of God</term> that is above all things—even though it goes forth by divine goodness into a sacred communion with those who participate in it—never departs from its own unmoving essence and stable foundation. It shines upon all godlike beings in a proportion suited to each, remaining truly centered within itself and never shifting at all from its own identity. 

In the same way, the divine rite of the Assembly <note>original: "synaxeos," the gathering for the Eucharist</note>, while having a unified, simple, and hidden beginning, is lovingly multiplied into a sacred variety of symbols. It reaches out through the whole range of divine imagery; yet, in a unified way, it is gathered back from these symbols into its own unique unity. It brings into oneness those who are being led toward it in a holy way.

**I**n the same godlike way, the divine bishop, even though he brings his unified knowledge of the Godhead down to those below him by using a multitude of sacred riddles <note>original: "ainigmaton," referring to the mysterious or symbolic nature of the liturgical acts</note>...

## The Mystery of the Assembly, or Communion <note>original: "Synaxis" or "Koinonia"</note>.

<margin>Incense as it circles around the perimeter <note>original Latin: "Incens q m circitu ambit"</note></margin>

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

And first, let us sacredly behold this: <margin>the reason why you indeed call it communion</margin> why it is that this common rite is specifically assigned this name <term>communion: "koinonia," a sharing or fellowship</term> above all others, and is uniquely proclaimed as both "Communion" and "Assembly" <term>assembly: "synaxis," a gathering or coming together</term> of every sacredly-perfecting labor. For though our lives are divided and fragmented, this rite gathers them together into a unified deification <term>deification: "theosis," the process of becoming god-like or being united with the divine</term>, and by folding together our divided parts into a god-like unity, it grants us communion and union with the One. We say, then, that through the participation <margin>there are participations</margin> in the other hierarchical symbols, perfection is achieved through the divine and perfecting gifts of this specific rite.

<margin>according to</margin> **F**or it is almost impossible for any hierarchical rite to be completed unless the most divine Eucharist <note>original: "eucharistia," meaning thanksgiving</note> performs its sacred work—as the summary of each particular rite—of gathering the person being initiated toward the One. Through this divinely-given gift of the perfecting mysteries, the rite brings to fulfillment the person's communion with God.

**I**f, therefore, each of the hierarchical rites remains incomplete and does not fulfill our communion and assembly toward the One—even losing its very nature as a rite by being unfinished—then the goal and the summary of them all is the imparting of the divine mysteries to the one being initiated. Quite rightly, then, hierarchical understanding <margin>hierarchical understanding... wisdom and understanding</margin> found a name for it that reflects the reality of the matter. So it is also with the sacred rite of the "divine birth" <note>original: "theogenesia," usually referring to the sacrament of Baptism</note>; since it imparts light before anything else, and is the beginning of all divine illuminations, it takes its name from the true light <note>The text cuts off here, referring to the "illumination" of the initiate</note>...

# **Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy**

...as a good judge, appropriately bestowing the prizes to those who conquer.

<margin>K</margin> And what is even more divine is this: because He, as a good one, became present among the athletes, He was with them in a sacred way for the sake of their freedom and victory, struggling against the power of death and corruption. The one being initiated will enter into these contests as if they were divine, rejoicing; he remains within the wise legislations <note>original: "nomothesiais," referring here to the "rules of the game" or the divine laws governing the spiritual life</note>, and according to them he will struggle without transgression toward the hope of the beautiful prizes, holding his hope firmly under a good Lord of the prize-giving, and being led by Him. Having stepped into the divine tracks of the "First of the Athletes" <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the pioneer of the faith</note> through His goodness, and participating in these god-imitating struggles, <margin>overcoming</margin> and wrestling down those energies and existences that are contrary to his **deification** <term>deification: "theosis," the process of becoming like God or being united with Him</term>, he dies together with Christ mystically, just as he dies to sin according to **baptism** <term>baptism: the rite of water immersion signifying spiritual rebirth</term>. 

And consider for me intelligently with how much intimacy and appropriateness the sacred things hold their symbols. For among us, death is not a "non-existence" of our essence (as it seems to some others), but rather the separation of things that were once united. It leads the soul into that which is invisible to us—since the soul becomes unseen when deprived of the body—while the body is covered in the earth and disappears from its human form through various physical changes. Appropriately, then, the total covering by water is taken as an image of death and of the invisible burial. Therefore, the symbolic teaching initiates the one being sacredly baptized by the three immersions in the water... <note>The "three immersions" represent the three days Christ spent in the tomb.</note>

# Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

**T**he divine Blessedness <note>The state of divine perfection or God Himself</note> receives the one who is thus led upward <gloss>1</gloss> into his own fellowship, and imparts his own light <gloss>2</gloss> to him as a kind of sign. It makes him godlike and a sharer in the divine fulfillment <gloss>3</gloss> and the sacred order. The sacred symbol of these things is the **seal** <term>seal: "sphragis," a sign of ownership or protection, usually the sign of the cross</term> given by the **hierarch** <term>hierarch: the bishop or high priest leading the ceremony</term> to the one approaching, and the saving registration <gloss>4</gloss> of the sacred ones, which enrolls him among those being saved and places him in the sacred records.

It is the sponsor's role to be a guide <gloss>8</gloss> who does not wander, following the divinely-handed instructions for the one who follows him.

However, it is not possible to participate <gloss>9</gloss> in things that are utterly opposed at the same time. Nor can one who has had a certain fellowship with the One <note>original: "tou henos," the Neo-Platonic and Christian term for God as the ultimate Unity</note> have a divided life, if he holds fast to the firm participation in that One. Rather, he must be unattached and unclassified among all those things that divide the unified state. The sacred tradition of the symbols hints <gloss>11</gloss> at this by stripping <gloss>10</gloss> the one who approaches of his former life, and loosening him from even the last remaining connections <gloss>12</gloss> to it. 

The rite stands him naked and barefoot, looking toward the West <note>The West, where the sun sets, symbolized the realm of darkness and demons in early Christian thought</note>. Then, with the pushing away <gloss>13</gloss> of his hands, he renounces fellowship with the dark wickedness, as if breathing out the habit of dissimilarity that had grown within him, and he makes a total renunciation of everything that is contrary to the godlike state.

He acts neither with jealousy nor with the unholy anger of a former rebellion or lack of moderation <note>referring to the candidate's past life of sin or turning away from God</note>. <margin>A</margin> But since the Divine is the sacred principle of all **good order** <term>good order: "eutaxia," the harmonious arrangement of the universe and the church</term>, according to which the sacred minds are judges of themselves, the one approaching runs back toward the visible character of his own nature. At the beginning, he will see whoever he actually is; and he will receive this first as a sacred gift from the wellspring of light. When he has looked upon his own condition well with eyes that are not clinging to passions, he will depart from the dark mists of ignorance. But because he is still incomplete regarding the most perfect **union** <term>union: "henosis," the ultimate mystical goal of becoming one with God</term> and participation in God, he will not immediately desire it for himself. <margin>
ρ

**T**herefore, even if the symbolic tradition of these ceremonies possessed nothing more divine, it would not be unholy, in my opinion. After he has performed this triple renunciation, the Hierarch leads him toward the **East** <note>The East, the source of light, represents Christ, the "Sun of Righteousness"</note>.

### The Mystery of Enlightenment <note>original: "Mystērion phōtismatos," the common term for the Sacrament of Baptism in the early Church, emphasizing the spiritual light given to the initiate</note>

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

->This is the goal of our hierarchy: our assimilation to and union with <margin>the</margin> God, as far as is possible.<- We may attain this—as the divine words teach us—only through the love and sacred performance of the most venerable commandments. For He says: <note>original: "τηρήσει γάρ φησιν ὁ ἀγαπῶν με τὸν λόγον μου..." quoting John 14:23</note> *“He who loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.”*

What then is the beginning of this sacred performance of the most venerable commandments? It is that which most suitably shapes our soul’s dispositions for the reception of other sacred words and rites, and which prepares our path for the ascent to our heavenly inheritance: the tradition of our sacred and most divine rebirth <note>The author is referring to the Sacrament of Baptism, which he calls 'theoghenesia' or divine birth</note>. For as our famous teacher <note>A reference to Hierotheus, the mentor-figure Dionysius often cites</note> says, the first movement of the mind toward divine things is love for God; and the most foundational step of that sacred love toward the performance of the divine commandments is the most unspeakable, creative act that brings about our divine existence.

**F**or if "divine birth" is the very basis of our divine existence, then no one could ever know the things handed down by God, nor perform them, if they have not first attained this god-like existence. This, I believe, is clear. Next, let us behold the divine aspects of this divine birth.

# Of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

<margin>allotment or inheritance <br/> element or heritage</margin>
**A**nd to the super-mundane and blessed allotments <note>original: "λήξεσιν" (lexesin); refers to the different ranks or orders of heavenly beings</note>, the Godhead grants its light in a more immaterial and intellectual way; for God does not move them toward divine things from the outside, but rather they are illuminated intellectually and from within, as the most divine will shines brightly within them in a clear, pure, and immaterial light. But to us, that which is granted to those heavenly beings in a unified and concentrated way is bestowed from the God-given oracles <term>theoparadota logia: the scriptures and sacred teachings handed down by God</term> according to our own capacity, through a variety and multitude of divided symbols.

**F**or the very essence of our hierarchy is the God-given oracles. By these most venerable oracles, we mean those which have been given to us by our divine initiators <term>hierotelestai: high-ranking clergy or teachers of sacred rites</term> in the hallowed and theological books. And furthermore, we mean those things in which our leaders were initiated by those same holy men through a more immaterial initiation—one that is already a "neighbor," so to speak, to the heavenly hierarchy—passing from mind to mind through the medium of speech; a speech that is indeed corporeal, yet more immaterial than writing, as it exists outside of the written word. Nor did the divine hierarchs deliver these things to the common body of the sacred rite in unveiled meanings, but rather handed them down through sacred symbols. For not everyone is holy, nor, as the oracles say, is knowledge for everyone. Therefore, of necessity, the first leaders of our hierarchy—having been filled with the sacred gift from the super-substantial Godhead, and having been sent forth by the divine goodness to lead that gift forward to those who follow—and they themselves, being divinely and ungrudgingly in love with the progress of their disciples...

## Dionysius concerning...

...[sacred] mediation. For when one speaks of a **Hierarch**, he indicates a man who is inspired and divine, an expert in all sacred knowledge, in whom his own hierarchy is purely perfected and known. The source of this hierarchy is the Fountain of Life, the Essence of Goodness, the unique Holy Trinity of all things, from which existence and "well-being" <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὸ εὖ εἶναι"; a philosophical distinction meaning God gives both the fact of existence and the capacity for a virtuous, flourishing life</note> are granted to all that exists through His goodness.

<margin>1. T</margin>o this most divine Blessedness <note>Greek: "makariotes"; a term for the perfect, happy state of the divine nature</note> beyond all things—the Trinity and the Unity—which truly exists in a way unattainable to us but known to itself, it is His will that there be a rational salvation for both our own natures and for those essences above us <note>The "essences above us" refers to the angelic ranks</note>. This salvation can happen in no other way than through the **deification** <term>theosis: the process of becoming like God and being united with Him as much as humanly possible</term> of those who are being saved. Deification is the attaining of likeness to God and union with Him, as far as is possible. 

The common goal of every hierarchy is a persistent love toward God and divine things, a love that is divinely and uniformly enacted in sacred service. But before this, there must be a complete and unswerving departure from all opposites: **the knowledge of things as they truly are**, the vision and understanding of sacred truth, and the divine participation in the uniform perfection of the One Himself. This is the feast of contemplation which, as far as is possible, intellectually nourishes and deifies everyone who reaches out toward it.

<margin>2. L</margin>et us say, then, that the divine Blessedness—which is Divinity by nature, the source of all deification, and from whose divine goodness comes the deification of those being divinized—has established the hierarchy for the salvation and deification of all rational and intellectual beings.

## On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy

The variety of symbols is multiplied, through which we are led up—in a proportion suitable to our human nature—toward a unified **deification** <note>theosis: the process of becoming like God</note>, toward God and divine virtue. While the pure minds <note>referring to angels</note> understand these things as is lawful for them, we are led up to divine contemplations, as far as we are able, through **sensible images** <note>physical objects used in worship, like bread, wine, or oil, that represent spiritual truths</note>.

<margin>p</margin>
**T**ruly, there is one goal which all god-like beings desire; yet they do not participate in this same and single goal in a uniform way. Instead, the divine scales distribute to each their portion according to their worthiness.

<margin>o</margin>
**B**ut these matters have been discussed more thoroughly by us in the treatise on *The Intelligibles and the Sensibles* <note>a reference to a now-lost or perhaps fictional work by Dionysius exploring the relationship between spiritual concepts and physical objects</note>. Now, I shall attempt to describe our own hierarchy—its origin and its essence—as far as I am able, calling upon **Jesus**, the source and the perfection of all hierarchies.

<margin>Definition of Hierarchy</margin>
**E**very hierarchy, according to the holiness of our tradition, is the complete account of the sacred matters underlying it; it is a most universal summary of the particular hierarchy, or of the things conducted through sacred rites.

**O**ur hierarchy, therefore, is said to be—and truly is—the comprehensive treatment of all the sacred things within it. Through this hierarchy, the divine **Hierarch** <note>The Bishop; the leader who oversees the sacred order</note>, being initiated, shares in all the most sacred things pertaining to himself; hence he is named after the hierarchy <gloss>1</gloss> itself.

<margin>p</margin>
**F**or just as one who mentions "hierarchy" indicates the orderly arrangement of all sacred things together, so "hierarch"...

### Dionysius on the Divine Names.

For you see that we also have not withheld for ourselves any of the hierarchical discourses <note>original: ἱεραρχικῶν λόγων; these are the sacred teachings or doctrines passed down through the church's leadership</note> handed down to us. <margin>Note</margin> <note>original: τ; likely a scribal shorthand for "Sēmeiōsai," meaning "note well."</note> But we have shared them, and will continue to share them, without grudge, both with you and with other holy men. This is so that we might be capable of speaking, and those to whom it is spoken capable of hearing, in no way doing wrong to the tradition—unless, perhaps, we fail in the understanding or the expression of them.

But as for these matters, let them be as they are and be spoken of however it is pleasing to God; and let this be the conclusion of our work concerning the <term>intelligible divine names</term> <note>original: νοηταῖς θεωνυμίαις; names of God that are grasped by the mind and intellect—such as "Goodness" or "Being"—rather than through physical imagery</note>. Under the guidance of God, I shall now move on to the <term>symbolic theology</term> <note>original: συμβολικὴν θεολογίαν; the study of physical metaphors and sensory symbols used in Scripture to describe the Divine, such as God being called a "Rock" or "Fire"</note>.

### Of the Divine Names

...of all things to Him, uniting us in so far as it is possible for us to be united to Him.

<margin>3</margin> <note>original: Γ; the Greek numeral for 3, marking the section.</note> **H**aving gathered these **conceptual names of God** <term>theonyms</term> <note>original: θεωνυμίας; literally "God-names." These are titles used in Scripture to describe God’s attributes.</note>, we have unfolded them as best we could. We have fallen short not only of their true precision—which even the angels would admit of themselves—but also of the angelic songs of praise. For the very best of our <term>theologians</term> <note>original: θεολόγων; in this context, Dionysius refers to the inspired writers of the Bible and the highest Church fathers.</note> fall short of even the lowest of the angels. We have even fallen short of the theologians themselves, their practitioners, and their followers. Indeed, we have fallen short even of those who are our own equals. 

Therefore, if what has been said is correct, and if we have truly grasped the explanation of the divine names with our minds, we must credit the matter to the **Cause of all good things** <note>original: ἀγαθῶν αἴτιον; a Platonic-style title for God as the source of every blessing.</note>. It is He who grants first the ability to speak, and then the ability to speak well. And if anything of equal importance has been left out, we must apply the same methods to understand those things as well.

<margin>5</margin> <note>original: Ε; the Greek numeral for 5.</note> **B**ut if these words are incorrect or incomplete, and if we have wandered from the truth either entirely or in part, it is up to your kindness to correct one who is unintentionally ignorant. Share your knowledge with the one who needs to learn; assist the one who lacks sufficient strength; and heal the one who does not wish to remain in error. Whether you find the answers within yourself or from others, receiving all things from **the Good**, pass them on to us. Do not grow weary of doing a kindness for a friend.

<summary>Dionysius concludes his study of the Divine Names by humbly acknowledging that human language and even angelic praise fall short of God's true nature. He credits God for any insights gained and asks his reader to correct any errors in his work.</summary>

## Dionysius on the Divine <unclear>Names</unclear>

Now number participates in being; but the **super-essential One** <note>original: τὸ δὲ ὑπερούσιον ἓν; the term "super-essential" refers to God existing beyond the very category of "being" or "existence" as humans understand it.</note> defines both the number one and every other number. It is itself the origin and the cause, the numerical principle and the order, of the number one and of every existing thing. 

Therefore, it is praised as both a **Monad** <term>monas</term> <note>original: μονὰς; a philosophical term for the absolute, indivisible Oneness of the Divine.</note> and a **Triad** <term>trias</term> <note>original: τριὰς; referring to the Holy Trinity.</note>, and as the **Divinity** <note>original: θεότης</note> that is above all things. Yet, it is neither a Monad nor a Triad in a way that can be fully grasped by us or by any other being. 

But so that we might truly praise its "super-unified" nature and its divine fruitfulness, we use the divine names of the Triad and the Unity to name the **beyond-name** <note>original: ὑπερώνυμον</note> and **beyond-being** <note>original: ὑπερούσιον</note> according to the things that exist. For no Monad or Triad, no number or unity, no fruitfulness, nor any other thing that exists or can be known, can truly express the **hiddenness** <note>original: κρυφιότητα</note>—which is beyond all things, speech, and mind—of that **Super-divinity** <note>original: ὑπερθεότητος</note> which exists super-essentially above all. 

It has no name and no description. Rather, it is set apart in inaccessible places. We do not even apply the title of "Goodness" itself as if it were a perfect fit; we offer it only out of a **longing** <note>original: πόθῳ; an intense spiritual desire or yearning</note> to understand and say something about that **ineffable nature** <note>original: ἀρρήτου φύσεως</note>. 

We dedicate the most venerable of names to it as a first priority. In this, we may agree with the inspired theologians, but we will always fall short of the truth of the actual reality. Therefore, the theologians themselves have preferred the **ascent through negations** <term>apophasis</term> <note>original: διὰ τῶν ἀποφάσεων ἄνοδον; "Apophatic theology" is the spiritual practice of describing God by what He is NOT (e.g., "infinite" or "not-finite"), acknowledging that God exceeds all positive definitions.</note>. This method lifts the soul out of its familiar surroundings and travels through all the divine concepts—concepts which are themselves surpassed by the Name that is beyond every name, every description, and every knowledge. At the last...

## On the Divine Names

<insert>A. Divine Names</insert>

And the **One** is the fundamental element <note>original: "στοιχειωτικόν"; the basic building block or underlying principle</note> of all things. If you were to take away the One, there would be no whole, no part, nor any other existing thing. For the One has pre-contained and embraced all things within itself in a **unified manner** <note>original: "ἑνοειδῶς"; in the form of a single unity</note>.

**T**herefore, theology praises this entire Divine Origin <term>thearchia</term> <note>original: "θεαρχία"; the "God-head" or the governing principle of the divine</note> as the cause of all things, using the title of "The One." It speaks of "one God and Father," and "one Lord Jesus Christ," and "one and the same Spirit," because of the surpassing simplicity <note>literally "indivisibility"</note> of the entire divine Unity <note>original: "ἑνότητος"</note>. Within this Unity, all things are gathered together in a singular way and are "super-unified." They proceed from it in a way that is beyond being <term>hyperousios</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως"; existing beyond the very category of "being" as humans understand it</note>. Through this Unity, all things are justly returned and dedicated to it. By it, and from it, and through it, and in it, and unto it, all things exist, are ordered, remain, are held together, are fulfilled, and are turned back. 

You would not find a single thing among all that exists which is not what it is, and is not perfected and preserved, by the "One"—which is the name for the entire Divinity <note>original: "θεότης"</note> in its state beyond being. It is necessary for us also to be turned back from the "many" to the "One" by the power of the divine Unity, and to praise the entire and single Divinity in a **unified way** <term>heniaios</term> <note>original: "ἑνιαίως"; in a single, integrated act of worship</note>. This Divinity is the One who is the cause of all; the One who exists before every "one," before every multitude, part, or whole, and before every limit, indefiniteness, boundary, and infinity. It is the One that defines all existing things and defines "being" itself. It is the cause of all things and of the whole—simultaneously before all, above all, and uniquely. It is even beyond the "One" that exists; for the "One" that is found among existing things is a numerical value <note>The author distinguishes between the mathematical number "1" and the Divine Unity which is the source of all numbers.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" from Chapter 13 of Dionysius's work. # Dionysius [Concerning] <unclear>the Divine Names</unclear>

...[source] and overflowing; according to one unceasing, ever-full, and undiminishing provision through which it brings all perfect things to completion and fulfills them with their own perfection.

<margin>E</margin> But if all things exist in a unified way according to the transcendence of a single unity, and if the One is the cause of all things—from which nothing ever departs—then nothing among existing things is without a share in the One. Just as every number participates in the unit <note>original: "μονάδος" (monados); the Monad or the basic number one from which all other numbers are generated</note>, and a "dyad" <note>the number two</note> is called one, and a "decade" <note>the number ten</note> is called one; and a half is one, and a third and a tenth are one; so all things and every part of all things participate in the One. By the existence of the One, all things exist. The Cause of all is not merely "one" among many, but is the defining principle prior to every "one" and every multitude. For no multitude can exist without participating in some way in the One. Rather, that which is many in its parts is one in its underlying subject; and that which is many in number or in its powers is one in its whole. 

<margin>Γ</margin> That which is many in its accidents <term>symbebekota</term> <note>original: "συμβεβηκόσιν"; the non-essential or variable qualities of a thing, like its color or size</note> is one in its species; and that which is many in its species is one in its genus; and that which is many in its outpourings <term>proodois</term> <note>original: "προόδοις"; the "processions" or ways in which the Divine energy flows out into the world</note> is one in its source.

<margin>K</margin> There is nothing among existing things which does not participate in some way in the One which, by its absolute uniqueness, has pre-contained all things and all wholes—including opposites—within its unity. While the One is the cause, it is not itself a multitude; yet the One is the cause of the multitude, just as the unit <note>monad</note> exists prior to every multiplied number. And if one were to suppose that all things are united to each other, then all things would be one in their totality.
<margin>Γ</margin>

Furthermore, it must be understood that unified things are said to be united according to a form <term>eidos</term> <note>the intellectual "look" or essential structure of a thing</note> that is conceived beforehand for each individual thing.

<summary>Dionysius argues that the "One" is the essential foundation of all reality, demonstrating through mathematical and logical analogies that even the most complex multitudes must participate in a singular unity to exist.</summary>

# CHAPTER 13
## Concerning the Perfect and the One

So much for these matters. Let us now proceed to the most fruitful part of our discourse. For theology <note>In this context, Dionysius uses "theology" to mean the study of how God is named in sacred texts.</note> attributes all things—and all things at once—to the Cause of all; it praises Him both as **Perfect** and as **One**.

<margin>P</margin> Now, He is **Perfect** not only because He is self-complete <note>original: "αὐτοτελές" (autoteles); being complete in and of itself without needing anything else</note> and defined by Himself in a single form, and most perfect throughout His whole being, but also because He is "beyond-perfect" <term>hyperteleios</term> <note>original: "ὑπερτελές"; exceeding any concept of completion or perfection that we can imagine</note>, surpassing all things. He sets the boundary for every infinite thing and overflows every limit. He is neither contained nor grasped by anything. Instead, He extends to all things at once and beyond all things with His never-failing gifts and His unmultiplied activities <term>energeiai</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργείαις"; the outward actions or "workings" of God in the world</note>.

<margin>P</margin> Furthermore, He is called **Perfect** because He is without increase and is always perfect, and because He is undiminished—as one who pre-contains all things in Himself...

<summary>Dionysius defines God as "Perfect," arguing that He is not just complete in Himself but "beyond-perfect," acting as the source that limits the infinite and sustains all things through His overflowing power.</summary>

# Dionysius Concerning

<margin>T</margin>hese things, then, must be sung in praise of the Cause that transcends all things. We must address Him as the "Surpassing Holiness," the "Lordship," the "Kingship" that stands above all, and the most "Simple Deity." For from Him, in a single and simultaneous act, there has sprouted and been distributed all unmixed precision <note>The author uses "precision" here to mean the exact, pure nature of things as they were intended to be created.</note> and every kind of pure clarity. From Him comes the entire arrangement and ordering of existing things, which banishes all disharmony, inequality, and lack of proportion <note>original: "ἀσυμμετρίαν" (asymmetrian)</note>. This order takes joy in a well-regulated identity and correctness, embracing all those things deemed worthy to participate in it. Here is found the complete and universal beauty of all good things. Here is all divine Providence <term>pronoia</term> <note>original: "πρόνοια"; the protective care and foresight of God toward His creation</note>, which observes and holds together all that it cares for, giving itself with a goodness that is fitting to its nature, for the purpose of the deification <term>theosis</term> <note>original: "ἐκθέωσιν" (ektheosin); the process of becoming more like God or being "divinized" through His grace</note> of those who are guided by Him.

<margin>B</margin>ecause the Cause of all things is "over-full" of all things—by virtue of His single, transcending excellence—He is praised as the "Holy of Holies" <note>This is a biblical title (from the Hebrew 'Qodesh HaQodashim') used here to show God is the source of all that is sacred.</note> and so on, according to His overflowing causality and His exalted pre-eminence. One might say that just as existing things—whether they be holy, divine, lordly, or kingly—surpass things that do not exist, and just as the things that participate in God are superior to those that do not, so too is the Cause who is "beyond all existing things" established high above all beings. He is the "Unparticipated Cause" <note>original: "ἀμέθεκτος αἴτιος" (amethektos aitios); a philosophical term meaning God gives His gifts to others, but His own essence remains untouched and unshared</note> who stands above all those who participate in Him.

<margin>A</margin>nd so, Sacred Scripture <note>original: "τὰ λόγια" (ta logia); literally "the oracles," the author’s standard term for the Bible</note> calls "holy," "kings," "lords," and "gods" those primary ranks in each order <note>The author is referring to the celestial hierarchy of angels and the high-ranking members of the church.</note> through which...
