# CHAPTER 12
### Concerning Holy of Holies, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, God of Gods.

<margin>1</margin> But since, as I believe, the discussion of those previous matters has reached its proper conclusion, we must now sing the praises of the One who has infinite names <note>original: "ἀπειρώνυμον" (apeironymon); the concept that God's nature is so vast that no single name can contain Him, or that every name applies to Him.</note> as the "Holy of Holies," the "King of those who reign," who reigns "forever and ever," and as "Lord of Lords" and "God of Gods."

<margin>K</margin> And first, we must state what we understand "Self-Holiness" <term>autohagiotes</term> <note>original: "αὐτοαγιότητα"; holiness in its very essence, existing by and of itself rather than being granted by another.</note> to be, as well as what we mean by "Kingship," "Lordship," and "Deity," and what the Holy Scriptures intend to reveal by the doubling of these names <note>Referring to the superlative form of titles like "King of Kings."</note>.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>21</margin> **H**oliness, then, is—to put it in terms we can understand—that purity which is free from any defilement, complete and entirely stainless. Kingship is the distribution of every boundary, every world-order, law, and rank. Lordship is not merely the superiority over those who are lesser; rather, it is the complete and total possession of all things beautiful and good, a true and unchangeable stability. For this reason, the word "Lordship" <note>original: "κυριότης" (kyriotes)</note> is derived from the Greek words for "authority," "validity," and "sovereignty" <note>The author is using a wordplay on "kyros" (authority) to explain the nature of God's Lordship as something that is fundamentally "valid" and "sovereign."</note>. Deity is the Providence that beholds all things, which, in its perfect goodness, "runs around" <note>The author uses a traditional (though linguistically debated) etymology linking "Theos" (God) with "theasthai" (to behold) and "theein" (to run).</note> all things, holding them together, filling them with itself, and yet transcending all those things that enjoy the benefit of its providential care.

<summary>In this chapter, Dionysius defines the supreme titles of God, explaining "Holiness" as absolute purity, "Kingship" as the source of universal order, and "Lordship" as the secure possession of all goodness.</summary>
<keywords>Pseudo-Dionysius, Divine Names, Holiness, Kingship, Lordship, Deity, Providence, purity, sovereignty, etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of divine titles, moving from the definitions of "Holiness," "Kingship," and "Lordship" to a deep metaphysical analysis of "Deity" (Theotes). It transitions from God's singular essence to the "providential powers" through which created things participate in the divine nature.</meta>

-># Of Dionysius, Concerning...<-
<meta>catchword: [untranslated Greek fragment]</meta>
<sig>1</sig>

...we speak of **Deity** <note>original: "θεότητά" (theoteta)</note>. In a primordial, divine, and causal sense, we use this term to describe the one Source and Cause of all things—a Source that is "supra-primordial" <term>hyperarchion</term> <note>existing before and above any worldly beginning or principle.</note> and "beyond-being" <term>hyperousion</term>. 

In a "participated" sense, however, we use this term for the providential powers that flow out from the God who cannot be shared <note>original: "ἀμεθέκτου" (amethektou); the theological concept that God's essence remains transcendent even as His actions touch the world.</note>. These powers include **Self-Substantiality**, **Self-Life**, and **Self-Deification**. It is by participating in these—each according to its own nature—that existing things are, and live, and are "god-filled." Thus, they not only exist but are also *called* existing, living, and divine. Because of this, the "Good Author of Being" <note>original: "ἀγαθὸς ὑποστάτης" (agathos hypostates)</note> is said to be the very first of these powers.

<margin>E</margin> This applies first to these powers in their entirety, then to their specific parts; then to those beings which participate in them wholly, and finally to those that participate in them only partially. 

And why is it necessary to speak of these things? For some of our sacred teachers <note>Refers to the "Hierodidaskaloi," specifically the author's mentor Hierotheus.</note> claim that the "Supra-Good" and "Supra-Divine" One is the Author of "Self-Goodness" and "Self-Deity." They say that "Self-Goodness" and "Deity" are actually the "good-making" and "divine-making" gift that has proceeded from God. They speak also of **Self-Beauty** as a "Self-Beautifying Outpouring," and describe "total beauty," "partial beauty," things that are "wholly beautiful," and things "beautiful in part." 

All such terms, whether already mentioned or yet to be spoken, reveal the providences and goodnesses that are shared by existing things. These flow out from the unshared God in an ungrudging and overflowing stream, so that the Cause of all things may truly remain "beyond." This ensures that His "beyond-being" and "beyond-nature" transcends every single thing, regardless of its specific essence or nature.

***

**Vocabulary for this section:**
*   **Dionysius:** The purported author, Dionysius the Areopagite.
*   **Deity:** The divine nature or the state of being God.
*   **Beyond-being:** <term>hyperousios</term>; that which exists above the very category of "existence."
*   **Providential:** Relating to God's care and guidance of the universe.
*   **Self-Substantiality:** The power of existence existing in itself.
*   **Self-Life:** The power of life existing in itself.
*   **Self-Deification:** The process by which a creature is made divine through grace.
*   **Author of Being:** The one who gives substance or reality to a thing.
*   **Sacred Teachers:** The authorities of the early Church.
*   **Good-making:** The act of bestowing goodness upon a creature.

And first, so that we may once again take up what has been said ten thousand times before: it is not a contradiction to call God 'Power-itself' or 'Life-itself,' and also the 'Author' of Life-itself, or of Peace, or of Power. On the other hand, He is named as the one who is **Beyond-being** <term>hyperousiōs</term>, existing above all things and even above the primary things.

Nor is there any other life-giving deity besides the **Beyond-God** <note>original: "ὑπέρθεον" (hypertheon)</note>, who is the Life that causes Life-itself and all living things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Divine Peace. The previous page ended with Christ reconciling humanity to God and establishing peace. This section addresses a potential objection: how can "Peace" be the goal of everything if some things seem to prefer being different or moving around? Dionysius argues that even difference and motion are forms of internal peace.</meta>

### [Of Divine Names]

<margin>Ξ</margin> ...unity and remains—by the transcendence of union—whole with respect to the whole and, through the whole, united to itself in a way that transcends all connection. But how might someone say that all things long for peace? For many things delight in **difference** and **distinction**, and would never willingly choose to be at rest. If, by "difference" and "distinction," the <margin>Ξ</margin> one saying this means the <term>unique identity</term> <note>original: "ἰδιότητα" (idiotēta); referring to the specific set of characteristics that makes a thing what it is and not something else.</note> of each existing thing, and that no existing thing ever wishes to lose its own nature, we would not object to this either. Rather, we would declare that even this is a longing for peace. For all things love to be at peace and united with themselves—with their own properties and their own belongings—and they desire to be unshakable and stable. Indeed, perfect Peace is the guardian of the unmixed identity of each individual thing. Through her <term>peace-giving providences</term> <note>original: "εἰρηνοδώροις... προνοίαις"; the idea that God’s care (providence) actively distributes peace to maintain the order of the universe.</note> she preserves all <margin>Τ</margin> things undisturbed and unconfused, both within themselves and toward one another. She establishes all things in a steady and unyielding power to maintain their own peace and lack of disturbance.

**A**nd if all things in motion do not wish to be at rest, but instead desire to always move with their own particular motion, even in this there is a longing for the Divine Peace of the universe. This Peace preserves all things so they do not fall away from themselves. It guards the unique character and the <term>vital motion</term> <note>original: "κινητικὴν ζωήν" (kinētikēn zōēn); the "life of movement," referring to the natural activities and internal drives of living or celestial beings.</note> of <margin>Α</margin> all moving things, keeping them unshakable and stable so that these moving things remain at peace with themselves and act according to their own natures in a consistent way.

<summary>Dionysius explains that "Peace" is not just the absence of movement, but the internal stability that allows a thing to keep its unique identity. Even things that move or seem "different" are seeking peace by trying to remain consistently themselves.</summary>

# CHAPTER 10

## Concerning the Almighty; the Ancient of Days; in which also concerning Eternity and Time.

<margin>1</margin>
**It** is now time for our discourse to praise the many-named **God** as the **Almighty** <note>original: "παντοκράτορα" (pantokratora); literally "All-Ruler" or "All-Sovereign."</note> and as the **Ancient of Days**. He is called by the former title because He is the "almighty foundation" <note>original: "παντοκρατορικὴν ἕδραν" (pantokratorikēn hedran); a "seat" or "base" that supports the weight of all creation.</note> of all things, containing and encompassing the whole; establishing, grounding, and binding it together, making the universe an unbreakable whole within Himself. He brings forth all things from Himself as if from an almighty root, and turns all things back to Himself as if to an almighty depth. He holds them together as an all-encompassing, all-powerful seat, keeping all things that are held together in a single, supreme embrace. He secures them and does not allow them to fall away from Him and perish, as they would if they moved away from their absolute Cause.

<margin>The</margin>
**Godhead** <term>Godhead</term> <note>original: "θεαρχία" (thearchia); specifically the "divine origin" or "divine principle."</note> is called **Almighty** because it rules over all things, presiding over those it governs with a pure and unmixed authority. It is also because He is the object of longing and desire for all, placing upon all things "willing yokes" and "sweet pangs" <note>A poetic reference to the soul's yearning for God as a burden that is joyful to bear.</note> of that divine, almighty, and unbreakable love <note>original: "ἔρωτος" (erōtos); Dionysius famously uses this term for divine love, which was more often associated with passionate desire in secular Greek.</note> which flows from His goodness.

<summary>Dionysius explains the divine title "Almighty," describing God as the central root and foundation that holds all of creation together and prevents it from dissolving into nothingness. He further characterizes God's rule not as a harsh tyranny, but as a magnetic, loving force that creation willingly follows.</summary>

### Of Dionysius concerning <unclear>the Divine Names</unclear>

...and by the providential approaches and activities directed toward all beings. But we must also allow our discourse to praise, in a manner befitting God, the motions of the unmoved **God**. The **straight** <note>original: "εὐθὺ" (euthy)</note> motion must be understood as the unswerving and undeviating progression of His activities, and the generation of all things from Him.

**The spiral** <note>original: "ἑλικοειδὲς" (helikoeides)</note> motion signifies the steady progression and the productive stability. 

**The circular** <note>original: "κατὰ κύκλον" (kata kyklon)</note> motion signifies "sameness," and the way He contains both the middle points and the extremities—both encompassing and being encompassed—maintaining the whole, and the return <term>return</term> <note>original: "ἐπιστροφήν" (epistrophēn); in Neoplatonic thought, this is the process where all created things "turn back" toward their divine source to find fulfillment.</note> of those things that have proceeded from Him back to Himself.

**If** anyone should take the divine name of the "Same" <note>The author is referring to the concept of God as unchanging or identical to Himself.</note> or the name of **Justice** <note>original: "δικαιοσύνης" (dikaiosynēs)</note> to mean **Equal**, we must say that **God** is **Equal**. He is so not only as being indivisible and undeviating, but also as proceeding equally to all things and through all things. He is the very substance of Equality-itself, according to which He brings about, in a manner like unto Himself, the mutual interaction of all things. He provides an equal share to those who participate in Him, according to the capacity <note>original: "ἐπιτηδειότητα" (epitēdeiotēta); this refers to the "fitness" or "receptivity" of a creature to receive divine grace.</note> of each. He bestows the divine gift upon all things equally according to their worth. We also mean that He has pre-embraced within Himself—in a transcendent and unified way—every kind of equality (whether intellectual, rational, sensible, essential, or natural) according to His creative power, which produces every kind of equality and is beyond them all.

<summary>Dionysius explains how the "unmoved" God can be said to move in straight, spiral, and circular ways to create and sustain the world, and defines God's Justice as an "Equality" that distributes gifts to all creatures according to their capacity.</summary>

<header>Of the Divine Names.</header>

# Of the Divine Names.

...He says <note>Referring to the author's source or the internal logic of the argument.</note> that the discourse is not contrary to the likeness toward Him; for the same things are both similar and dissimilar to **God**. They are similar according to the possible participation in the Unparticipated; they are dissimilar according to how the effects fall short of the Cause, being left behind by infinite and incomparable measures.

**A**nd what do we mean by the divine stability, or rather, the "seat"? What else than that **God** remains within Himself? He is fixed permanently in an unmoving identity, firmly established and immovably set, acting according to the same things, around the same things, and in the same way. He exists entirely from Himself according to His unchangeability, being immovable and totally unmoving—and these things He is in a way that is beyond being <term>beyond being</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs); This describes a state of existence that transcends the very category of "being" as understood by humans.</note>. For He is the cause of the stability and the "seat" <note>The "seat" or "throne" is a traditional metaphor for God’s sovereign rest and permanence.</note> of all things; He who is above every seat and stability, and in Him all things consist, being preserved as unshakable within the stability of their own inherent goods. 

But what of it when the theologians <note>Likely referring to the writers of Holy Scripture.</note> again say that the Unmoved One proceeds toward all things and is in motion? This too must be understood in a manner befitting God. For we must piously think of Him as moving, not according to transit, or alteration, or change, or turning, or local motion—neither the straight, nor the circular, nor the motion composed of both, nor the intellectual, nor the psychic, nor the physical—but rather that **God** brings all things into being <note>original: "εἰς οὐσίαν ἄγειν" (eis ousian agein); literally "to lead into essence."</note>, holds all things together, provides for all things in every way, and is present to all by the unconstrained embrace of all.

<summary>This page explains how God remains perfectly stable and "unmoved" in His essence while simultaneously "moving" through His providence to sustain the universe. It reconciles the paradox of God being both similar to His creation (through participation) and infinitely dissimilar (as the transcendent Cause).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Divine Names from Chapter 9 of "The Divine Names." # Of Dionysius on

6. Regarding the fact that **God** is called "Like": In one sense, as one might say He is "the Same," as being permanently and indivisibly like Himself through and through, we must not disregard the divine name <term>divine name</term> <note>Dionysius treats various titles for God found in Scripture—like "Same," "Like," or "Different"—as "names" that reveal something about the divine nature.</note> "Like."

<margin>But</margin> the theologians <note>original: "θεολόγοι" (theologoi); here referring to the biblical writers.</note> say that God, who is beyond all, is in Himself like to nothing; however, they say He grants a divine likeness to those who turn toward Him by imitating, according to their capacity, Him who is beyond all limit and reason. And the power of this divine likeness is that which turns all created things back toward their Cause.

<margin>These</margin> things, then, must be called "like God," and according to the divine image and likeness <note>A reference to Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image and likeness."</note>; yet God is not like them, any more than a man is like his own image. For among those things of the same rank, it is possible for them to be like one another, and for the likeness to be reciprocal on both sides—where both are like each other according to a previously existing form of likeness. But in the case of the Cause and the effects <note>The "Cause" is God; the "effects" are the things He created.</note>, we do not accept this reciprocity. For He does not grant the quality of being like only to this thing or that, but He is the Cause of being like for all who participate in Likeness. God is the substantiator <term>substantiator</term> <note>original: "ὑποστάτης" (hypostatēs); the one who gives underlying reality or substance to a quality.</note> of Likeness-Itself, and every likeness in all things is like a certain trace of the divine Likeness, which completes their unity. And what more is there to say? For theology itself proclaims that He is "Unlike" and is disconnected from the universe, being different from all things, and—what is even more paradoxical—that there is nothing at all like Him.

<note>This passage argues that while we can be "like" God by imitating Him, God cannot be "like" us because He is the unique source. A reflection in a mirror is "like" the person standing before it, but the person is not "like" the reflection; the person is the original reality.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the divine name "Like," explaining that while creation reflects God’s likeness to return to Him, God remains uniquely "Unlike" and incomparable to His creations. It establishes a one-way relationship where God is the source of all likeness without being defined by His effects.</summary>

# ->Of Divine Names<-

->n iii<-

**J**ust as our discourse fashioned the soul itself in a bodily form, and modeled bodily parts for that which has no parts, we understand the components assigned to it in a manner appropriate to the soul’s partless nature. 

<margin>k</margin> <margin>o</margin> **W**e called the intellect <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous); the highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual insight.</note> the "head," and opinion <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa); a level of awareness situated between rational logic and irrational instinct.</note> the "neck," as it stands in the middle between reason and irrationality. We called anger the "chest," desire the "belly," and we termed nature the "legs and feet," using the names of body parts as symbols for various powers. Much more so, regarding Him who is beyond all things, it is necessary that the variety of forms and shapes be purified by holy, god-befitting, and mystical explanations.

<margin>T</margin> <margin>k</margin> **A**nd if you wish to apply the three dimensions of bodies to the intangible and shapeless God: 

<margin>p</margin> **D**ivine **breadth** must be called the vast procession <term>procession</term> <note>original: "πρόοδος" (proodos); the way God’s presence and energy "go forth" into the created world.</note> of God over all things; **length** is the power extending over the whole of reality; and **depth** is the hiddenness and unknowing <term>unknowing</term> <note>original: "ἀγνωσία" (agnosia); the spiritual state of moving beyond intellectual concepts to encounter the mystery of God.</note> which is incomprehensible to all beings.

<margin>a</margin> **B**ut we must take care that we do not deceive ourselves by confusing the incorporeal divine names <note>original: "θεωνυμίαι" (theonymiai); the specific titles used to describe God in scripture.</note> with those descriptions of different shapes and forms derived from the senses.

<margin>d</margin> **T**herefore, while these matters have been discussed in the *Symbolic Theology* <note>A work by Dionysius—either lost or intended as a reference—dedicated to explaining the physical metaphors for God found in the Bible.</note>, we must not now suspect "divine difference" to be some kind of alteration of His unchangeable identity. Rather, we should view it as His unified multiplication <term>multiplication</term> <note>original: "πολυπλασιασμός" (polyplasiasmos); the paradoxical idea that the one God remains a unity while being present in many different created things.</note> and the single-form processions of His many-birthing fertility <note>original: "πολυγονία" (polygonia); the creative fruitfulness of God.</note> toward all things...

It warns against taking these physical descriptions literally, pointing instead to God's "unified multiplication" across the created order.</summary>

# Of Dionysius concerning...

**T**he **Same** <term>sameness</term> <note>original: "ταυτὸν" (tauton); referring to God’s absolute self-identity and consistency.</note> in a manner **beyond all being** <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs); an adverb describing how God exists above and beyond the category of "being" or "substance."</note> is eternal, immutable, and remains always within itself. It exists according to the same principles, being present to all things in the same way, and is itself by itself, firmly and purely established in itself within the most beautiful limits of the super-essential identity. It is unchangeable and cannot fall from its state; it is unwavering, unalterable, unmixed, and immaterial. 

**I**t is most simple, needing nothing, without increase and without decrease. It is **unbegotten** <note>original: "ἀγέννητον" (agennēton); meaning not created or brought into existence by another.</note>—not in the sense of not yet having come into being, or being incomplete, or not being born from this or that source; nor in the sense of being absolutely non-existent. Rather, it is unbegotten in a way that is above all things and absolutely unbegotten. It is eternally being, and is a perfect being in itself. It is the "Same" through itself, being defined singularly and uniformly by itself. 

**T**his Sameness shines forth from itself upon all those things capable of participating in it, and it coordinates different things with one another. It is the abundance and the cause of identity, containing even opposites within itself according to the single and unique transcending cause of the whole identity.

**T**he **Other** <term>otherness</term> <note>original: "ἕτερον" (heteron); here used to explain how the one God manifests in many different ways in the world.</note> is spoken of because God is present to all things through His providence, and becomes all things in all for the salvation of all. Yet, He remains within Himself and never departs from His own proper identity in a single, unceasing act. He stands firm and gives Himself with an unwavering power for the **deification** <term>deification</term> <note>original: "ἐκθέωσιν" (ektheōsin); the process by which a person is transformed and united with God’s grace.</note> of those who turn toward Him. We must believe that the "otherness" of the various shapes and forms of God in the many-sided visions of Him signifies something different from what appears to the eyes.

<summary>This page discusses the divine attributes of "Sameness" and "Otherness," explaining how God remains eternally unchanging and self-identical while simultaneously manifesting in diverse ways through His providence.</summary>

### Of the Divine Names
->n ii<-

...is able, and beyond every **greatness** <note>original: "μεγέθους" (megethous); referring to God’s attribute of Greatness/Magnitude.</note>, He is overflowing and extending beyond. He contains every place; He exceeds every number; He traverses every infinity. This is according to His super-abundance and His **mighty-working** <term>magnificence</term> <note>original: "μεγαλουργόν" (megalourgon); God's power to perform great and creative acts.</note>, and His **source-like gift** <note>original: "πηγαίας... δωρεᾶς" (pēgaias dōreas); implying that God’s grace flows like an inexhaustible spring or fountain.</note>. Insofar as these gifts are shared by all through an ungrudging pouring-forth, they remain entirely undiminished. They possess the same super-fullness and are not lessened by those who participate in them; rather, they overflow all the more.

<margin>T</margin> This greatness is both infinite and without quantity; it is beyond number. This is the **pre-eminence** <note>original: "ὑπεροχή" (hyperochē); the state of being supreme or surpassing all categories.</note> according to the absolute and over-extended nature of His ungraspable majesty.

<margin>S</margin> **Smallness**, or rather **subtlety** <note>original: "λεπτόν" (lepton); literally "fine" or "thin." In this context, it describes God's ability to be present in the most minute details of existence without being bulky or physical.</note>, is spoken of Him as that which has moved away from all bulk and distance, and which passes through all things without hindrance. Indeed, He is the **elementary cause** <term>constituent principle</term> <note>original: "στοιχειωτικόν αἴτιον" (stoicheiōtikon aition); the cause that provides the fundamental elements for everything else.</note> of all things. You will nowhere find the "idea" of smallness to be without participation in Him. This, then, is how "smallness" must be understood in God: as that which reaches into everything and through all things without obstruction. It is **active and reaches even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart** <note>The author is quoting the New Testament (Hebrews 4:12) to show that God's "smallness" is His ability to penetrate the innermost parts of a person.</note>. Or rather, He reaches through all beings; for there is no creature hidden from His sight.

<margin>T</margin> This "smallness" is without quantity and without magnitude. It is uncontainable, infinite, and undefined—containing all things, while being itself uncontained.

It emphasizes that God's gifts are inexhaustible and are not diminished when shared with creatures.</summary>

# CHAPTER 9

## Concerning Great, Small, Same, Other, Like, Unlike, Rest, Motion, and Equality

**S**ince Greatness and Smallness are attributed to the Cause of all things—as are Sameness and Otherness, Likeness and Unlikeness, and Rest and Motion—come then, let us behold as many of these **images of the Divine Names** <note>original: "θεωνυμικῶν ἀγαλμάτων" (theonymikōn agalmatōn); Dionysius uses the word for 'statues' or 'icons' to describe how names represent God.</note> as are manifest to us. God is praised as **Great** in the **Holy Scriptures** <note>original: "λογίοις" (logiois); literally 'oracles' or 'divine utterances,' referring to the Bible.</note> and in magnitude. He is also praised in the **gentle breeze** <note>original: "αὔρα λεπτῇ" (aura leptē); a reference to 1 Kings 19:12, where God appears to Elijah not in a wind or earthquake, but in a 'still small voice' or thin breeze.</note> which manifests the divine smallness. He is called **The Same** when the Scriptures say, "But you are the same." He is called **Other** when He is fashioned by the same Scriptures as being of many forms and many shapes. He is called **Like** insofar as He is the **Originator** <term>Substantial Producer</term> <note>original: "ὑποστάτης" (hypostatēs); the one who gives underlying existence or substance to things.</note> of all like things and of likeness itself. Yet He is also **Unlike** all things, because there is nothing that is His equal. He is described as **Standing**, **Motionless**, and **Sitting forever** <note>original: "εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα" (eis ton aiōna); into the age or eternity.</note>, and yet also as **Moving**, as if proceeding into all things. These, and any other **Divine Names** <term>Names of God</term> <note>original: "θεωνυμίαι" (theonymiai).</note> of similar power, are praised by the Scriptures.

**G**od is indeed called **Great** according to His own particular greatness, which imparts itself to all great things...

<margin>E</margin> And regarding this **salvation** <note>original: "σωτηρία" (sōtēria)</note>, it is not beside the mark for someone to praise **sacred theology**; for it describes how all things are redeemed from the falling away of their own proper goods by the **saving goodness** of the All. This occurs to the extent that the nature of each being that is saved allows. Therefore, the theologians also call it **redemption** <term>Liberation from Lack</term> <note>original: "ἀπολύτρωσιν" (apolytrōsin); while often translated as 'redemption,' it carries the sense of a 'loosing away' from a state of bondage or deficiency.</note>, insofar as it does not allow things that truly exist to fall away into non-existence. Or rather, it establishes it in the good, filling up the good that had ebbed away, ordering and adorning its disorder and lack of ornament, making it complete once more and releasing it from all its defects.
<margin>A</margin> But these things have been spoken of, along with **justice** <note>original: "δικαιοσύνης" (dikaiosynēs)</note>, according to which the **equality** <note>original: "ἰσότης" (isotēs)</note> of all things is measured and defined, and all inequality—which arises from a privation of the equality inherent in each thing—is banished. For if one were to take "inequality" to mean the differences of the parts within the whole, justice is also the guardian of this, not permitting all things, once they are mixed together among the whole...

# Dionysius on

...those who desire certain things, when they obtain the objects of their desire—do they not then more closely approach the **angelic virtues** <note>original: "ἀγγελικαῖς ἀρεταῖς" (angelikais aretais)</note>? This happens when, as much as possible, they withdraw from attachment to material things through a desire for the divine, exercising themselves most **manfully** <note>original: "ἀνδρικῶς" (andrikōs); in this context, it implies a courageous or vigorous strength of spirit.</note> in the circumstances provided by the **Beautiful**. Thus, it is true to say that this is a specific property of **Divine Justice**: it does not charm or destroy the **masculine vigor** <note>original: "ἀῤῥενότητα" (arrhenotēta); referring to the strength and integrity of the soul.</note> of the best souls by providing them with material rewards. Nor does it leave them without help if someone attempts to do this, but rather it establishes them in a beautiful and unrelenting stability, and allots to such individuals what they deserve according to their merit.

<margin>A</margin> This, then, is **Divine Justice** <note>original: "θεία δικαιοσύνη" (theia dikaiosynē)</note>. It is also praised as the **salvation of all things** <note>original: "σωτηρία τῶν ὅλων" (sōtēria tōn holōn)</note>, for it preserves and guards the unique and pure essence and order of each thing, keeping it distinct from others. It is purely the cause of **self-operation** <term>Minding one’s own business</term> <note>original: "ἰδιοπραγίας" (idiopragias); a Platonic concept where justice is defined as every part of a system performing its own specific function without interfering with others.</note> throughout the whole of creation.

<margin>E</margin> But if someone should praise salvation as that which rescues all things from the effects of **time** <note>original: "χρόνων" (chronōn)</note> in a saving manner, we shall certainly accept this singer of many-sided salvation as well. Let us deem him worthy to define this primary salvation of all things as that which preserves everything within itself—**unchangeable** <note>original: "ἀμετάβλητα" (ametablēta)</note>, **without faction** <note>original: "ἀστάσιαστα" (astasiasta)</note>, and **without inclination** <note>original: "ἀῤῥεπῆ" (arrhepē)</note> toward what is worse. It guards all things so they are ordered without battle or conflict, each governed by its own internal **principles** <note>original: "λόγοις" (logois); the rational blueprints or ratios that define a thing's nature.</note>. Finally, it excludes all inequality and **interference** <term>Meddling in others' affairs</term> <note>original: "ἀλλοτριοπραγίαν" (allotriopragian); the opposite of idiopragia, referring to things overstepping their bounds or losing their proper nature.</note> from the whole of the universe.

<summary>Pseudo-Dionysius explains that Divine Justice acts as a "salvation" by ensuring every being maintains its own unique nature and purpose without interfering with others. He emphasizes that this divine order preserves the stability of the universe and protects the soul from being weakened by material distractions.</summary>

# On Divine Names

...keeping all things distinct and unconfused from one another, it grants to all beings that which belongs to each, according to the **merit** <note>original: "ἀξίαν" (axian); in this context, it refers to the status or "fittingness" of a creature's nature within the cosmic hierarchy.</note> belonging to each of the beings.

<margin>K</margin> Because of this, we are correct to say that those who revile **Divine Justice** <note>original: "θείᾳ δικαιοσύνῃ" (theia dikaiosynē)</note> are unaware that they are pronouncing a clear judgment of injustice against themselves. For they claim that **immortality** <note>original: "ἀθανασίαν" (athanasian)</note> should belong to mortals, and perfection to the imperfect. They suggest that those who are moved by others should instead possess a **self-moving necessity** <note>original: "αὐτοκινήτοις τὴν ἑτεροκίνητον ἀνάγκην"</note>, and that identity should belong to the changeable, or complete power to the weak. They wish for things in time to be eternal, for things naturally in motion to be unchangeable, and for fleeting pleasures to be everlasting. In short, they try to assign the attributes of one nature to another.

<margin>Δ</margin> But it must be known that Divine Justice is truly real justice in this: that it assigns to all their own things according to the merit of each of the beings, and preserves the nature of each according to its own **rank and power** <note>Dionysius argues that it would be "unjust" to force a creature to be something it is not.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> But someone might say: "It is not an act of justice to allow holy men to be left without help while being worn down by the wicked." I do not know how they could even be called holy, for they do wrong to the things that are truly worthy of love—the divine things—by casting them aside in favor of things that are envied but ultimately unlovable. However, if they truly love the things that **really exist** <note>Referring to spiritual realities rather than physical shadows.</note>, they should rejoice...

<summary>Dionysius defends Divine Justice against critics by arguing that it preserves the natural order of all things according to their merit. He explains that the suffering of the righteous is not an injustice, as true holiness seeks spiritual rather than material rewards.</summary>

Often, such weak people imagine that they have opponents—conceived according to their own fantasies—and they shadowbox bravely against those who are not even there. # On the Divine Names

# Of Dionysius

...or possesses an essential power; and indeed, if it is permissible to say so, Being itself <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι" (to einai); Dionysius is arguing that the very concept of "existence" is a form of power granted by God.</note> is power. For existence itself holds its being from the **super-essential power** <note>original: "ὑπερουσίου δυνάμεως" (hyperousiou dynameōs); power that is beyond any category of being or essence.</note>. From this power come the god-like powers of the **angelic ranks** <note>original: "ἀγγελικῶν διακόσμων" (angelikōn diakosmōn); the structured "orders" or "arrangements" of angels that Dionysius describes in his other famous work, *The Celestial Hierarchy*.</note>; from it they also possess their being in an unchanging way. All their intellectual and immortal movements-without-end, their steadfastness, and their undiminished desire for the Good, they have received from the **super-good power**. It is this power that grants them the ability to be these things, to desire to be always, and even the power to desire the <insert>seemingly</insert> impossible <note>This refers back to the paradox mentioned on the previous page: the power to reach for things that are beyond the natural capacity of a created being.</note>.

<margin>P</margin> The gifts of this inexhaustible power proceed also to humans, animals, and plants, and to the whole nature of the universe. It empowers things that are joined together toward mutual friendship and communion; it also empowers things that are distinct so that each exists according to its own **proper reason and limit** <note>original: "λόγον καὶ ὅρον" (logon kai horon); the defining logic and boundaries that make a thing what it is.</note>, keeping them unconfused and unmixed. It preserves the orders and the well-being of the whole universe, directing them toward their own proper good.

<margin>K</margin> It guards the immortal lives of the **angelic unities** <note>original: "ἀγγελικῶν ἑνάδων" (angelikōn henadōn); refers to the angels as unified beings who reflect the "One" (God).</note> unharmed. It keeps the heavenly, light-bearing, and star-like essences and orders unchangeable. It enables eternity to exist. It governs the **many-turning cycles of time** <note>original: "πολυελίξεις" (polyelixeis); literally "many-windings" or "spirals," referring to the complex orbits of planets and the seasons.</note>, distinguishing them by their progressions yet drawing them back together in their **restoration** <note>original: "ἀποκαταστάσεσιν" (apokatastasesin); the "return" or "reconstitution" of all things to their original state in God.</note>. It makes the powers of fire unquenchable and the flowings of water inexhaustible; it defines the spreading of the air...

<summary>Dionysius describes God's power as the source of all existence, sustaining the unchanging immortality of angels and the harmonious balance of the physical elements (fire, water, air). This power is what maintains the boundaries between different types of beings while drawing the entire universe back toward its divine source.</summary>

# On the Divine Names, 4 <note>While the heading says "4" (Δ), this text corresponds to Chapter 7, section 4 of Dionysius’s treatise in standard modern editions.</note>

# Of Dionysius, concerning <gloss>the Divine Names</gloss> <unclear>the remainder of the title is faded</unclear> ⊕

God is known both through all things and apart from all things; through knowledge and through **unknowing** <term>unknowing</term> <note>original: "ἀγνωσίας" (agnosias); a central concept in Dionysius's theology where God is "known" by moving beyond intellectual concepts into a state of mystical silence.</note>. Of Him, there is intellection, reason, science, touch, sensation, opinion, imagination, a name, and all other things. Yet He is neither thought, nor spoken, nor named; He is not any of the things that exist, nor is He known in any existing thing. He is all things in all, and nothing in any; He is known to all from all things, and to no one from nothing.

<margin>K</margin>
**F**or indeed, we say these things correctly concerning God. He is praised from all existing things according to the **analogy** <note>original: "ἀναλογίαν" (analogian); the principle that the created world reflects the nature of its Creator in proportion to its own capacity.</note> of all things of which He is the cause. <margin>Γ</margin> And again, the most divine knowledge of God is that which is known through unknowing, according to the **union beyond the mind** <note>original: "ὑπὲρ νοῦν ἕνωσιν" (hyper noun henōsin); a state where the soul transcends its own rational faculties to be joined directly to God.</note>. For she is, according to the **Oracle** <note>original: "λόγιον" (logion); Dionysius uses this term to refer to the Holy Scriptures.</note>, the maker of all, forever harmonizing all things, the cause of the unbreakable connection and order of the universe, always joining the ends of the first things to the beginnings of the second, and cultivating the single **concord** <note>original: "σύμπνοιαν" (sympnoian); literally a "breathing together," describing the organic unity of the created order.</note> and harmony of the whole.

<margin>Λ</margin>

<summary>Dionysius explains that God is known both through the study of creation (positive theology) and by stripping away all concepts in a state of "unknowing" (negative theology). # <gloss>Of the Divine Names, Chapter 4</gloss> <note>Though the header indicates "4," the text corresponds to Chapter 7 of the treatise.</note>

...both knowing and producing. For indeed, since God imparts being to all things according to a single cause, by that same singular cause He will know all things as existing from Him and pre-existing in Him. And He does not take His knowledge from existing things; rather, He Himself is the provider of knowledge for each thing, and of the knowledge others have of those things.

<margin>O</margin>
Therefore, God does not have a private knowledge of Himself and a separate, common knowledge that encompasses all existing things. For if the Cause of all things knows itself, it could hardly be ignorant of the things that come from it and of which it is the cause.

<margin>T</margin>
In this way, then, God knows existing things—not by a science derived from the things themselves, but by His own nature. For they say that even the angels know the things on the earth, not by perceiving them through the senses (though they are sensible things), but by a power and nature suited to a **god-like** <term>god-like</term> <note>original: "θεοειδοῦς" (theoeidous); describing an intellect that has been shaped into the likeness of God and thus shares in His way of knowing.</note> mind.

<margin>E</margin>
In addition to these points, one must ask how we know God, who is neither an object of thought nor of sense, nor is He at all numbered among existing things. Perhaps, then, it is true to say that we know God, but not from His nature—for that is unknown and surpasses all reason and mind—but from the arrangement of all existing things. This order has been brought forth from Him and contains certain images and likenesses of His divine **paradigms** <term>paradigms</term> <note>original: "παραδειγμάτων" (paradeigmaton); the eternal "models" or ideas in the mind of God according to which the universe is patterned.</note>. It is through this arrangement that we are led toward Him...

<margin>Δ</margin>
...on a path and in an order according to our capacity, through the **removal** <term>removal</term> <note>original: "ἀφαιρέσει" (aphairesei); the "apophatic" method of reaching God by stripping away all created concepts and names.</note> and the **pre-eminence** <term>pre-eminence</term> <note>original: "ὑπεροχῇ" (hyperochē); the understanding that God possesses all qualities in a way that infinitely transcends our definitions.</note> of all things, and in the Cause of all. Because of this, God is known in all things.

<summary>Dionysius explains that God knows the world through His own nature as its Cause, rather than by observing created things. He establishes that humans know God not through His essence, but by observing the "order" of creation and then transcending that order through negation and excellence.</summary>

## Dionysius on the <unclear>Divine Names</unclear>

...[knowing] in a way that is transcendently established. And yet the Scriptures <note>original: "τὰ λόγια" (ta logia); literally "the oracles," referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> say that He knows all things and that nothing escapes the divine knowledge. But as I have often said, we must understand divine things in a manner worthy of God. For we must categorize the "unintelligent" and the "insensible" as belonging to God by way of transcendence, not by way of deficiency. 

Just as we attribute the "irrational" to that which is beyond reason <note>Dionysius argues that calling God "irrational" isn't an insult; it means He is so far above human logic that our "reason" cannot contain Him.</note>, and "imperfection" to that which is beyond-perfect and pre-perfect; and just as we attribute the "obscure and invisible darkness" to the "unapproachable light," we do so because He transcends visible light. Thus, the divine Mind contains all things. In His knowledge, which is set apart from all things, and according to His role as the Cause of all, He has pre-contained within Himself the knowledge of all things before the angels came to be—knowing and bringing forth the angels, and knowing all things from within and from the very **Beginning** <term>Beginning</term> <note>original: "ἀρχῆς" (archēs); refers to God as the starting point or first principle of all existence.</note> (so to speak), and bringing them into being. And I believe the Scripture teaches this when it says: "He who knows all things before they come to be." <note>A reference to the biblical Story of Susanna (Daniel 13:42).</note>

<margin>O</margin>
For the divine Mind does not learn about existing things from those existing things; rather, from Himself and in Himself, as the Cause, He possesses and has pre-grasped the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "εἴδησιν" (eidēsin); a specific type of conceptual knowledge or "notion."</note>, knowledge, and essence of all things. He does not focus on each thing according to its individual form; instead, by a single embrace of the Cause, He knows and contains all things—just as light, as a cause, has pre-contained within itself the knowledge of darkness, knowing darkness not from any other source but from the light itself.

<margin>E</margin>
Therefore, by knowing itself, the Divine Wisdom will know all things: the material things <term>immaterially</term> <note>original: "ἀΰλως" (aylōs); God knows physical matter without Himself being physical or having to touch it.</note>, the divisible things indivisibly, and the many things in a unified way—knowing all things by means of the **One** itself.

<summary>This page explains that God's knowledge is "transcendently established," meaning He knows the world through His own nature as its Cause rather than by observing it. Dionysius argues that negative descriptions of God (like "darkness" or "irrational") actually point to His overwhelming perfection which exceeds human light and reason.</summary>

# On the Divine Names, Section 4
m iii

In relation to these things, the angelic powers, drawing themselves together and remaining pure from all material and multiplicity, perceive the <unclear>intelligible</unclear> truths of the divine in an intellectual, immaterial, and unified way. Their intellectual power and activity is radiant with unmixed and stainless purity. With a comprehensive view of divine thoughts—in their indivisibility and lack of matter—they are shaped, as much as is possible, into the likeness of the divine and super-wise **Mind** <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun). In Dionysian thought, "Mind" refers to an intuitive, immediate grasp of truth, whereas "Reason" refers to step-by-step logical thinking.</note> and **Word** <term>Word</term> <note>original: "λόγον" (logon); the ordering principle or "Logos" of God.</note> through the gift of divine wisdom. 

And human souls also possess the power of reason, though they travel around the truth of things in a roundabout and discursive way <note>Dionysius describes human reason as "moving in a circle," meaning we have to think through steps and arguments to reach a conclusion, unlike angels who see the truth all at once.</note>. Because they deal with divided and diverse things, they fall short of the unified minds of angels. However, by drawing the many details of existence together into a single unity, souls are deemed worthy of thoughts that are "equal to the angels," as far as is natural and possible for them. Furthermore, one would not miss the mark by calling even the physical senses themselves an "echo" of divine wisdom.

<margin>K</margin> Even the demonic mind, insofar as it is a "mind," originates from this Wisdom. But because it has lost the ability to reach the rational goal it seeks—neither knowing nor truly willing the good—it should more accurately be called a "falling away" from wisdom. 

Yet, it has been said that divine wisdom is the origin, cause, substance, perfection, guardian, and goal of all wisdom itself, and of every mind, every reason, and every sensation. We must then ask: how is God Himself—the "Super-wise"—praised as Wisdom, Mind, Reason, and Knower? For how will He understand anything that can be known if He does not possess intellectual activities? Or how will He know the things of the senses, being [beyond] all sense...

<summary>Dionysius explains how angels, human souls, and even the senses reflect Divine Wisdom at different levels of purity. He notes that even the "demonic mind" is a fallen version of this wisdom, which remains the ultimate source and goal of all intelligence.</summary>

### From Dionysius' [Writing] On

**B**ut as I have said elsewhere, we are deceived because we receive things that are above us in a way that is familiar to ourselves. Being entangled in the habits of our senses and comparing divine things to our own standards, we pursue the divine and unspeakable **Word** <term>Word</term> <note>original: "λόγον" (logon); here referring to the divine reason or manifestation of God.</note> only according to how it appears to us. We ought to know that while our mind has the power of thinking—through which it sees things of the intellect—it also possesses a union that transcends the nature of the mind, through which it is joined to those things that are beyond itself.

**I**t is according to this union, therefore, that divine things must be understood, and not according to our own measure. We must step out of our whole selves entirely <note>original: "ἐξισταμένους" (existamenous), the root of the word "ecstasy." In this context, it means to stand outside one's limited human perspective to meet the Divine.</note> and become entirely God’s. For it is better to belong to God than to ourselves. In this way, divine gifts will be granted to those who come to be with God.

**L**et us, then, praise this "wordless," "mindless," and "foolish" Wisdom <note>Dionysius is referencing the Apostle Paul’s idea that "the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom." By "mindless," he does not mean God lacks intelligence, but that God's Wisdom is so far above human "mind" (nous) that it cannot be categorized by it.</note> in a way that recognizes its transcendence. Let us say that it is the cause of all mind, reason, and all wisdom and understanding. In it is every counsel; from it comes all knowledge and understanding; and in it are "all the hidden treasures of knowledge and wisdom" <note>A quotation from the biblical Book of Colossians 2:3.</note>. Following what has already been said: this super-wise Cause is the foundation of Wisdom-itself and of all wisdom, whether universal or specific. From it, the intellectual and mental powers of the angelic minds possess their simple and blessed perceptions. They do not gather their divine knowledge from divided parts, nor from the senses, nor from long-winded arguments <note>original: "λόγων διεξοδικῶν" (logon diexodikon); this refers to "discursive" reasoning, where one reaches a conclusion through steps, rather than seeing the truth all at once.</note>, nor are they held under any common...

## CHAPTER 7 ##

### Concerning Wisdom, Mind, Reason, Truth, and Faith. ###

<margin>A</margin>Come now, let us also praise the Wise and Wisdom-itself; or rather, let us praise God as the source who gives substance <term>substance</term> <note>original: "ὑποστατικὴν" (hypostatikēn); meaning the foundational reality or essence that allows all other wisdom to exist.</note> to all wisdom, and as one who exists far beyond all wisdom and understanding. For not only is God overflowing with wisdom, and "of His understanding there is no number," <note>A reference to Psalm 147:5.</note> but He is established high above all **Reason**, **Mind**, and **Wisdom**. 

<margin>x</margin>Thinking upon this in a supernatural way, that truly divine man—who is a sun to both us and our teacher <note>A respectful reference to the Apostle Paul, whom the author (writing as Dionysius) considers his primary instructor.</note>—says that "the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:25.</note> He says this not only because all human thought is a kind of error when judged against the stability and permanence of the divine and most perfect thoughts, but because it is also customary for theologians <margin>τ</margin> to use "privations" <note>In theology, a "privation" is a term that describes what God is *not* (e.g., "invisible") to show He is actually *above* that quality.</note> to speak of God in a reverse sense. 

In this way, the Scriptures call the all-radiant light "invisible," and call Him who is praised by many and has many names "unutterable" and "nameless." They call Him who is present to all and found in all things "incomprehensible" and "untraceable." In this very same way, the divine Apostle is now said to praise the "foolishness of God"—referring to that which appears to be irrational and absurd in it—thereby leading us up to the unutterable truth that exists before all reason.

<margin>X</margin> But I call "supernatural" that which is beyond our own nature—meaning the visible nature, not the imagined nature of the **Divine Life**. For to that Life, as it is the nature of all lives (and especially the more divine ones), no life is "against nature" or "beyond nature."

Therefore, let those contradictory arguments regarding the madness of **Simon** <note>original: "Σίμωνος"; referring to Simon Magus, a figure from the Acts of the Apostles often regarded in early Christian tradition as the first heretic.</note> be driven far away from the divine choir and from your holy soul. For it escaped him—even though he thought himself wise in these matters—that a person of sound mind should not use the obvious reasoning of the senses as an ally against the invisible **Cause** of all things. 

This is what must be said to him concerning his use of the phrase "against nature": for nothing is contrary to the Divine Life; rather, all things are animated and cherished by it. All animals and plants—whether they possess a life that is intellectual, rational, sensory, nutritive, or generative—and whatever kind of life, or principle of life, or essence of life exists, it both lives and gives life through that <term>Life</term> <note>original: "ζωῆς"; here Dionysius refers to God as the archetype of Life itself.</note> which is above all life. In that Divine Life, all things pre-exist in a unified way as their primary Cause. 

<margin>Δ</margin> For the **super-living** and life-originating Life is the cause of every life. It is life-generating, fulfilling, and the distributor of life. It is to be praised by every life according to the multi-faceted fruitfulness of all lives, as if it were of every kind. Every life is contemplated and praised in it. 

<margin>κ</margin> Because it lacks nothing—or rather, is overflowing with life—it is **Life-itself**. And just as it makes all life, it is "super-living," or however else one might humanly attempt to praise that Life which is beyond all speech.

# On Divine Names

Life—the **Divine Life**—is both life-giving and the very essence of life. All life and every living movement come from the Life that is beyond all life and every beginning. From this Life, souls possess their immortality, and all animals and plants—down to the very last echo of life—possess the ability to live. As the <term>Scripture</term> <note>original: "λόγιον" (logion); likely referring to Psalm 104:29-30.</note> says, when this Life is withdrawn, all life fails; and when things turn back toward it—even those that have failed because of their weakness in participating in it—they become living beings once more. This <term>Self-Life</term> <note>original: "αὐτοζωὴ" (autozōē); God as the source or archetype of life itself, rather than a single living thing.</note> grants to "Life" itself the quality of being alive, and to every individual life, it grants the existence proper to its own nature.

<margin>K</margin> To the super-celestial lives <note>The angels.</note>, it grants an immaterial, god-like, and unchanging immortality, as well as an unswerving and unceasing movement. This Life even extends itself, through an abundance of goodness, into the life of **demons**; for even that life does not have its existence from any other cause, but from this Life it has both its being as a life and its permanence.

<margin>Δ</margin> It grants also to humans—who are composite beings <note>original: "συμμίκτοις"; referring to the human nature as a mixture of the physical and the spiritual.</note>—an angel-like life as far as they are capable of receiving it. Through an overflowing love for humanity, it turns us back and recalls us to itself even when we wander away.

<margin>K</margin> And what is even more divine is that it has promised to transfer our whole selves—I mean both our souls and the bodies joined to them—to a state of total life and immortality. This is a concept that likely seemed **"contrary to nature"** to the <term>ancients</term> <note>original: "παλαιότητι" (palaiotēti); referring to pre-Christian philosophers who did not believe in the resurrection of the physical body.</note>; but to me, to you, and to the Truth, it is both divine and "beyond nature."

->**Dion.**<-

## On Life.

**N**ow we must praise the **eternal Life**, from which comes <term>Life-itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοζωὴ" (autozōē); the divine source or archetype of life.</note> and all life. By this Life, to all things that participate in life in any way, the capacity to live is distributed according to the nature of each. # On Divine Names

**I**f Clement the philosopher <note>Likely a reference to Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> deems it right that the primary principles among existing things be called "paradigms" <note>original: "παραδείγματα" (paradeigmata); in Platonic thought, these are the eternal "blueprints" or "models" of all things in the mind of God.</note> in relation to something else, his discourse does not proceed through proper, complete, and simple names. Nevertheless, we concede that this is also said correctly. For we must remember that <term>Theology</term> <note>Dionysius uses "Theology" to refer to the Holy Scriptures.</note> says: "Where I showed these things to you," <note>A reference to Exodus 25:40, where God shows Moses the patterns for the Tabernacle.</note> marveling at the path of that vision. This is done so that through the **analogical knowledge** of these things, we may be led back—as far as we are able—to the **Cause of all**.

Therefore, all existing things must be attributed to that Cause according to the one transcendent **union** of all. For it begins from the "to be" of the <term>substance-making procession</term> <note>original: "οὐσιοποιοῦ προόδου" (ousiopoiou proodou); the way God "goes out" from Himself to create and give substance to the world.</note> and goodness, passing through all things, filling all being from itself, and rejoicing over all existing things. 

It pre-contains all things in itself, rejecting all duality according to a single excess of simplicity. Similarly, it encompasses all things according to its super-extended infinity, and it is shared by all in a unified way. This is just like a **single voice**: though it is one and the same, it is shared by many ears as a single thing.

The <term>Pre-existent</term> <note>original: "ὁ προών" (ho proōn); "He-Who-Is," the name of God from Exodus 3:14.</note> is therefore the **Beginning** and the **End** of all beings:
*   The **Beginning** as the Cause.
*   The **End** as that for whose sake all things exist.

He is the limit of all things, yet he is the infinity of every infinity and limit—surpassing those things that are seen as opposites. For in the **One**, as has often been said, all beings both pre-exist and subsist. He is present to all and everywhere. He is according to the "one and the same," and according to that same "one," he proceeds to all things. He remains within himself, both standing and moving—and yet, he is neither standing nor moving <note>Dionysius uses these paradoxes to show that God is beyond human categories of physics or logic.</note>...

# Dionysius on

**...embracing and excelling**; and he is beyond all things, as existing **beyond-substance** <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs); a key term for Dionysius meaning that God exists in a way that transcends our definition of "being" or "existence."</note> before all things. For this reason, all things are attributed to him at the same time, and yet he is nothing among all things. He is **all-formed**, **all-natured**, yet **formless** and **without beauty** <note>In this mystical context, "without beauty" (akallēs) does not mean "ugly," but rather that God’s nature transcends physical aesthetics and human concepts of "form."</note>; for he has pre-embraced the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of all beings within himself, in an unattached and transcendent way. He shines purely upon all things through their very "to be," according to a single and super-unified cause.

<margin>E</margin> For if our sun—though it is one and shines with a single form—renews, nourishes, guards, perfects, distinguishes, unites, warms, makes fertile, grows, changes, establishes, brings forth, moves, and gives life to all things; and if each of these various beings partakes of the same and single sun in a way appropriate to its own nature; and if the single sun has already pre-embraced within its own uniform light the causes of all those many things that partake of it;

Then it must be conceded even more so that the **paradigms** <note>original: "παραδείγματα" (paradeigmata); the blueprints or ideal forms of all things.</note> of all existing things pre-exist within the Cause of both the sun and all things, according to a single union that is beyond-substance. This is because He brings forth "substances" through a procession away from substance.

We say that these "paradigms" are the <term>substance-making</term> <note>original: "οὐσιοποιούς" (ousiopoious); the creative principles that give a thing its essential nature.</note> and singularly pre-existing **reasons** <note>original: "λόγους" (logous); here referring to the divine ideas or "Logoi" that define each created thing.</note> of things in God, which <term>Theology</term> <note>Dionysius uses the word "Theology" to refer specifically to the Holy Scriptures.</note> calls **pre-determinations** <note>original: "προορισμοὺς" (proorismous); also translated as "fore-ordinations."</note> and divine, good wills. These define and create all existing things, for according to them, the One who is Beyond-Substance pre-determined and brought forth everything that exists.

## On the Divine Names.

...to the highest degree, as with the angels; but for us, in a way that **transcends the world**. Both souls and all other existing things, according to the same principle, possess both their **existence** and their **well-being** <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὸ εὖ εἶναι" (to einai kai to eu einai); a classic philosophical distinction where "being" is mere existence, and "well-being" is existence that has reached its proper goodness or perfection.</note>. They exist, and they come from the place where they truly exist. From the **Pre-existent** <note>original: "προόντος" (proontos); referring to God as the one who exists before all created things.</note>, they receive their existence and their well-being. They are both in Him as existing things and come from Him as beings; they begin from Him, are preserved within Him, and reach their final goal in Him. He grants the highest honors of existence to the superior substances <note>Referring to the celestial hierarchy or angels.</note>, which the Scriptures also call **eternal** <note>original: "αἰωνίας" (aiōnias).</note>.

But **Existence** <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι" (to einai); here used as a noun meaning the abstract quality of "to be."</note> itself never departs from any of the things that exist. And He Himself—the Pre-existent—is the source of Existence, and Existence belongs to Him, yet He does not "belong" to Existence. Existence is contained within Him, but He is not contained within Existence. Existence possesses Him, and yet He does not possess Existence <note>Dionysius is using paradox to show that God is not a "thing" that "has" existence like we do; He is the source of the very concept of existence itself.</note>. He Himself is the **Master of existence**, being **Eternity** <note>original: "αἰὼν" (aiōn).</note>, the **Beginning**, and the **Measure of pre-existence** <note>original: "μέτρον προουσίας" (metron proousias); the standard that defines reality before it even comes into being.</note>.

He is the source of both being and eternity; He is the **substance-making beginning**, the **middle**, and the **end** of all things. Because of this, the truly **Pre-existent** is described by the Scriptures in many different ways according to every possible conception of existing things. The terms "**He was**," "**He is**," and "**He will be**"—as well as "**He became**," "**He becomes**," and "**He will become**"—are all properly sung in praise of Him. For to those who perceive God in a way that is fitting for His divinity, all these terms signify that He exists **beyond-substance** <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs); the foundational Dionysian term for God's existence being "above" or "beyond" our human understanding of substance.</note> according to every thought, and that He is the **Cause** <note>original: "αἴτιον" (aition).</note> of everything that exists in any way.

For He is not merely *this* thing while not being *that* thing; rather, He is **all things** as the Cause of all, and in Himself He holds together all the beginnings and all the completions of all existing things...

->## Dionysius on<-

**B**ut even in the whole nature of the universe, all the **principles** <note>original: "λόγοι" (logoi); in this context, these are the divine "blueprints" or rational patterns that define what each specific creature is meant to be.</note> of each individual nature are gathered together according to a single **unconfused union** <note>original: "ἀσύγχυτον ἕνωσιν" (asynchyton henōsin); a term often used in theology to describe a unity where the individual parts remain distinct and are not blurred or melted together.</note>. Similarly, in the soul, the powers that provide for all the individual parts of the whole body exist in a **unified way** <note>original: "μονοειδῶς" (monoeidōs); literally "single-form-ed," meaning they exist as a single, simple capacity before they are expressed in the various functions of the body.</note>. Therefore, it is not at all strange if, ascending from these faint images to the Cause of all things, we should behold with **super-mundane eyes** all things within that Cause—even things that are contrary to one another—in a unified and joined manner. 

For He is the **Beginning** of all beings, from whom comes Being itself and everything that exists in any way: 
- every beginning and every end; 
- all life and all immortality; 
- all wisdom; 
- all order and all harmony; 
- all power; 
- all preservation and all stability; 
- all distribution; 
- all intelligence, all **reason** <note>original: "λόγος" (logos).</note>, and all sensation; 
- all habit; 
- all rest and all motion; 
- all union and all mixture; 
- all friendship and all fitting together; 
- all distinction and every boundary; 

...and everything else that characterizes existing things by the very fact of their being. From that same Cause of all things come the **intelligible** and **intellectual** <note>These terms distinguish between things that are pure thoughts (intelligible) and the minds that think them (intellectual).</note> essences of the godlike angels, the essences of souls, the natures of the whole world, and whatever things are said either to exist within others or to exist only as a concept in the mind.

**F**or indeed the all-holy and most ancient Powers <note>Referring to the highest ranks of angels, such as Seraphim or Cherubim.</note> are truly essences; standing as it were in the **vestibules** of the **Trinity that transcends essence** <note>original: "ὑπερουσίου τριάδος" (hyperousiou triados); the idea that God’s nature is "beyond" the category of existence as we understand it.</note>, they possess both their existence and their godlike state from Her and in Her. And after those, the subordinate powers possess their existence subordinately, and the lowest...

<summary>Dionysius explains how all distinct and even contrary aspects of reality (like life, motion, and rest) exist in a unified, "unconfused" state within God. He describes God as the source of the entire celestial and physical hierarchy, from the highest angels to the smallest concepts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Section 4 of Dionysius the Areopagite's "On the Divine Names." The previous page concluded a list of various qualities (life, wisdom, power) that God provides to the universe. This page picks up mid-sentence to explain how these qualities are "participated in" by created things and introduces the famous mathematical analogies of the monad and the circle.</meta>

# On the Divine Names <gloss>4</gloss>

...to be, and both existing and participated in.
<margin>E</margin> But if these things exist by the **participation** <note>original: "μετοχῇ" (metochē); the Neoplatonic concept where lower things derive their reality by "sharing" in a higher, more perfect principle.</note> in Being, then much more so do the things that participate in *them*. Therefore, the **Divine Goodness**, by putting forward the gift of **Being-itself** <note>original: "αὐτοεῖναι" (autoeinai); existence in its purest, most universal form, before it is limited to a specific creature.</note> as the first of gifts, is praised as the most ancient of all that is participated in. From It and in It are Being-itself and the **foundational principles** <note>original: "ἀρχαί" (archai); the starting points or origins of all things.</note> of existing things. All things that exist, and all things that exist in any way whatsoever, are held together by It. This happens in a way that is **unattached** <note>original: "ἀσχέτως" (aschetōs); meaning God provides existence without being bound, limited, or changed by the things He creates.</note>, collective, and singular.

For just as in a **monad** <note>original: "μονάδι" (monadi); a single unit or "the One." In ancient mathematics, the monad was the source of all numbers but not a number itself.</note> every number pre-exists in the form of a unity—and the monad contains every number within itself in a singular way, and every number is united within the monad—so it is with Being. Insofar as a number proceeds from the monad, it becomes distinct and multiplied.

Similarly, in the **center of a circle**, all the lines of the circle coexist according to a single union. The **point** <note>original: "σημεῖον" (semeion); here referring to the infinitesimal mathematical point at the very center of a circle.</note> holds all the straight lines within itself, unified as one, both in relation to each other and to the single origin from which they proceeded. Within the center itself, they are completely united; but when they stand even a short distance from it, they are slightly distinguished; and as they move further away, they are further separated. Simply put, insofar as they are closer to the center, by that much they are united both to the center and to each other; and insofar as they are distant from it, by that much they are also distant from one another.

<summary>Dionysius uses the mathematical analogies of the monad and the center of a circle to explain how all multiplicity in the universe originates from a single, unified Divine source. He argues that Being is the primary gift of God, containing all subsequent realities in a state of perfect unity.</summary>
<keywords>participation, Being-itself, monad, circle analogy, center and radius, Divine Goodness, Neoplatonism, metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 5 of "On the Divine Names." Having previously established that God is the source of all gifts, the author now focuses on why "Being" (existence) is the primary and most fundamental name of God, surpassing even "Life" or "Wisdom."</meta>

# Dionysius <unclear>on the Divine Names</unclear>

Before all His other participations, **Being** <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι" (to einai). Dionysius argues that before a thing can be "wise" or "alive," it must first "exist." Therefore, Being is the most fundamental gift.</note> is put forward. And **Being-itself** is more ancient than <term>Life-itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοζωή" (autozōē); the abstract principle of Life from which all living things draw their vitality.</note> being, and <term>Wisdom-itself</term> being, and Divine <term>Likeness-itself</term> being. All other things that existing things participate in must first participate in **Being** before all else. Rather, even those very principles <note>original: "αὐτὰ καθ' αὑτὰ" (auta kath' hauta); the "themselves-by-themselves" principles, referring to the Platonic Ideas or Forms.</note> which existing things participate in, themselves participate in **Being-itself**. There is no existing thing whose essence and <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "αἰών" (aiōn); here referring to the permanent, unchanging reality of a thing's nature.</note> is not **Being-itself**.

Therefore, God is reasonably praised as **"He Who Is"** <note>original: "ὁ ὤν" (ho ōn); a reference to the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14 ("I Am Who I Am").</note> from the most ancient of His gifts, as this name is more sovereign than all others. For by pre-existing and super-existing, and by preceding and surpassing **Being**, He pre-established all **Being-itself**—I mean the very principle of existence—and by that **Being-itself**, He established everything that exists in any way whatsoever.

<margin>10</margin> Indeed, all the principles of existing things exist only because they participate in **Being**. They are principles, but first they *exist*, and *then* they are principles. And if you wish to say that <term>Life-itself</term> is the principle of living things as living things, and <term>Likeness-itself</term> is the principle of similar things as similar, and <term>Unity-itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοένωσιν" (autoenōsin); the principle that allows things to be "one" or whole.</note> is the principle of united things as united, and <term>Order-itself</term> <note>original: "αὐτοτάξιν" (autotaxin); the principle of arrangement and hierarchy.</note> is the principle of ordered things as ordered—and so too for all other things that participate in this or that, or both, or many—you will find that these principles themselves first participate in **Being**. By **Being**, they first endure; then, they are principles of this or that. Their participation in Being...

<summary>This page argues that "Being" is the first and most fundamental gift from God, as all other qualities like Life, Wisdom, and Order require existence as a prerequisite. God is thus most appropriately praised as "He Who Is," the source of Being-itself.</summary>
