<meta>This page continues the fifth chapter of Dionysius the Areopagite's "On the Divine Names." The previous page established that "Being" is the first and most fundamental gift God gives to the world. Here, the author explores how God, as the "Pre-existing One," is the source of all existence, time, and eternity.</meta>

## On the Divine Names

Let us sing His praises: **He Who Is** <note>original: "ὁ ὤν" (ho ōn); the name of God from Exodus 3:14.</note> is, according to His power, the <term>super-essential</term> <note>original: "ὑπερούσιος" (hyperousios); meaning a reality that is "above" or "beyond" essence or being itself.</note> foundation, cause, and creator of truly existing being, substance, essence, and nature. He is the beginning and the measure of <term>eternities</term> <note>original: "αἰώνων" (aiōnōn); referring to "ages" or the permanent state of heavenly things.</note> and of times. He is the "beingness" and the eternity of existing things, and the time of those things that are in the process of becoming. He is existence for whatever exists in any way, and He is the process of "coming-to-be" for whatever becomes, drawing from **He Who Is**. He is eternity, essence, being, time, becoming, and the thing that becomes; He is the existence within existing things, and whatever in any way subsists and holds firm.

<margin>K</margin> For God is not "being" in just any particular way, but He is Being simply and boundlessly, having embraced and anticipated the whole of existence within Himself. Therefore, He is called the "King of Ages," because all existence—both that which truly is and that which merely subsists—is in Him and around Him. He was not, and He will not be; He did not become, nor is He becoming, nor will He become. Rather, one might even say He "is" not <note>Dionysius uses "negative theology" here to suggest that God's way of being is so superior to ours that it shouldn't even be called "being" by our limited human definitions.</note>. Instead, He Himself is the **Being** for all existing things. And He is not only the things that exist, but He is the very **Being-itself** of all things, derived from the **Pre-existing One**. For He Himself is the "Eternity of Eternities."

Let us take this up again and say that for all existing things and for all ages, their existence comes from the **Pre-existing One**. Every eternity and every time is from Him. Of every eternity, every time, and everything that exists in any way, the **Pre-existing One** is the beginning and the cause. All things participate in Him, and He is absent from no existing thing. He is before all things, and "in Him all things hold together." <note>A reference to Colossians 1:17.</note> Quite simply, if anything exists in any way, it exists, is conceived, and is preserved within the **Pre-existing One**.

<summary>Dionysius explains that God is the "Pre-existing One" who provides the foundation for all existence, time, and eternity, while remaining "super-essentially" beyond being Himself.</summary>
<keywords>Being, Pre-existing One, Super-essential, Eternity, Divine Names, Ontotheology, Dionysius the Areopagite</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 5 of "On the Divine Names" by the writer known as Dionysius the Areopagite. The previous page discussed God as "He Who Is," the source of all existence. This passage addresses why "Being" is treated as the primary name of God, even though "Life" and "Wisdom" might seem like higher qualities.</meta>

# Dionysius [on] [Divine] [Names]

...of God, the complete and good <term>processions</term> <note>original: "προόδους" (proodous); this refers to the ways God’s power and presence "flow out" into the created world.</note> and the <term>Divine Names</term> <note>original: "θεωνυμίας" (theōnymias); titles or names attributed to God in sacred texts.</note> celebrated by us. One of these names [the Good] is expressive of the complete <term>providence</term> <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia); the divine care and forethought God has for all creation.</note> of the one God, while others express the more universal processions before Him and the more particular ones.

<margin>K</margin> And yet, someone might ask: why is Being ranked above Life, and Life ranked above Wisdom? For among existing things, those that have life are superior; among those that live, the <term>sentient beings</term> <note>original: "αἰσθητικά" (aisthetika); things capable of feeling or perceiving through senses.</note> are superior; among these, the <term>rational beings</term> <note>original: "λογικά" (logika); beings possessing reason and language.</note> are superior; and among the rational, the <term>intellects</term> <note>original: "νόες" (noes); referring to pure minds or angelic beings.</note> excel, for they are around God and are closer to Him. Surely, those things that share in God's greater gifts should be better and should surpass the rest. However, if one were to assume that the <term>intellectual beings</term> <note>original: "νοερά" (noera); beings of pure mind.</note> were without substance or life, that argument would be correct. But if the divine intellects exist above all other things, and live above all other living things, and think and know beyond all sensation and reason, and if—above all existing things—they desire and participate in the Beautiful and the Good, then they themselves are most truly "around" the Good. They are the ones who participate in Him most abundantly, having received more and greater gifts from Him, just as rational beings surpass sentient beings by the abundance of their reason, and sentient beings surpass others by sensation, and others by life. And this, I believe, is true: that those things which participate more in the one and infinitely-giving God are closer to Him and more divine than those that fall behind.

<margin>E</margin> Since we have spoken of these matters, come now, let us praise the Good as that which truly "is" and as the <term>Creator of Substance</term> <note>original: "οὐσιοποιὸν" (ousiopoion); the one who brings essence or "beingness" into existence.</note> for all existing things.

<summary>Dionysius explains the hierarchy of divine gifts, arguing that while Life and Wisdom are "higher" qualities, they all depend on the foundational gift of Being. He concludes that beings with higher faculties (like angels and humans) are closer to God because they participate more fully in His nature.</summary>
<keywords>Being, Life, Wisdom, hierarchy of existence, Divine Names, Intellects, Processions, Providence, Neo-Platonism</keywords>

<margin>A</margin> Instead, it celebrates the manifested, good-producing Providence as "Goodness" in a pre-eminent sense. <summary>This page explains that while God's inner nature is hidden and "beyond being," he is known through his "processions" or manifestations such as Goodness, Being, and Wisdom. It clarifies that these names refer to a single divine Cause rather than multiple separate deities.</summary>

For evil as evil is nowhere; and the becoming of evil is not according to a power, but through weakness. And for the <term>demons</term> <note>original: "δαίμοσιν" (daimosin); Dionysius views demons not as inherently evil substances, but as angelic beings who have turned away from their proper purpose.</note>, that which they are is both from the Good and is itself good. And it makes the understanding of the Good involuntary because of the deviation or the weakness of the will. <margin>K</margin>And yet someone might say that weakness is not deserving of punishment; on the contrary, it should be forgiven. # Dionysius On

->the Good<-

...how can something be the contrary of the Good, if it is deprived of its own will and power and activity? It is not so in every case. Things are not evil in every way or in the same respect; for a <term>demon</term> <note>original: "δαίμονι" (daimoni); in this context, Dionysius refers to spiritual beings who have turned away from their divine source.</note>, evil is to be contrary to the good-formed intellect; for a soul, it is the <term>irrational</term> <note>original: "παράλογον" (paralogon); acting against the logos or reason.</note>; for a body, it is that which is against nature. How then does evil exist at all, if <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "προνοίας" (pronoias); the divine care and guidance of God over all creation.</note> exists? Evil, insofar as it is evil, does not exist; it is neither a "being" nor is it found among things that have being. 

And nothing that exists is outside the reach of Providence; for evil does not even exist as a substance that is entirely unmixed with the Good. And if nothing that exists is without a share in the Good, and evil is the <term>deficiency</term> <note>original: "ἔλλειψις" (elleipsis); a falling short or lack of something that should be present.</note> of the Good, then nothing that exists is entirely deprived of the Good. Divine Providence is present in all things that exist, and nothing that exists is without Providence. Rather, Providence even makes use of the evils that occur in a way <term>worthy of the Good</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθοπρεπῶς" (agathoprepōs); in a manner befitting God's goodness.</note>, utilizing them for the correction of the individuals themselves or others, or for justice, or for the common benefit. 

It provides for each of the things that exist in a manner appropriate to them. Therefore, we should not accept the common argument of the many who say that Providence ought to lead us to virtue even against our will. For to destroy nature is not the work of Providence. Hence, as Providence preserves the nature of each thing, it provides for <term>self-moving beings</term> <note>original: "αὐτοκινήτων" (autokinētōn); those endowed with free will or the power to initiate their own actions.</note> as self-moving, and it cares for the whole and for individuals in a way appropriate to both the whole and the individual. Insofar as the nature of those receiving care allows, the providential goodnesses—which are given out from the universal and manifold Providence—are distributed to each in proportion to their capacity.

Evil, therefore, is not an existing thing, nor is evil among the things that have being; it is not...

<header>On Divine Names</header>
<sig>l ii</sig>

# On Divine Names

->the Good<- <note>This text continues the sentence from the previous page, completing the word "Good" (ἀγαθόν).</note>... for the sake of the Good all things exist—both those things that are good and those that are contrary to it. For even these contrary things we do because we desire the Good; no one, after all, performs an action while looking toward evil as their goal. Therefore, evil does not have its own <term>substance</term> <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin); a fundamental, self-existing reality.</note>, but rather an <term>accidental existence</term> <note>original: "παρυπόστασιν" (parhypostasis); an existence that is secondary, parasitic, or a "by-product" of something else.</note>, occurring for the sake of the Good and not arising from itself.

**W**e must posit that "being" belongs to evil only by accident, through the influence of something else and not from its own internal origin. Thus, an action seems to be right because it is done for the sake of the Good; but in reality, it is not right because we mistakenly believe that which is not good to be the Good.

**I**t has been demonstrated that the object of desire is one thing, and the actual result is another. Therefore, evil is away from the path, away from the goal, away from nature, away from the cause, away from the origin, away from the end, away from the limit, away from the will, and away from substance. Evil is therefore <term>deprivation</term> <note>original: "στέρησις" (stēresis); the absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>, deficiency, weakness, lack of symmetry, <term>error</term> <note>original: "ἁμαρτία" (hamartia); literally "missing the mark."</note>, aimlessness, ugliness, lifelessness, mindlessness, irrationality, imperfection, instability, causelessness, indefiniteness, barrenness, inactivity, disorder, dissimilarity, infinity, darkness, and essence-less—being nothing at all in any place, and itself possessing no existence whatsoever.

**H**ow can evil have any power at all? It is only through its mixture with the Good. For that which is entirely without a share of the Good neither is anything, nor can it do anything. For if the Good is that which has being, and is the object of will, and is power, and is activ[ity]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word (δραστή-).</note>

<summary>This page defines evil not as a thing in itself, but as a "parhypostasis" (a parasitic existence) and a "steresis" (a deprivation) of the Good. It argues that evil only has power because it mimics or attaches itself to good intentions and divine reality.</summary>

# [Of] Dionysius concerning

...[is] evil eternal, and does it create and possess power? Does it exist and act? If so, from where does it derive these qualities? Does it receive them from the Good, or does the Good receive them from evil? Or do both arise from some other cause?

<margin>Γ</margin> <note>The Greek letter Gamma (3) serves here as a section marker.</note> Everything that exists according to nature is produced by a definite cause. But if evil is causeless and undefined, it is not according to nature. For that which is contrary to nature does not exist within nature, just as a lack of art has no place within the <term>logic of art</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos); here referring to the internal rational structure or principle of a craft.</note>.

<margin>Α</margin> <note>The Greek letter Alpha (1), likely a reference to a primary argument.</note> Is the soul the cause of evils, just as fire is the cause of heating? Does it infect everything it approaches with vice? Or is the soul’s nature itself good, while in its activities it behaves sometimes one way and sometimes another? If its nature were evil, then its very being would be evil; and from where would it derive its being, if not from the good Cause that creates all existing things? But if it comes from that Cause, how can it be evil in its essence? For all the offspring of that Cause are good. If it is evil only in its activities, even this is not unchangeable; otherwise, where would virtues come from, if the soul were not also capable of becoming <term>good-formed</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδοῦς" (agathoeidous); having the form or appearance of the Good.</note>? It remains, then, that evil is weakness and a <term>deficiency</term> <note>original: "ἔλλειψις" (elleipsis); a falling short or lack of something necessary for perfection.</note> of the good. The cause of good things is one.

<margin>Ε</margin> <note>The Greek letter Epsilon (5).</note> If evil is the opposite of the Good, the causes of evil must be many. These are not, however, "productive" causes—there are no rational principles or powers of evils. Instead, evil arises from <term>impotence</term> <note>original: "ἀδυναμία" (adynamia); a lack of power or capacity.</note>, weakness, and the disproportionate mixing of things that do not match. Nor are evil things fixed or always the same; rather, they are infinite and undefined, moving in different ways among an infinite variety of things.

<margin>Ζ</margin> <note>The Greek letter Zeta (6).</note> The Good shall be the beginning and end of both [good] things and of evils... <note>The text breaks off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>Pseudo-Dionysius argues that evil is not a natural substance or a creative force, but rather a "deficiency" or "weakness" that lacks a primary cause. He rejects the idea that the soul is inherently evil, asserting that its essence must be good because it was created by the Good.</summary>

# [Of] Divine Names

Every evil stands in need of the Good; for evil flees the very nature of the Good. How then could **matter**, if it were evil in itself, generate and nourish nature? For evil, insofar as it is evil, is neither generative, nor nourishing, nor in any way productive or preservative. If some were to say that matter does not produce vice in souls but rather attracts them toward it, how can this be true? For many souls look toward the Good; yet how would this be possible if matter were dragging them entirely toward evil? Thus, evil in souls does not arise from matter, but from a **disordered and erroneous movement** <note>original: "ἀταξίου καὶ πλημμελοῦς κινήσεως" (ataxiou kai plēmmelous kinēseōs); this refers to the soul losing its internal harmony and "missing the mark" of its divine purpose.</note>.

<margin>E</margin> <note>The Greek letter Epsilon (5), used here as a section marker.</note> If they also say that this disorder is an inevitable consequence of matter, and that unstable matter is necessary for those things that cannot remain established in themselves, we must ask: how can evil be "necessary," or how can that which is "necessary" be evil?

<margin>A</margin> <note>The Greek letter Alpha (1).</note> Nor is it true, as we sometimes say, that <term>privation</term> <note>original: "στέρησις" (sterēsis); a central concept in Neoplatonism where evil is not a "thing," but a "lack" or "hole" in existence, like shadows are a lack of light.</note> fights against the Good by its own inherent power. For a total privation is completely powerless. A partial privation has power not because it is a privation, but because it is *not yet* a total privation. For as long as the privation of the Good is only partial, it is not yet "evil" <note>In the sense of a complete opposite to existence.</note>; but once it becomes total, the very nature of evil also vanishes <note>Dionysius argues that if something were "totally" evil, it would have no "Good" (existence) left in it at all, and therefore would cease to exist entirely.</note>.

<margin>S</margin> <note>The Greek letter Sigma.</note> To put it briefly: the Good arises from a single and total cause; but evil arises from many and partial defects.

<margin>O</margin> <note>The Greek letter Omicron.</note> God knows evil insofar as it is good, and in His eyes, the causes of evils are actually powers that produce good. If indeed...

<summary>This page argues that matter is not inherently evil since it supports life, and defines evil as a powerless "privation" or deficiency rather than a creative force.</summary>

# Dionysius: On [Divine Names], Chapter 4

<margin>1</margin> **N**or is evil found in bodies; for ugliness and disease are a deficiency of form and a <term>privation</term> <note>original: "στέρησις" (sterēsis); the idea that evil is not a positive substance but a "lack" of something that should be there, like a hole in a garment.</note> of order. This is not entirely evil, but rather "less good." For if there were a complete dissolution of beauty, form, and order, the body itself would vanish.

<margin>2</margin> **I**t is clear that the body is not the cause of vice in the soul, because it is possible for vice to arise even without a body—as is seen in the case of <term>demons</term> <note>original: "δαίμοσιν" (daimosin); in this context, Dionysius refers to fallen spiritual beings who possess no physical bodies yet still exhibit evil.</note>. For this is what evil is for intellects, souls, and bodies alike: the weakness and falling away from the state of their own proper goods.

<margin>3</margin> **N**or is evil to be found in the much-discussed "matter," as some say, insofar as it is matter. For matter itself has a share in world-order, beauty, and form. If matter were outside these things—being in itself without quality or form—how could matter *do* anything, since it would not even have the capacity to be acted upon? Furthermore, how can matter be evil? If it does not exist at all, it is neither good nor evil. If it does exist—and since all existing things come from the Good—then matter too must come from the Good. This leads to a contradiction: either the Good is the creator of evil, or evil (being from the Good) is actually good, or evil creates the Good, or the Good (being from evil) is actually evil. Or, we must fall back on the idea of two primary principles <note>This refers to Dualism, the belief in two equal and opposite forces of Good and Evil, which Dionysius rejects in favor of a single divine source.</note>, and even these would have to hang from a single, higher peak.

<margin>4</margin> **I**f they say that matter is "necessary" for the completion of the entire cosmos, how then can matter be evil? For "evil" is one thing, and "the necessary" is another. And how could the Good produce some kind of addition to the world out of evil, or...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil does not reside in the body or in matter, as both are part of the created order and thus contain some degree of goodness; instead, evil is defined as a "privation" or a falling away from a thing's proper state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 4 of "On the Divine Names" by Pseudo-Dionysius. The previous page concluded that evil is not found in the body or in matter itself. # Dionysius: On Divine Names

->**Of Divine Names**<-

<margin>A</margin> <unclear>...is found</unclear> not in anything other than the deficiency and absence of good <term>dispositions</term> <note>original: "ἕξεων" (hexeōn); refers to stable qualities or habits of character.</note> and activities, caused by an inherent weakness, a failure, and a "slipping away" from the goal. We see this even in our environment: we say the air around us is "darkened" only when there is a deficiency and absence of light. But light itself remains forever light, and it is the light that illuminates even the darkness. Therefore, evil does not exist in <term>demons</term> <note>original: "δαίμοσιν" (daimosin); here referring to spiritual beings who have turned away from their original purpose.</note> or in us as a "thing" that is evil in its own right. Rather, evil is simply the deficiency and lack of the perfection of those goods that are proper to our nature.

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, evil is not found in irrational animals. For if you were to take away their anger, their desire, and the other traits we complain about, you would find they are not simply evil by their own nature. 
A lion that loses its courage and its pride would no longer even be a lion. If a dog became submissive and friendly to everyone, it would no longer be a dog—since it is the very nature of a dog to be a guardian, to recognize its own family, and to drive away what is foreign. Thus, for a creature's nature to be preserved is not an evil. What *is* evil is the "destruction of nature"—a state of weakness and a deficiency <term>of the</term> natural dispositions, activities, and powers. For all things that reach their perfection through a process of growth over time, even being "imperfect" is not a state that is entirely against every nature. 

Moreover, evil is not found in nature as a whole. If all natural laws and principles come from "Universal Nature," then nothing can truly be "opposite" to it. However, when looking at a "Particular Nature" (an individual creature or thing), one thing might be "according to nature" while another is "contrary to nature." What is "contrary to nature" for one creature might be "according to nature" for another. The "evil" of a nature is simply that which is contrary to its design, or a privation <term>of the</term> things that belong to that nature. Therefore, there is no such thing as an "evil nature." Instead, "evil" for any specific nature is simply its inability to fulfill the functions and purposes of its own specific kind.

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil is not a positive substance but a "privation" or deficiency of good, using examples like the protective nature of dogs and the courage of lions to show that natural instincts are not evil unless they fail to fulfill their purpose.</summary>

They are only called "evil" because of their deprivation, their avoidance, and their falling away from the goods that are proper to them. They are evil only to the extent that they are not good; and by desiring "that which is not" <note>In this philosophy, "non-being" is synonymous with evil, as everything that truly exists is good.</note>, they are said to desire evil.

<margin>Delta</margin> But someone might say that **souls** are evil. If it is because they associate with those who are evil in a providential and saving way, then this is not evil—it is good and comes from the Good, which turns even evil toward a good purpose. 

<margin>Epsilon</margin> But if we say that souls themselves *become* evil, in what way do they become evil?

# Of the Divine Names: Chapter 4

### Dionysius <gloss>On the Divine Names</gloss>

...concerning the Good and the incomplete; and that when the perfect Good is absent, only then will evil exist and be perceived. Evil exists specifically when it is "evil" to those beings to which it is opposed; yet even then, it is dependent upon things that are good. For it is impossible <margin>Ξ</margin> for the same things to fight against one another in the same respects in all things. Therefore, evil is not a real being <note>original: "οὐκ ἄρα ὂν τὸ κακόν" (ouk ara on to kakon). Here Dionysius argues that evil lacks "being" or ontological reality; it is a privation rather than a thing.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, evil does not even exist among things that have being. For either <margin>T</margin> all beings come from the Good, and the Good is in all beings and encompasses all things, or evil cannot exist among beings at all. Otherwise, it would have to exist within the Good. Yet, it certainly cannot exist in the Good, just as cold cannot exist in fire. Nor can that which is made evil exist in that which turns even evil into good. But if evil <insert>does</insert> exist within the Good, how could it be so? If it comes from the Good, that is absurd and impossible; for, as the truth of the <term>Holy Oracles</term> <note>original: "λογίων" (logiōn). But if evil does not come from the Good, then it clearly must come from some other <term>principle</term> <note>original: "ἀρχῆς" (archēs). A starting point, source, or first cause.</note> and cause. For either evil must come from the Good, or the Good from evil; or, if that is not possible, then both the Good and the evil must come from some other principle and cause.

<margin>P</margin> However, every <term>dyad</term> <note>original: "δυὰς" (dyas). A duality or pair of opposing things.</note> is not a first principle; rather, the <term>monad</term> <margin>T</margin> <note>original: "μονὰς" (monas). The "One" or single unity that precedes all multiplicity.</note> must be the principle of every dyad. It is also absurd that two completely opposite things should proceed from one and the same source, and that the principle itself should not be simple and unified, but divided and consisting of two <margin>H</margin> different forms, being contrary to itself and altered.

<margin>K</margin> Verily, it is also not possible for there to be two contrary principles of beings...

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil has no independent existence and cannot originate from the Good, as "a good tree cannot bear bad fruit." He asserts that all reality must stem from a single, unified source (the Monad) rather than a dualistic conflict of two equal principles.</summary>

## Of the Divine Names.

...so that even "coming into being through the destruction of another" is a form of generation. This is not <gloss>1</gloss> a power of evil, but rather a strain <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "πόνος" (ponos). Rather, all beings will exist to a greater or lesser degree exactly in proportion to how much they participate in the Good.
<margin>K</margin> For even in the case of "non-being" itself: that which is absolutely and in no way <gloss>2</gloss> <gloss>1</gloss> a being will simply not exist. Insofar as it has fallen away from the Eternal Being, it is not; yet insofar as it has partaken in "being," to that extent it exists. Thus, its entire existence, even its non-being, is held together and preserved [by the Good]. In the same way, evil—that which has entirely fallen away from the Good—will not be good, and will not exist to a greater or lesser degree.
<margin>T</margin> But that which is "good" in one way and "not good" in another fights <gloss>1</gloss> against a specific good, but not against the Good in its entirety. It is held together by its participation in the Good; for the Good gives substance even to the <term>privation</term> <note>original: "στέρησις" (stēresis). This is the idea that evil is not a "thing" but a "hole" where something should be—like darkness is the absence of light.</note> of itself through its total participation in all things.
<margin>P</margin> For if every good were to depart from it <gloss>1</gloss>, there would be no good at all, nor anything mixed, nor would evil itself exist. For if evil is an "imperfect good," then by the absolute absence of all <gloss>2</gloss>...

<summary>Dionysius explains that evil is a "privation" (a lack of good) rather than a substance. He argues that even "evil" things only exist because they contain a small remnant of the Good that sustains their being.</summary>

# Dionysius on...

->Of the Divine Names<-

Rather, to put it briefly: all things that exist, insofar as they exist, are both good and come from the Good; and insofar as they are deprived of the Good, they are neither good nor do they exist.

**F**or in the case of other qualities <note>original: "ἕξεων" (hexeōn). Often translated as 'habits' or 'states,' referring to the way a thing currently is.</note>—such as heat or cold—things that have been heated exist even when the heat leaves them; and many things exist that have no share in life or mind. Even God is set apart from substance <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias). This refers to 'essence' or 'being'.</note>, and exists <term>super-essentially</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs). Dionysius uses this to explain that God is not a "thing" like other things, but exists on a level far above the very concept of existence.</note>.

**A**nd simply, regarding all other things: even if a quality departs, or never entered them at all, the beings still exist and are able to subsist. But that which is in every way deprived of the Good never was, nor is, nor will be, nor can possibly exist. For example, consider the licentious person <note>original: "ἀκόλαστος" (akolastos). Someone who lacks self-control or gives in to every impulse.</note>: even if he is deprived of the Good according to his irrational desire, in that specific respect he neither exists, nor does he desire things that truly exist. Yet he still <term>participates</term> <note>The concept of "participation" suggests that everything "borrows" its reality from the Divine Good; to stop participating is to cease existing.</note> in the Good through the very dim echo of union and friendship.

**A**nd anger participates in the Good by the very fact of its movement and its desire to set right and turn back what seem to be evils toward what seems to be beautiful <note>original: "καλὸν" (kalon). In Greek, this word means both 'beautiful' and 'morally good'.</note>.

**A**nd even he who desires the worst life—insofar as he desires life at all (and what he perceives as the best life)—participates in the Good by the very act of desiring, by desiring life, and by looking toward what he thinks is a "best" life.

**A**nd if you were to remove the Good entirely, there will be no substance, no life, no desire, no motion, nor anything else at all.

<summary>Dionysius argues that the Good is the foundation of all existence; even "evil" actions like anger or lust contain a distorted desire for some perceived good, because without the Good, a thing would cease to exist entirely.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the discussion of how the Good (God) is the source of all existence. Dionysius is specifically addressing the paradox of evil: if God is the source of everything, how can evil exist? He argues that evil is not a "thing" in itself but a lack or failure of the Good.</meta>

# Of the Divine Names <margin>Δ</margin>

<margin>Δ</margin> <margin>M</margin> Evil itself <note>original: "αὐτὸ κακὸν" (auto kakon)</note> is neither a being, nor is it good, nor is it a creator of life, nor a producer of beings and good things. However, the Good makes those things in which it is perfectly present into perfect, unmixed, and complete goods. <margin>H</margin> Those things that have a lesser share in the Good are both imperfect goods and are mixed <note>meaning they are a mixture of good and the lack of it</note> because of their deficiency of the Good. Therefore, evil is not at all a good, nor a producer of good. <margin>K</margin> Instead, a thing will be good only in proportion to how much it approaches the Good, whether more or less.

<margin>E</margin> Just as the perfect goodness that passes through all things does not stop with the "all-good" essences <note>the highest celestial or angelic beings</note> that surround it, but extends even to the lowliest things; <margin>X</margin> it is present to some in a total way, to others in an inferior way, and to others in the furthest degree, according to how each of the beings is able to <term>participate</term> <note>original: "μετέχειν" (metéchein). This is the philosophical idea that creatures "borrow" their existence and qualities from God.</note> in it. Thus, some things participate in the Good entirely.

<margin>Γ</margin> <margin>H</margin> Others are more or less deprived of it; some have a dimmer share of the Good; and to others, the Good is present only as a distant echo. For if the Good were not present to each thing in proportion to its capacity, then the most divine and ancient things would hold the same rank as the lowest.

<margin>Π</margin> And how would it even be possible for all things to participate in the Good in a single, identical form <note>original: "μονοειδῶς" (monoeidōs)</note>, if they were not all suited for a <term>total participation</term> <note>original: "ὁλικὴν μέθεξιν" (holikēn methexin)</note> in it? But this demonstrates the power of the Good: its surpassing greatness. <margin>K</margin> It even gives power to things that are deprived of it—and to the very deprivation itself—insofar as they participate in it at all. <margin>X</margin> Indeed, one must speak the truth boldly: even the things that fight against the Good both exist and are able to fight only by the power of the Good itself.

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil has no independent existence and is merely a deficiency of the Good. He explains that all things exist and function only because they "participate" in God's goodness to varying degrees.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of evil. Dionysius is responding to the objection that if evil seems to cause new things to be born (like a seed dying to become a plant), it must have some creative power. He clarifies that this power comes from the Good, not from the evil itself.</meta>

# Dionysius, On [the Divine] Names

...the offspring of one principle and one cause; it rejoices in communion and unity and friendship. And the lesser good is not the opposite of the greater good; for neither is a lesser heat or cold the opposite of a greater degree of the same. Therefore, evil exists among beings; it is a being, and it is set against and is the opposite of the <margin>†</margin> Good.

<margin>K</margin> And if evil is the corruption of beings, it does not entirely cast out their being. Instead, it would itself be both a being and truly a producer of life <note>original: "γενεσιουργόν" (genesiourgón)</note>. For is it not often the case that the corruption of one thing <margin>T</margin> becomes the birth of another? And thus, evil would contribute to the completion of the universe, and through itself, it would provide the whole with the quality of not being incomplete.

<margin>E</margin> But to these points, the true word <note>referring to divine reason or philosophical truth</note> replies that evil, insofar as it is evil, produces no essence or birth. It only debases and corrupts the <margin>η</margin> substance <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hypóstasin); the underlying reality of a thing</note> of beings, as far as it is able. If it is said to be a producer of life, and that by the corruption of one thing it gives birth to another, one must truly answer: it is not insofar as it corrupts that it gives birth. Rather, insofar as it is <term>corruption</term> and evil, it only corrupts and debases. But <term>birth</term> and <term>essence</term> <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia); the "what-ness" or nature of a thing</note> occur because of the <term>Good</term>.

And so, evil will be <term>corruption</term> through itself, but a producer of life through the Good. Insofar as it is evil, it is neither a being nor a maker of beings. But through the Good, it is both a being and—as a good being—a maker of good things. Or rather, the same thing cannot be both good and evil at the same time and in the same respect. Nor can the corruption and the birth of the same thing be the same power in the same respect; neither is it an inherent power or an inherent self-corruption.

<summary>Dionysius argues that evil has no independent power to create or sustain life; any "productive" result seen in the cycle of decay and birth is actually the work of the Good. He maintains that evil is purely a corruptive force that lacks its own substance.</summary>

The goal of all beings, having its beginning and its end, is the Good. For no one does what they do while looking toward the nature of evil. How then can evil exist among beings, or even exist at all, if it were deprived of such a desire for the Good?

And if all beings come from the Good, and the Good is beyond all beings, then in the Good even <term>non-being</term> <note>original: "τὸ μὴ ὄν" (to mē on); a technical term for things that do not have a defined existence</note> exists as a kind of being. But evil is not even a "being." If it were not so, it would not be entirely evil, nor would it be non-being. For nothing can be completely "non-being," unless it were spoken of in relation to the Good according to its <term>beyond-being</term> <note>original: "ὑπερούσιον" (hyperousion); referring to God's nature which is above the category of "existence"</note> nature.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, the Good must be established long before both that which simply exists and that which does not exist. But evil is neither among the things that exist nor among the things that do not exist; instead, it is even more alien than non-being itself, standing apart from the Good and being even further removed from <term>substance</term> <note>original: "ἀνουσιώτερον" (anousioteron); literally "more substance-less"</note>.

<margin>P</margin> "Where then does evil come from?" someone might ask; "for if evil does not exist, then virtue and vice would be the same, both as a whole and in their corresponding parts." Or [they might argue] that even that which fights against virtue would not be evil. And so, opposites like temperance and debauchery, or justice and injustice [would be the same]. And I do not merely mean this in terms of a just or unjust person, or a temperate and debauched person; but even before that outward conflict between a virtuous person and their opponent, the vices are already separated from the virtues within the soul itself. The passions rebel against reason, and from these things it is necessary to grant that there is something evil which is opposite to the Good. For the Good is not the opposite of itself, but [it is viewed as an opposite] just as...

# Of Dionysius on [Divine Names]
->Page 1<-

...having fallen away from the <term>Identity</term> <note>original: "Ταυτότητος" (Tautotētos); in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the state of being consistent and unified with one's own divine source.</note> of the Good; instead of <unclear>meeting</unclear> with evils, it is harmful to itself and to all others that are said to be corrupted.

<margin>P</margin> <note>Likely shorthand for "Problem" or "Question."</note> But how is it that the race of demons, though produced entirely from the Good, is not <term>good-like</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδές" (agathoeides); having the form or essential character of the Good.</note>? Or how was that which was made good by the Good later changed? And what is it that corrupts it, and what is evil in its entirety? From what principle did it <term>subsist</term> <note>original: "ὑπέστη" (hypestē); to take on a defined existence or substance.</note>? In which of the things that exist does it reside? And how did He who is Good desire to produce it? And having so desired, how was He able to do so? Furthermore, if evil comes from some other cause, what other cause is there for beings besides the Good? If <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "προνοίας" (pronoias); the divine guidance and care of God over the universe.</note> exists, how can evil exist, or come to be, or why is it not entirely abolished? And how can any existing thing desire it instead of the Good? Perhaps a questioning mind will raise these points. But let us urge such a mind to look toward the truth of things, and let us first venture to say this with boldness:

<margin>T</margin> <note>Likely shorthand for "Truth" or "Thesis."</note> Evil does not come from the Good. If it were to come from the Good, it would not be evil. For it is not the nature of fire to provide cold, nor is it the nature of the Good to produce things that are not good. If all beings come from the Good—for it is the nature of the Good to produce and to preserve, just as it is the nature of evil to corrupt and to destroy—then no existing thing comes from evil. Nor can evil itself exist as a <term>being</term>, for if it were, it would be "evil" even to itself <note>Dionysius argues that if evil were a "thing" or "substance," it would have to follow the rules of existence, which are governed by the Good, creating a logical contradiction.</note>.

<margin>K</margin> <note>Likely shorthand for "Conclusion."</note> If this is not the case, then evil is not entirely evil, but possesses some portion of the Good by which it exists at all. And if all beings desire the Beautiful and the Good, and everything they do they do for the sake of what *seems* to be good...

<summary>Dionysius explores the logical paradox of evil, questioning how demons or corruption could arise from a perfectly good source. He concludes that evil is not a substance or "being" created by God, but rather a corruption or lack within things that are fundamentally good.</summary>

# On Divine Names

<margin>τ</margin> <note>This marginal mark, a Greek 'tau', likely serves as a section marker for the reader.</note> ...since those things under His providence find Him desirable; and in another sense, the Beautiful and the Good are the objects of longing. Love itself is pre-established in the Beautiful and the Good, and it exists and comes into being because of the Beautiful and the Good.

<margin>τ</margin> But why is it that theologians generally sometimes call Him <term>Eros</term> <note>original: "ἔρωτα" (erōta); often translated as "passionate love" or "longing," which Dionysius daringly applies to God.</note> and <term>Agape</term> <note>original: "ἀγάπην" (agapēn); often translated as "charity" or "divine love."</note>, while at other times they call Him the <term>Desirable</term> and the <term>Beloved</term>? Of the former, He is the cause and, as it were, the producer and progenitor; but the latter, He is Himself. Through the former He is moved, while through the latter He moves; for He is the producer and mover of Himself toward Himself.

<margin>Δ</margin> <note>Likely indicating a "Definition" or "Division" in the argument.</note> In this way, they call Him "the Beloved" and "the Desirable" as being the Beautiful and the Good. Conversely, they call Him "Eros" and "Agape" as being both the moving and the <term>uplifting power</term> <note>original: "ἀνάγωγον δύναμιν" (anagōgon dynamin); a power that leads the soul upward from material things to the divine.</note> toward Himself—He who is the only self-subsisting Beautiful and Good through Himself. In this, the Divine Love uniquely demonstrates its own end-less and beginning-less nature, like an <term>eternal circle</term> <note>original: "ἀΐδιος κύκλος" (aidios kyklos); a key concept where God’s love flows out to the world and draws the world back to Himself in a perfect loop.</note>, proceeding because of the Good, from the Good, in the Good, and toward the Good, in an unerring revolution, always remaining in the same state. And this is the eternal nature of the <term>formless</term> things, and concerning it, even <term>non-being</term> is spoken of <term>beyond being</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousiōs); a term describing God as existing in a way that transcends the very category of "existence."</note>. Just as the demonic multitude does not lack a desire for the Beautiful and the Good, but being material and [falling away] from the angelic desire for the Good...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Divine Love (Eros) from Chapter 4 of Pseudo-Dionysius’s "The Divine Names." Having previously established that God is both the object of love and Love itself, the author now explores the "ecstatic" nature of this love—how it causes the lover to move toward the beloved—applying this even to God’s own relationship with His creation.</meta>

# Dionysius on <term>Divine Names</term> <note>original: "Διονυσίου περὶ [Θείων Ὀνομάτων]" (Dionysiou peri [Theiōn Onomatōn])</note>

...ward <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding the "uplifting power."</note> and establishing the inferior things by means of their return to the superior.

<margin>E</margin> Moreover, divine <term>Eros</term> <note>original: "ἔρως" (erōs); Dionysius uses this term for passionate or intense love, which he views as a holy force of attraction.</note> is **ecstatic** <note>original: "ἐκστατικὸς" (ekstatikos); literally "standing outside of oneself." It describes a state where one is so moved by love that they no longer dwell within themselves but in the beloved.</note>, not allowing lovers to belong to themselves, but to those they love. This is shown by the superior things acting through their providence for the inferior, by those of equal rank through their cohesion with one another, and by the subordinate things through their more divine return toward the primary things.

<margin>Δ</margin> Therefore, the great Paul, when he was possessed by this divine love and had shared in its ecstatic power, spoke with an inspired mouth: <margin>Δ</margin> <note>These "Δ" markers in the margin likely indicate a "Division" (Diairesis) in the logic or a "Definition."</note> **"I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me."** <note>A reference to Galatians 2:20.</note> As a true lover and one who was "beside himself" (as he himself says) for God, he did not live his own life, but rather the life of the Beloved, which is exceedingly precious. 

We must also dare to say this for the sake of truth: that the Cause of all things Himself, through the beauty and goodness of His love for all, and through the abundance of His loving goodness, **goes outside of Himself** by His providential care for all existing things. It is as if He is charmed by goodness, by affection, and by love; He is led down from His place above all and beyond all, to dwell in all things according to an **ecstatic, supernatural power** that yet does not depart from His own nature. 

Because of this, those who are experts in divine things call Him **"Zealous,"** <note>original: "ζηλωτὴν" (zēlōtēn); usually translated as "jealous" in biblical contexts like Exodus 34:14, but here Dionysius explains it as an intense, active longing for the good of creation.</note> because His good love for all beings is great, and because He awakens a "zeal" of longing within them. Thus, He shows Himself to be "Zealous" in that He is the object of the zeal of those things that long for Him.

<summary>Pseudo-Dionysius explains that Divine Love is "ecstatic," causing the lover to move toward the beloved; he even applies this to God, who "goes out of Himself" to care for creation through His providence.</summary>

## On the Divine Names

...the **true Love** <note>original: "ὄντως ἔρωτα" (ontōs erōta). This completes the sentence from the previous page: "and for this reason, the theologians call it the true Eros."</note>. Because of the strange prejudice of such men <note>Referencing those who view the word "Eros" only in a sexual or worldly sense.</note>, the "real Love" is celebrated in a god-befitting way, not only by us, but also by the <margin>Ξ</margin> scriptures themselves. However, the masses—not grasping the **unified nature** <note>original: "τὸ ἑνοειδὲς" (to henoeides). Dionysius argues that divine love is a single, simple force, unlike human love which is fragmented into different categories.</note> of this erotic divine name—slipped away toward a divided, bodily, and partitioned understanding. They believe it is not "true love," but rather an idol of it, or even a falling away from that true Love. For the unified nature of the divine and single Love <margin>Δ</margin> <note>This "Δ" likely marks a new "Definition" or "Distinction" in the text.</note> is incomprehensible to the common crowd.

<margin>Δ</margin> Therefore, because it seems to be a more "difficult" name to the many, it is applied to Divine Wisdom to lead them upward and raise them toward the knowledge of the **true Love**; this helps release them from any difficulty they might feel toward the term. Among us, on the other hand, the lowly-minded might often imagine something "unseemly" or "offensive" where the scriptures say: <margin>2 Samuel 1:26</margin>> **"Your love <note>original: "ἀγάπησίς" (agapēsis). Dionysius is pointing out that even the "safer" word for love can be used in intense, human contexts in scripture.</note> fell upon me, as the love of women."**

But to those who listen rightly to divine things, the holy theologians rank the name of **"Affection"** <note>original: "ἀγάπη" (agapē)</note> and **"Love"** <note>original: "ἔρως" (erōs)</note> as having the same power in the divine revelations. # [Of] Dionysius on [Divine Names]

This movement, as if in a circle, grants the soul freedom from error <margin>b</margin> as it turns and gathers itself from the many external things; first into itself, then—having become unified—uniting with the singularly unified powers, and so leading the way toward the **Beautiful and Good**, which is beyond all beings, and is One, and the same, and without beginning or end. 

And the soul moves **spirally** insofar as it is moved in its own way...

# Divine Names
<note>original: "Θείων ὀνομάτων" (Theiōn onomatōn). This is the title of the fourth chapter of Pseudo-Dionysius’s influential work, which explores how God can be named through the qualities observed in creation.</note>

...of the nature of all beautiful things. Every beauty and everything beautiful pre-exists in a unified way within its cause. It is from <term>the</term> <note>original: "τῶν" (tōn); the Greek article here emphasizes that Beauty is not just a concept, but a specific, singular Source.</note> Beautiful itself that all beings receive their existence, each becoming beautiful according to its own specific essence <note>original: "λόγον" (logon); here meaning the rational principle or "blueprint" of a thing's nature.</note>. The Beautiful is the beginning of all things, acting as the creative cause that moves the universe and holds it together through the love of its own beauty. It is also the end of all things and the object of all desire, acting as the ultimate purpose <note>original: "τελικωτικὸν αἴτιον" (telikōtikon aition); the "final cause" or the "why" for which everything is made.</note>.

<margin>T</margin>

It is the model <note>original: "παραδειγματικὸν" (paradeigmatikon); a Platonic term suggesting that God is the original pattern from which all things are copied.</note> because all things are defined according to it. For this reason, the Beautiful is the same as <term>the Good</term> <note>original: "τἀγαθῷ" (tagathō); a contraction of 'to agathō'. The author argues that Beauty and Goodness are two names for the same divine reality.</note>. All things, regardless of their nature, seek the Beautiful and the Good. Indeed, there is nothing in existence that does not participate in Beauty and Goodness.

<margin>T</margin>
The argument will even dare to say this: that even "non-being" <note>original: "τὸ μὴ ὂν" (to mē on); this refers to things that do not yet exist, or matter that lacks form. Even in their state of potential, they are held within the divine mind.</note> participates in the Beautiful and the Good. For "non-being" is itself beautiful and good when it is praised in God beyond all being, through the stripping away of all characteristics.

<margin>T</margin>
This one Good and Beautiful is the singular cause of all the many beautiful and good things in the world.

<margin>E</margin>
From this Source come all the essential existences of beings: their unions and their distinctions; their identities and their differences; the cooperation of opposites and the purity of things joined together. From here comes the care <note>original: "προνόιαι" (pronoiai); Divine Providence.</note> that higher beings have for the lower, the mutual connections between equals, and the turning back <note>original: "ἐπιστροφαὶ" (epistrophai); the Neoplatonic concept of "reversion," where a created thing naturally seeks to return to its creator.</note> of the lower toward the higher. From this Source, all things find their protective, unmoving stability and their firm foundation, and likewise, the way that all things share in one another in their own proper ways...

# On the Divine Names

He <note>Referring to Hierotheus, the author’s mentor.</note> deigned to treat beforehand all theological matters and, in partial unrollings <note>original: "ἀνελίξεσι" (anelixesi) — a metaphor referring to the unrolling of a papyrus scroll to reveal its contents; hence, an exposition or explanation.</note>, he went through the summary of all theology. ...a heavenly height <note>The author is using the metaphor of a golden chain or rope suspended from the heavens, a common image in Neoplatonic philosophy to describe the connection between the Divine and the material world.</note> hanging down even to this world. <margin>H</margin>

It is just the same in the opposite case: if someone standing on a coastal rock pushes a ship away, he does nothing to the fixed and immovable rock, but he separates himself from it; and the more he pushes it away, the further he is cast off from it. Therefore, before everything—and especially before a theological discussion—it is necessary to begin with prayer. This is not because we are drawing toward ourselves that Power which is present everywhere and nowhere, but so that by divine remembrances and invocations, we may hand ourselves over to it and be united with it.

# On Divine Names

->On Divine Names<-

...by which it <note>The "it" refers to the soul in its spiral movement, which Dionysius describes as a middle ground between pure intuition and external observation.</note> is illuminated by divine knowledge; not in a purely intellectual and stable manner, but through logic and step-by-step investigation, as if by mingled and transitional activities.

**I**t moves in a **straight** line, however, when it does not enter into itself to be moved by a unified intellect—for as I said, that is the "circular" movement—but instead reaches out to the things around it. From these external things—acting as various and multiplied symbols—it is led upward to simple and unified contemplations <term>theoria: a Greek term for "beholding" or "contemplation," referring to a direct spiritual vision of truth</term>.

**O**f these three movements, then, and of the sensible things in this universe, and of the many states of rest, stability, and foundation that come before them, the Beautiful and Good <note>original: "to kalon kai agathon." In Neoplatonic Christian thought, Beauty and Goodness are names for God that attract all things back to their source.</note> is the sustainer and the goal. It is that which exists beyond all rest and motion.

# On Divine Names.
<note>original: "Θείων ὀνομάτων" (Peri theion onomaton)</note>

I have not forgotten; indeed, I often recall having heard from you parts of those divinely inspired <term>en-theastic: literally "having God within," referring to the divinely possessed or inspired hymns of the author's mentor</term> songs, for such is your zeal to pursue divine matters with more than just a passing interest.

<margin>A</margin>
But let us set aside those mystical matters—which are inexpressible to the many and already known to you—since it was necessary to share them with the common people and to lead as many as possible to this sacred knowledge <term>hierognosia: holy or priestly knowledge</term> of ours. [He] so far surpassed the many sacred teachers in length of experience, in purity of mind, in the accuracy of his demonstrations, and in his other sacred discourses, that we would never have dared to look directly into such a great sun. For we are conscious of ourselves and we know that we are neither capable of sufficiently grasping the intellectual aspects of divine things, nor of speaking or describing the ineffable qualities of the knowledge of God <term>theognosia: the direct knowledge of God</term>. Being far off, we fall short of the knowledge of those divine men regarding theological truth. Because of this, we certainly would have arrived at such a state of reverence as to not hear or say anything at all about divine philosophy <note>The author uses "philosophy" here in the sense of a spiritual or theological discipline</note> which we have not first grasped in our minds, were it not for the fact that one must not neglect the possible knowledge of divine things. ## On the Divine Names. I <note>The letter "A" (Alpha) likely refers to the first section of this specific manuscript's division or a chapter marker, though the text belongs to Chapter 2 of the traditional treatise.</note>

<margin>P</margin> <note>The Greek letter 'pi' likely serves as a decorative initial or section marker.</note> **Every** procession <term>Procession (proödos): The "outgoing" or movement of God toward the world, by which He creates and sustains all things while remaining unmoved in His own nature.</term> of the Godhead <term>Godhead (thearchia): Literally "the source of God" or "divine sovereignty," referring to the ultimate nature of the Trinity.</term> is bestowed upon all beings and overflows with the participations <term>Participation (metousia): The way created things share in God's goodness or existence according to their own capacity.</term> of all good things. <margin>O</margin> <note>The Greek letter 'omicron' marks a new paragraph.</note> **For** example, since God is "He who is" in a super-substantial <term>Super-substantial (hyperousiōs): Existing "beyond being" or "above substance." Yet He remains nonetheless One even in that multiplication; He remains united during the procession and full in the midst of distinction. He is super-substantially exalted above all beings by the unitary production of the whole and by the undiminished pouring out of His inexhaustible gifts.

**Furthermore**, though He is One, and imparts the One to every form, and to the whole, and to the individual, and to the many, He is likewise One in a super-substantial way. He is not a "part" of the many, nor is He a "whole" composed of parts. In this sense, He is not "one" as we understand it, nor does He merely participate in oneness, nor does He simply possess oneness; rather, He is far beyond these things. He is the "One" above the oneness found in beings. He is an indivisible plurality, un-fillable and over-full. He is the "All-One" who produces, perfects, and sustains the many. Again, by the deification <term>Deification (theōsis): The process by which a creature is united with God and becomes "god-like" through grace, without losing its own nature.</term> proceeding from Him—according to the capacity of each god-like one—many "gods" are brought into being.

<margin>D</margin> <note>The Greek letter 'delta' marks the concluding thought of this section.</note> **There** seems to be, and there is said to be, a distinction and a multiplication of the One God; but He is nonetheless the Source-God <note>original: architheos</note> and the Beyond-God <note>original: hypertheos</note> in a super-substantial way: one indivisible God.

To use examples from our own human experience: pleasures and pains are said to be "productive" of the feelings of enjoying or grieving, yet these abstract concepts of pleasure and pain do not themselves feel joy or sorrow. Similarly, fire, though it heats and burns, is not said to be "burned" or "heated" itself. If someone were to say that "Life-Itself" lives, or that "Light-Itself" is enlightened, they would not be speaking correctly according to my view—unless, perhaps, they said it in a different way: that the qualities of the effects exist in their causes in a super-abundant and <term>essential (ousiodōs): Pertaining to the very "essence" or "being" of a thing.</term> manner.

# On the Divine Names

...[contin]uing to approach them as mysteries according to the divine tradition <gloss>1</gloss>, reaching out with an effort that exceeds our own intellectual capacity. For all divine things, even those that have been revealed to us, are known only through their "participations" <gloss>12</gloss> <note>Participations: The ways in which created beings share in God's attributes, like goodness or life, without ever possessing His full essence.</note>. But as for what these things are in their own source and foundation, they are beyond mind, beyond all essence, and beyond knowledge.

For example, if we should name that super-essential <term>hiddenness (kryphiotēta): The state of being "hidden" or beyond human comprehension.</term> as "God," or "Life," or "Essence," or "Light," or "Word," we understand nothing other than the powers brought forth from it toward us—powers that are deifying, essence-making, life-giving, or wisdom-granting. But we ourselves, at the point where our intellectual activities cease, reach for a "release" <note>original: "apolysis," meaning a detachment from finite thoughts to reach the infinite.</note>, seeing no deification <gloss>13</gloss>, nor life, nor essence, that is exactly similar to the Cause which is exalted above all things in its total transcendence.

<margin>P</margin> Again, we have received from the Holy Scriptures that the Father is the "source-deity," while Jesus and the Spirit are—if one may put it this way—"divinely-planted shoots" of the God-bearing Deity, and like "flowers" and "super-essential lights." But how these things can be, it is neither <gloss>11</gloss> possible to <margin>L</margin> speak nor to conceive.

<margin>A</margin> But the progress of our intellectual activity goes only so far: we know that every divine "fatherhood" and "sonship" is granted to us and to the super-celestial powers from the Source-Fatherhood and Source-Foundation <note>original: "hyparchias," the primal origin of existence.</note> which is exalted above all. It is from this source that the "god-like" ones both become and are named "gods," "sons of gods," and "fathers of gods."

## On Divine Names.

...utterable union and existence, both unions and distinctions.

<margin>E</margin> But if there is also a **divine distinction**, it is the goodness-befitting **procession** <term>procession (proodos): The way the singular, unknowable God "goes forth" or emanates into the world to create and sustain life.</term> of the divine union, which, in a manner transcending unity, multiplies and expands itself through its own goodness.

<margin>H</margin> United indeed, according to the divine distinction, are the **archetypal** <term>archetypal (archetypos): The original, perfect patterns in the mind of God.</term> distributions: the essential givings, the animations, the bestowals of wisdom, and the other gifts of the Goodness which is the cause of all. 

<margin>3</margin> According to these gifts, the "unparticipated" things <note>original: "amethektos metechomena," referring to God's attributes which are shared with us but which He never actually loses or diminishes.</note> are praised through those who participate in them. 

<margin>Δ</margin> And this is common, united, and one for the whole Godhead: that the whole of it is shared by each of those who participate, and by no one is it divided into any part. It is just like the point of a **center** in the middle of a circle, which is shared by all the straight lines lying within the circle <note>This is a classic Neoplatonic image: all radii of a circle meet at a single, indivisible point at the center.</note>. It is also like the many impressions of a **seal** that participate in the archetypal seal; in each of the impressions, the seal is present as a whole and the same, and in no part is it divided.

<margin>Ο</margin> Yet, beyond even these examples lies the **non-participation** of the all-causing Godhead, in that there is neither physical contact with it, nor any other blended communion with the things that participate in it. 

And yet, someone might say: "The seal is not whole and the same in all the impressions." But the seal is not the cause of this; for it gives itself as a whole and the same to each. Rather, the **difference** of those participating <gloss>participating: here, the material receiving the seal, like wax or clay</gloss> makes the imprints dissimilar, even though the seal is one...

<summary>Dionysius explains that while God is a single unity, He "multiplies" Himself through His gifts (life, wisdom, goodness) to creation. He uses the analogy of a circle's center and a seal's imprint to show how God can be fully present in many things without being divided.</summary>

# On Divine Names

We strive to preserve within ourselves the most beautiful rule of truth—those things laid down there—undiminished, unreduced, and unswerving, being guarded in our guardianship of the **Divine Oracles** <term>Divine Oracles (logia): A term used by Dionysius for the Holy Scriptures, viewed as direct communications from God.</term>, and being empowered by them so that, by guarding them, we ourselves are guarded.

<margin>T</margin> The "united" things, then, belong to the whole of the Godhead, as we have demonstrated through many examples from the Oracles in our **Theological Outlines** <note>original: "theologikais hypotypōsesi"—a foundational work by Dionysius that is now lost.</note>. These include: the **Super-good**, the **Super-divine**, the **Supersubstantial** <term>Supersubstantial (hyperousion): Existing beyond the realm of "being" or "substance" as understood by humans.</term>, the **Existing**, the **Super-wise**, and all those names which result from "transcendent negation." Along with these are 
<margin>Ξ</margin> all the "causal" names: the **Good**, the **Beautiful**, the <margin>Ξ</margin> **Being**, the **Life-giving**, the **Wise**, and whatever else the **Cause of all good things** is named after because of Her <note>The Greek "aitia" (Cause) is a feminine noun, often personified in this tradition.</note> goodly gifts. 

But the "distinguished" things are the supersubstantial name and reality of the **Father**, and of the **Son**, and of the **Holy Spirit**; in these, no reversal or general commonality is introduced. <margin>χ</margin> It is necessary, I believe, for us to resume and set out the complete mode of the divine **union** and **distinction**, so that our whole discourse may be easily understood by us, rejecting everything complex and unclear, and defining the specific points clearly, plainly, and in good order, according to our ability. # On Divine Names

## CHAPTER II

<margin>P</margin>
### Concerning unified and differentiated theology; and what is the divine union and differentiation.

<margin>T</margin> The whole **thearchic** <term>thearchic (thearchike): Relating to the "God-rule" or the "Godhead," the supreme principle of the Trinity.</term> existence, whatever it may be, is defined and revealed by the Oracles <note>The "Oracles" refers to the Holy Scriptures, which Dionysius treats as the primary source of divine knowledge.</note> to be praised as **Self-Goodness**. And what else is there to learn from sacred theology? For it says that the **Thearchy** <term>Thearchy (thearchia): The divine source or "God-rule" itself.</term> itself, leading the way, said: "Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except God alone." <note>original: "oudeis agathos ei mē monos ho theos" — Dionysius is quoting the words of Jesus from Matthew 19:17 or Mark 10:18.</note> This point has already been demonstrated by us through an examination of other passages: that all the God-befitting divine names are praised by the Oracles not just partially, but as belonging to the whole, complete, entire, and full Godhead. All of them are to be attributed impartially, absolutely, unreservedly, and wholly to the entire wholeness of the complete and total Godhead.

<margin>A</margin> And indeed, as we reminded you in the *Theological Outlines* <note>A lost or perhaps fictional work by Dionysius that he frequently references to provide foundational systematic theology.</note>, if one does not say this is spoken concerning the whole Godhead, and dares to unlawfully tear apart the **supra-unified unity** <term>supra-unified unity (hyperēnōmenēn henada): A unity that exists beyond any human concept of oneness or mathematical number.</term>, then we must ask: since the Word <note>The Logos, or Jesus Christ.</note> who is good by nature said, "I am good," and since one of the God-inspired prophets praises "the good Spirit," and again the Scripture says, "I am He who is" <note>original: "egō eimi ho ōn" — the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14, identifying God as Being itself.</note>—unless they say these things are spoken of the whole Godhead, how will they [explain them]? If they say they belong only to one part...

<meta>This page continues Dionysius’s exploration of how the "Nameless" God is given many names in Scripture. # On Divine Names

...fire, water, a wind of dew, a cloud, the essential stone, and a rock—[He is] all things that exist and yet nothing of the things that exist.

<margin>Thus</margin> therefore, both the "nameless" and all the names of existing things will apply to the Cause of all, which exists beyond all. This is so that there might accurately be a kingdom of the whole, and so that all things might be centered around Her <note>original: "autēn" — Dionysius uses feminine pronouns here because "Cause" (*aitia*) and "Goodness" (*agathotēs*) are feminine nouns in Greek. While referring to God, the text follows the gender of these philosophical terms.</note> and depend upon Her as the Cause, as the Beginning, and as the End. And She, according to the **Scripture** <note>original: "logion" — refers to the Bible, specifically 1 Corinthians 15:28, which states that God will be "all in all."</note>, shall be "all things in all things." Truly, She is praised as the Support of all, the Principle, the Perfecter, the sustaining Guard, the Hearth, and the one who turns all things back toward Herself. And these things are done in a unified, transcendent, and independent way. For She is not merely the cause of cohesion, or life, or perfection in a limited sense, such that the **Beyond-Name** <term>Beyond-Name (hyperōnymos): A key concept in Dionysius's thought; God is so great that no single name can truly define Him; He is "above" every name we use.</term> Goodness should be named only from this or that specific act of **providence** <term>providence (pronoia): The protective care and divine direction God exercises over the created world.</term>.

<margin>But</margin> rather, She has pre-contained all things simply and without limit within Herself, by the all-perfect goodness of Her single and all-causing providence. And from all things that exist, She is harmoniously praised and named.

<margin>And</margin> the theologians do not honor only these **divine names** <term>divine names (theōnymiai): The specific titles, such as "Good" or "Life," attributed to God in the Bible.</term> which are derived from universal or partial acts of providence, or from the things being cared for. They also derive names from certain divine visions that occasionally seize the **initiates** <term>initiates (mystai): Those who have been spiritually prepared to receive the deeper, "hidden" meanings of sacred truths.</term> or the prophets in the holy sanctuaries or elsewhere. According to various causes and powers, they name that radiant and Beyond-Name Goodness, attributing to Her forms and human likenesses, or fiery forms, or **electrum-like** <note>original: "ēlektreia" — refers to the "shining metal" (an alloy of gold and silver) described in the visions of the prophet Ezekiel (e.g., Ezekiel 1:4).</note>...

<summary>Dionysius explains that because God is the Cause of all things, He can be called by any name found in creation, yet He remains fundamentally "Nameless" and beyond all definitions. He also notes that names are derived both from God's acts of Providence and from the symbolic visions experienced by prophets.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Names, Providence, Symbolism, Namelessness, Pseudo-Dionysius, Theology, Visions</keywords>

# Dionysius on Divine [Names]

<margin>A</margin> [He is] **nameless**, as when the **Scripture** says that the Divine Sovereignty itself—in one of the mystical visions of symbolic divine manifestation <term>divine manifestation (theophania): A visible appearance of God to humanity, such as the burning bush or visions seen by prophets.</term>—reproved the one who asked, "What is your name?" <note>original: "ti to onoma sou" — referring to Judges 13:17-18, where Manoah asks the Angel of the Lord for His name.</note> and, as if leading him away from all knowledge of divine names, said, "Why do you ask my name? For it is **wonderful**." <note>original: "thaumaston" — this word implies something so miraculous it is beyond human comprehension.</note> Or is this not truly the "wonderful name," the one which is **above every name**, the nameless, the one established above every name that is named, whether in this age or in the age to come?

<margin>B</margin> And He is **many-named**, as when they again introduce Him saying: "I am He Who Is," <note>original: "ego eimi ho on" — the name God gives Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14.</note> "the Life," "the Light," "God," "the Truth"; and when the God-wise <note>original: "theosophoi" — Dionysius’s respectful term for the biblical writers and inspired theologians.</note> themselves hymn the Cause of all things with many names drawn from all His effects. They call Him: **Good**, **Beautiful**, **Wise**, **Beloved**, **God of gods**, **Lord of lords**, **Holy of holies**, **Eternal**, **He Who Is**, and the **Cause of Ages**. They call Him the **Giver of Life**, **Wisdom**, **Mind**, **Reason**, **Knower**, and the one who surpasses all the treasures of all knowledge. They call Him **Power**, **Potentate**, **King of kings**, **Ancient of Days** <note>original: "palaios hēmerōn" — a title for God from the Book of Daniel, symbolizing His eternal nature.</note>, **Ageless and Unchanging**, **Salvation**, **Righteousness**, **Sanctification**, **Redemption**, the one who surpasses all things in **Greatness**, and yet is present in a **gentle breeze**. They even say He is in minds, and in souls, and in bodies; in heaven and on earth, and at the same time, He is within Himself. He is the same one within the world, around the world, and above the world; **super-heavenly**, **super-essential** <term>super-essential (hyperousios): A key term for Dionysius meaning "beyond the nature of being." It suggests God does not just "exist" like a person or an object, but is the source of existence itself.</term>, a **sun**, and a **star**.

<summary>Dionysius explains that God is "nameless" because He is beyond human understanding, yet "many-named" because all qualities in the universe originate from Him. He provides a long list of biblical titles for God, ranging from "The Truth" to "Ancient of Days."</summary>

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>A</margin> ...[they name] it most properly through the **stripping away** <term>stripping away (aphairesis): The theological method of "negative theology," where one describes God by saying what He is not, removing limited human concepts to reach a higher truth.</term> of all existing things. They do this because they have been truly and supernaturally enlightened by that most blessed **union** with it. They learn that while it is the Cause of all things that exist, it is itself **nothing** <note>original: "auto de ouden" — meaning God is not any "thing" that can be defined or limited like objects in the created world.</note>, insofar as it exists **beyond being** <term>beyond being (hyperousios): A central term for Dionysius meaning that God's "existence" is so far above our own that it cannot even be called "being" in the human sense.</term> and is set apart from all things.

<margin>T</margin> Therefore, regarding this divine-ruling "beyond-beingness"—whatever that may be, or the super-existence of the Super-Goodness—it is not lawful to praise it as Reason, or Power, or Mind, or Life, or Essence. This is forbidden to any who are lovers of that **Truth** which is above all truth. Instead, we must praise it as being pre-eminently **removed** from every state or movement; from life, imagination, opinion, name, reason, thought, or intellection; from essence, rest, foundation, union, limit, and infinity; and from **all things that exist**. 

<margin>e</margin> But because this Divine Sovereignty is the very existence of **Goodness**, and by its very being is the **Cause** of all things that exist, we must also praise the "good-ruling" providence of this Divine Sovereignty by looking at all the things it has caused. For all things revolve around it and exist for its sake; it exists before all things, and in it all things **hold together**. Because it exists, the production and reality of the whole universe occurs. All things **long for it**: those with minds and reason seek it through **knowledge**; those below them seek it through **sensation**; and others seek it through **vital movement** or the natural fitness of their being and state.

<margin>T</margin> Knowing this, the theologians praise the Divine both as **nameless** and by **every name**.

<summary>Dionysius explains "negative theology," arguing that the Divine is best understood by "stripping away" all human concepts, yet must also be praised through the names of all created things because it is their Source.</summary>
